body: The word "Arab" first meant desert: open, waterless land without plants. Since ancient times it has named both the peninsula and the people who live in it.

The peninsula is bounded by the Red Sea and Sinai to the west, the Arabian Gulf to the east, the Arabian Sea to the south, and Syria and part of Iraq to the north. Its area is reckoned at between one and one-and-a-third million square miles.

Its deserts kept invaders out, so its people stayed free for ages beside two great empires. Yet it sat at the meeting point of the old world, joined by land and sea to most nations of the time. It became a crossroads of trade, culture and religion.
sections.title: The Land of the Arabs

body: Arab genealogists divide the Arabs by descent into three groups.

The Perished Arabs are the ancient peoples whose history is mostly lost, such as 'Ad and Thamud. The Pure Arabs, or Qahtanis, descend from Ya'rub bin Yashjub bin Qahtan and first lived in Yemen. The Arabized Arabs, or 'Adnanis, descend from Isma'il (Ishmael), son of Ibrahim (Abraham).

Of the Qahtani tribes of Yemen, Kahlan moved north as trade failed under Roman control of the land and sea routes. Al-Azd scattered widely. Their sons Aws and Khazraj settled in Yathrib, the later Madinah. Khuza'ah took Makkah from the tribe of Jurhum. Others founded the Ghassanid kingdom in Syria. Lakhm founded the kingdom of Heerah in Iraq, while Tai' settled in the mountains of the north.
sections.title: Three Peoples
list: 'Ad, Thamud, Tasm, Jadis and others, little known
Qahtan's sons, first of Yemen: Himyar and Kahlan

body: Ibrahim (Abraham) came from Ur, near Kufah in Iraq, then went to Harran and Palestine. On a journey to Egypt, Pharaoh plotted against his wife Sarah, but Allah protected her. Pharaoh then gave her Hajar (Hagar) as a servant. Sarah gave Hajar to Ibrahim in marriage, and Hajar bore him Isma'il.

By Allah's command Ibrahim took Hajar and the infant to a barren valley beside the Sacred House, where there were no people and no water. He left them with a bag of dates and a skin of water. When these ran out, water burst from the ground: the spring of Zamzam. The tribe of Jurhum came to live beside them.

Ibrahim visited them from Palestine several times. In a dream he was shown himself sacrificing his son. Both submitted to Allah, and Allah ransomed Isma'il with a great sacrifice [37:103-107]. On a later visit, father and son raised the walls of the Ka'bah, and Ibrahim called people to make pilgrimage to it.
sections.title: Ibrahim, Hajar and Isma'il

body: Isma'il married into Jurhum and had twelve sons. Over time only the lines of two of them, Nabet and Qidar, could still be traced. The Nabataeans, sons of Nabet, built a kingdom in the north of Hijaz with Petra as its capital, until Rome overthrew it.

From Qidar came 'Adnan, the twenty-first grandfather of the Prophet ﷺ. When the Prophet ﷺ traced his own lineage, it is reported that he stopped at 'Adnan. 'Adnan's line branched into many tribes. From Mudar came Kinanah, and from Kinanah came Quraish, the sons of Fihr bin Malik. Quraish divided into clans, among them Makhzum, Jumah, Sahm, 'Adi, Taim, Zuhrah and the sons of Qusai. From Qusai's son 'Abd Manaf came Hashim, and from Hashim, the Prophet ﷺ.
sections.title: From Isma'il to Quraish

quote.text: Allah chose Kinanah from the sons of Isma'il, Quraish from Kinanah, Hashim from Quraish, and He chose me from Hashim.
quote.who: The Prophet ﷺ, reported by Muslim

body: Sheba was among the oldest of the peoples of Yemen. Its kings built the great dam of Ma'rib, ruled from Sarwah and then from Ma'rib, and set up colonies across the region. Himyar later took the kingdom. Trade declined as the Nabataeans and then Rome took the trade routes, and the tribes fought among themselves.

The dam broke in the Great Flood around 450 CE, which the Qur'an mentions. Yemen's people scattered. In 523 CE the Jewish king Dhu Nawas threw the Christians of Najran into a pit of fire when they would not leave their faith. The Qur'an speaks of the "people of the ditch" [85:4]. Abyssinia (Ethiopia), with Roman support, conquered Yemen in 525 CE. One of its commanders, Abrahah, became its ruler. It was he who later marched on the Ka'bah.
Around 575 CE the Yemenis rose with Persian help under Ma'dikarib bin Saif Dhu Yazin. After he was killed, Persia ruled Yemen through its governors, until the last of them, Badhan, embraced Islam.
sections.title: The Kings of Yemen

body: On the Persian side, the Sassanid kings ruled the Arabs of Iraq through Arab kings of their own choosing at Heerah, the Lakhmids. They were a shield against raids from the desert and against the Byzantines' Arabs. When the Persian king later imprisoned the last of them, An-Nu'man, until he died, the tribe of Shaiban refused to hand over what he had left in its keeping. At Dhi Qar the Arabs routed a Persian army for the first time. This is said to have been shortly after the Prophet's ﷺ birth.

On the Roman side, Arabs of Quda'ah first guarded the Byzantine frontier. The Ghassanids then took their place and ruled the Arabs of Syria for the empire. They lasted until the battle of Yarmuk in 13 AH. Their last king, Jabalah bin Al-Aihum, embraced Islam in the time of 'Umar.
The kings around Arabia were never truly free: they ruled their people for empires beyond them. Deep in the desert, the tribes governed themselves.
sections.title: Heerah and the Ghassanids

body: After Isma'il, his sons kept the House for a time, then rule passed to their mother's people, Jurhum. When Jurhum grew harsh to visitors and took the Ka'bah's wealth, the 'Adnanis and Khuza'ah drove them out. Before leaving, Jurhum filled in the well of Zamzam and buried things in it.

Khuza'ah then ruled Makkah for about three centuries. Then Qusai bin Kilab of Quraish married the daughter of Khuza'ah's chief, Hulail. After Hulail's death, Qusai took Makkah and the House, with Quraish and Kinanah behind him. The wars ended in arbitration, which gave him both. From about 440 CE, Quraish held Makkah and the Ka'bah without rival.
Qusai brought his kin into Makkah and built Dar an-Nadwah, the House of Assembly, beside the Ka'bah. It was where Quraish met, took counsel and made marriages.
sections.title: Who Ruled Makkah

body: Qusai held every honour of Makkah, and his word was obeyed in all of them. He passed them to his son 'Abd Manaf rather than his eldest, 'Abdud-Dar. After 'Abd Manaf, the two branches nearly came to war, and a settlement divided the honours between them.

Feeding and watering the pilgrims went to the sons of 'Abd Manaf: first Hashim, then his brother Al-Muttalib, then Hashim's son 'Abdul-Muttalib, the Prophet's ﷺ grandfather. When Islam came, it was in the hands of Al-'Abbas. The assembly, the standard and the keys of the Ka'bah stayed with the sons of 'Abdud-Dar. Other offices went to other clans, such as the arbitration of blood money, the cavalry, and embassies to other tribes.
sections.title: The Honours of Qusai
list: presiding over the assembly, where counsel was taken and marriages announced
no war was declared without him or his sons
no caravan left Makkah except under his command
he alone could open the Ka'bah and keep it
basins of water, sweetened with dates or raisins, for the pilgrims
food for pilgrims who had none, from a tax Quraish paid each season

body: Most Arabs had followed the religion of Ibrahim: they worshipped Allah alone. Over long ages they forgot parts of it, though its core remained. Then 'Amr bin Luhai, a chief of Khuza'ah much loved for his piety and generosity, saw people worshipping idols in Syria. He brought back an idol, Hubal, set it up inside the Ka'bah and called people to worship it.

Idolatry spread through Makkah and then all of Hijaz. Manat stood at Al-Mushallal near Qudaid by the Red Sea, Al-Lat at Ta'if, and Al-'Uzza in the valley of Nakhlah. It is reported that 'Amr also dug up the idols of Noah's people, Wadd, Suwa', Yaghuth, Ya'uq and Nasr, and gave them to the tribes. When Makkah was conquered, 360 idols stood around the Ka'bah. The Prophet ﷺ broke them all.
sections.title: How the Idols Came

body: They gave themselves to their idols. They swore by them, called on them in hardship, and circled and bowed before them. They sacrificed to them [5:3] and set aside shares of their crops and herds for them [6:136]. Some camels and sheep were dedicated to the idols and left free and unused. The Qur'an denies that Allah ever made such a law [5:103]. They said they worshipped idols only to be brought nearer to Allah [39:3].
They decided their affairs by drawing arrows marked yes and no. They trusted soothsayers, diviners and astrologers. They believed it rained because of a star and read omens in the flight of birds.

Some of Ibrahim's ways remained: honouring the Ka'bah, pilgrimage, the stand at 'Arafat and sacrifice. But they were bent out of shape. Quraish, calling themselves Al-Hums, would not go out to 'Arafat with everyone else [2:199]. Pilgrims from outside had to circle the House in clothes from Al-Hums, or else naked [7:31]. In the sacred state, people entered their houses through holes in the back wall [2:189].
sections.title: The Ways of Idol Worship

body: Jews came into Arabia in two waves. The first came after Nebuchadnezzar destroyed their temple in 587 BCE, and the second after Rome took Palestine in 70 CE. They settled in Yathrib, Khaibar and Taima', built forts, and drew some Arab tribes to their faith. When Islam came, Banu Qainuqa', An-Nadir and Quraizah were among them.

A king of Yemen took Judaism back home from Yathrib. His son, Dhu Nawas, was the one who burned the Christians of Najran in October 523 CE. Christianity came into Arabia with the Abyssinians and the Romans. A preacher named Fimion won Najran to it. Ghassan, Taghlib and Tai' became Christian tribes. Near Persia some Arabs followed the Magian faith, and a few still kept the old Sabian religion.

All of these had little hold on the lives of the Arabs. The idol worshippers claimed Ibrahim's religion but were far from it. Among the Jews and Christians of the time, their religion had become much changed from what it once was.
sections.title: Jews, Christians and Others

body: Among the noble families, women were honoured, had a say in their affairs, and blood would be shed to defend them. Yet the family was ruled by its men, and a woman's guardian decided her marriage. Of the kinds of union people made, Islam kept only marriage as we know it. There was no limit on the number of wives, and divorce was in the husband's hands [2:229].
Some held their children dear, while others buried their baby daughters alive in fear of poverty or shame [16:58-59] [81:8]. The Qur'an forbade killing children for fear of want [17:31].

Loyalty to the tribe ruled everything. "Support your brother, wrongdoer or wronged" was taken at its word. Pride and rivalry kept cousin tribes at war for years: Aws and Khazraj, 'Abs and Dhubyan, Bakr and Taghlib. Only the four sacred months brought a pause, when people could trade and live in peace.
sections.title: Society in the Days of Ignorance

body: Trade was the main way to make a living, but caravans needed safe roads and peace between the tribes, and these were rare outside the sacred months. In those months the great markets met: 'Ukaz, Dhul-Majaz and Majannah.

Arabia had almost no industry. Weaving and tanning came from Yemen, Heerah and the edges of Syria. There was a little farming and herding, and the women spun wool, though war threatened even that. For most people, poverty, hunger and want of food and clothing were the shape of life.
sections.title: Trade and Want

body: For all their vices, the Arabs held virtues the world admired. These were the qualities, together with the land's place in the world, that fitted them to carry the Message. Islam would keep them and refine them.

A man with nothing but the camel his family lived on would slaughter it for a guest. Nearly half their poetry is about hospitality. To make a promise was to owe a debt: they would lose children and home before breaking their word.
sections.title: What Was Noble in Them
list: competing to feed the guest, and paying blood money to stop a feud
a promise was a debt, kept at any cost
no humiliation was borne, no injustice accepted
no chance of honour was let pass, even at the cost of life
valued all the more by a people quick to anger
desert life kept them truthful and far from intrigue

parts.title: Arabia Before Islam
parts.blurb: The land, its peoples, their rulers, their faiths and their ways, as they were when the Message came.

body: Scholars speak of his lineage in three parts. The line back to 'Adnan is agreed on by all the historians and genealogists. The line from 'Adnan back to Ibrahim has names that differ between sources. The line from Ibrahim back to Adam is less sure, and parts of it are certainly mistaken.

The agreed line runs: Muhammad, son of 'Abdullah, son of 'Abdul-Muttalib (whose name was Shaibah), son of Hashim (named 'Amr), son of 'Abd Manaf (named Al-Mughirah), son of Qusai (named Zaid). Then Kilab, Murrah, Ka'b, Lu'ai and Ghalib. Then Fihr, called Quraish, after whom the tribe is named. Then Malik, An-Nadr (named Qais), Kinanah, Khuzaimah, Mudrikah (named 'Amir), Ilyas, Mudar, Nizar, Ma'ad and 'Adnan.
sections.title: His Lineage

body: His family is called Hashimite after his great-grandfather Hashim, who fed and watered the pilgrims. His name was 'Amr. He was called Hashim, "the one who breaks bread", because he crumbled bread into broth for the pilgrims. He was the first to lead Quraish's two great caravans, in winter and summer [106:1-2]. On a trade journey he married Salma of Banu 'Adi bin An-Najjar in Madinah. He went on to Syria and died at Gaza in 497 CE while she was carrying his child.

Their son was named Shaibah for the white hair on his head, and he grew up among his mother's people in Madinah. When his uncle Al-Muttalib heard of him, he went to fetch him, weeping when he first saw him. He brought him home on his camel. Makkah took the boy for Al-Muttalib's servant, and so he came to be called 'Abdul-Muttalib.

After Al-Muttalib died, another uncle, Nawfal, seized 'Abdul-Muttalib's rights. His mother's people rode in from Madinah, eighty horsemen strong, and made Nawfal give them back before the elders of Quraish. Khuza'ah then joined Banu Hashim in a pact against Nawfal and 'Abd Shams. Long after, that pact would become a cause of the conquest of Makkah.
sections.title: Hashim and 'Abdul-Muttalib

body: In a dream, 'Abdul-Muttalib was told to dig at a certain spot. There he found the well of Zamzam, which Jurhum had filled in when they left Makkah. With it he found the swords, armour and two golden deer they had buried. The swords and the deer were beaten into the door of the Ka'bah, and from then on Zamzam's water was given to the pilgrims.

Quraish claimed a share in the well. 'Abdul-Muttalib refused: Allah had given it to him alone. They set out to have it judged by a diviner of Banu Sa'd. On the way, signs from Allah confirmed his right to it.
During this quarrel, 'Abdul-Muttalib vowed that if he were given ten sons who grew to manhood, he would sacrifice one of them at the Ka'bah.
sections.title: Zamzam Found Again

body: Abrahah, the Abyssinian ruler of Yemen, saw the Arabs making pilgrimage to the Ka'bah. To turn them away from it, he built a great church in San'a'. A man of Kinanah crept into it by night and defiled it. In fury, Abrahah marched on Makkah with sixty thousand men to destroy the Ka'bah. He rode the largest of his nine to thirteen elephants.

At the valley of Muhassir, between Muzdalifah and Mina, the elephant knelt and would not move. Turned north, south or east, it went quickly. Turned toward the Ka'bah, it knelt. Then Allah sent birds in flocks, each carrying three stones of baked clay, one in its beak and two in its claws. The stones tore Abrahah's men apart [105:1-5]. Abrahah himself fell sick, and his fingertips had to be cut away. He reached San'a' in a wretched state and died there. Quraish had fled to the hills, and came home safely.
This was in Muharram, fifty or fifty-five days before the Prophet's ﷺ birth. The news reached every corner of the known world, and showed that Allah had chosen this House.
sections.title: The Year of the Elephant
facts: Muharram, about 50 days before his birth

body: 'Abdul-Muttalib had ten sons, among them Al-Harith, Az-Zubair, Abu Talib, 'Abdullah, Hamzah, Abu Lahab and Al-'Abbas, and six daughters. When the ten were grown, he told them of his vow, and they accepted it. Their names were drawn by arrows before the idol Hubal, and the arrow fell on 'Abdullah. He was his father's most loved son, the finest and the most chaste.

'Abdul-Muttalib took him to the Ka'bah with a blade, but Quraish, 'Abdullah's uncles of Makhzum and his brother Abu Talib pleaded with him. A diviner told them to draw between 'Abdullah and ten camels, adding ten more camels each time the arrow fell on him. At one hundred camels the arrow fell on the camels, and they were sacrificed in his place. After this, blood money among the Arabs rose from ten camels to a hundred, and Islam later kept it.

'Abdul-Muttalib married him to Aminah, daughter of Wahb, chief of Banu Zuhrah, a woman of the noblest descent. Soon after, 'Abdullah was sent to Madinah to buy dates (or, in another report, was coming home from Syria) and died there, aged twenty-five, most likely two months before his son was born. He left five camels, a few goats, and a servant, Barakah, known as Umm Ayman, who would nurse the Prophet ﷺ.
sections.title: 'Abdullah, the Ransomed

body: He was born in the quarter of Banu Hashim in Makkah on a Monday morning, the ninth of Rabi' al-Awwal, in the Year of the Elephant. This was the fortieth year of the reign of the Persian king Kisra Anushirwan, the twentieth or twenty-second of April, 571 CE.

His mother said that at his birth a light came out of her that lit up the palaces of Syria. Signs are told of that night: balconies of Kisra's palace falling and the sacred fire of the Magians going out. But none of these reports has a confirmed chain.

She sent word to his grandfather, who came full of joy, carried him to the Ka'bah, prayed to Allah and thanked Him. He named him Muhammad, a name the Arabs seldom used. After his mother, the first to nurse him was Thuwaibah, a freed slave of Abu Lahab, who had nursed his uncle Hamzah too.
sections.title: His Birth
sections.place: The quarter of Banu Hashim, Makkah
facts: 9 Rabi' al-Awwal, Year of the Elephant

body: The townspeople sent their babies to wet nurses in the desert, to grow strong in open air and learn the pure speech of the Bedouin. His nurse was Halimah, daughter of Abu Dhu'aib, of Banu Sa'd bin Bakr. Her husband was Al-Harith bin 'Abdul-'Uzza.

It was a year of drought. Halimah came to Makkah on a lean donkey with an old camel that gave no milk, and a baby who cried all night from hunger. Every nurse turned the orphan away, expecting nothing from a boy with no father. Halimah would not go home empty-handed, so she took him. At once her milk was plenty for him and for her own son. The old camel gave milk, the family slept through the night, and her husband said she had taken a blessed child.

The lean donkey outran the whole caravan home. Their land turned green and their flocks came home full. After two years they weaned him, and they begged his mother to let them keep him longer. He stayed until he was about four or five. His foster sister Ash-Shaima' used to care for him.
sections.title: Halimah of Banu Sa'd

body: Anas reports, in Sahih Muslim, that Jibreel came to the boy while he played with other children. He laid him down and opened his chest, took out his heart, and removed a clot from it, saying, "That was Satan's share of you." He washed the heart in Zamzam water in a golden basin and returned it to its place.
The children ran to his nurse crying that Muhammad had been killed. They found him unharmed, only pale. Anas said he had seen the mark of it on his chest.
Halimah was frightened after this, and took him back to his mother.
sections.title: The Opening of the Chest

body: He lived with his mother until he was six. To honour her husband's memory, Aminah set out to visit his grave in Yathrib, about five hundred kilometres away. She took the boy, 'Abdul-Muttalib and their servant Umm Ayman. They stayed a month.
On the way home she fell gravely ill and died at Al-Abwa', on the road between Makkah and Madinah. 'Abdul-Muttalib brought the boy back to Makkah, now without father or mother.
sections.title: Aminah, and the Road to Yathrib

body: His grandfather loved him more than his own children. A mattress was laid for 'Abdul-Muttalib in the shade of the Ka'bah. His sons sat around it out of respect, but the boy sat on it. When his uncles moved him, 'Abdul-Muttalib would say, "Leave my grandson. By Allah, he will have a great standing," and he would stroke his back.

'Abdul-Muttalib died in Makkah when the boy was eight years, two months and ten days old. His care passed to Abu Talib, his father's full brother. Abu Talib put him before his own children and protected him for forty years. He judged other men by how they treated his nephew.

Once, in a year without rain, Quraish asked Abu Talib to pray for it. He went to the Ka'bah with the boy, who had a cloud above him, and they stood by its wall and prayed. Clouds gathered from every side, and the rain came pouring down.
sections.title: In His Grandfather's Shade

body: At twelve he went with Abu Talib on a trade journey to Syria. At Busra, in the Hawran under Roman rule, a monk named Bahirah came out to meet the caravan, though he had never met them before. He took the boy's hand and said he was the master of all people, whom Allah would send as a mercy to the worlds.

Abu Talib asked how he knew. The monk said every stone and tree had bowed as they came over the pass, which they do only for a prophet. He also recognized the seal of prophethood below his shoulder, like an apple, as described in their books. He urged Abu Talib to take the boy home, for fear of the Romans and the Jews. Abu Talib sent him back to Makkah with some of his servants.
sections.title: Bahirah the Monk
sections.place: Busra, on the road to Syria

body: When he was about twenty, war broke out between Quraish and Kinanah on one side and Qais 'Ailan on the other. It went on for years with heavy losses. It was called Al-Fijar, "the profane war", because it was fought in the sacred months, when fighting was forbidden. Harb bin Umaiyah led Quraish.
He was present in one of its battles to help his uncles, gathering the enemy's arrows as they fell and handing them back.
sections.title: The Sacrilegious Wars

body: When peace returned, the clans of Hashim, Al-Muttalib, Asad, Zuhrah and Taim met in the house of 'Abdullah bin Jud'an. They pledged to put down injustice and to protect the rights of the weak and the poor. Tribal pride had never bound the Arabs to anything like it.

It began with a merchant of Zubaid, who sold goods to Al-'As bin Wa'il and was never paid. No ally of his in Quraish would help. He climbed a hill and cried out his complaint in verse. Az-Zubair bin 'Abdul-Muttalib took up his cause, the clans met, and they made Al-'As pay.

As a prophet, he remembered it gladly. He said he had seen that pact in Ibn Jud'an's house, and it was dearer to him than the finest herds. If he were called to the like of it in Islam, he would answer.
sections.title: The Pact of the Virtuous
sections.place: The house of 'Abdullah bin Jud'an, Makkah

body: In his youth he had no fixed trade. It is reported that he herded sheep among Banu Sa'd, and in Makkah for wages.

Khadijah, daughter of Khuwailid, was a woman of honour and wealth who paid men a share of the profit to trade for her. She heard of his truthfulness, honesty and good character, and offered him more than she gave others to take her goods to Syria. Her servant Maisarah went with him. He was twenty-five.
sections.title: Shepherd and Merchant

body: Khadijah saw more profit and blessing from that journey than ever before. Maisarah told her of his manners, honesty, thoughtfulness and sincerity. Many great men of Quraish had asked to marry her, and she had refused them all. Now she told her friend Nafisah, daughter of Munyah, of her wish. Nafisah spoke to him, he agreed, and his uncles went to her uncle.

They were married before Banu Hashim and the chiefs of Mudar. His gift to her was twenty camels. She was forty, and the best of the women of Quraish in lineage, wealth and wisdom. She was his first wife, and he married no one else while she lived.

She bore all his children but Ibrahim, whose mother was Mariyah the Copt. His sons died young. All his daughters lived to see Islam, embraced it and emigrated to Madinah. All died in his lifetime except Fatimah, who died six months after him.
sections.title: Khadijah
people: his eldest; he was called Abul-Qasim after him; died in childhood
the youngest; died six months after her father
called At-Taiyib and At-Tahir; died in childhood

body: When he was thirty-five, Quraish rebuilt the Ka'bah. Since Isma'il's time it had been a low, roofless enclosure of stones, nine cubits high, and thieves could reach its treasure. Age had cracked its walls, and a great flood had almost brought it down.

They agreed to spend only clean money on it, nothing from usury, wrongdoing or ill-gotten gain. They were afraid to strike the first blow until Al-Walid bin Al-Mughirah began. When no harm came to him, the rest joined in, down to the foundations of Ibrahim. Each clan built its own part, and a Roman mason named Baqum laid the stones.

Then came the Black Stone. Every chief wanted the honour of setting it in place. For four or five days they quarrelled, and daggers were nearly drawn. The oldest of them, Abu Umaiyah bin Al-Mughirah, proposed that the first man to come through the gate should judge between them. It was Muhammad ﷺ. "Al-Amin, the trustworthy, has come," they said, "we accept him."
He spread a cloak, put the stone in it and had every chief lift its edges together. When it reached its place, he set it in with his own hands.

Their clean money ran short, so they left out about six cubits on the north side, which is the Hijr, or Hatim. They raised the door so they could decide who went in, and roofed the building on six columns.
sections.title: Rebuilding the Ka'bah
facts: Black Stone wall and the one facing it

body: In his youth he gathered the best qualities a man could have: sound judgement, deep thought, long silences and quiet reflection. He stayed away from wine, from meat sacrificed on the stone altars, and from the idols' festivals. He hated the idols, and could not bear to hear anyone swear by Al-Lat and Al-'Uzza.

Allah guarded him. Jabir reports, in Al-Bukhari, that while the Ka'bah was being rebuilt he carried stones with Al-'Abbas. Al-'Abbas told him to wrap his waist-cloth around his neck to pad his shoulders. As he did, he fell to the ground with his eyes turned to the sky. When he rose, he asked for his waist-cloth and tied it on again. He was never seen uncovered after that.

He was the most modest of his people and the most upright in his dealings. He was the gentlest, the most truthful, and the most faithful to his word, so that his people called him Al-Amin, the trustworthy. Khadijah said of him that he kept ties of kinship, carried the burdens of the weak, gave to the needy, honoured guests and stood by those who suffered for the truth.
sections.title: Al-Amin

parts.title: Forty Years Before the Message
parts.blurb: His family, the year of the Elephant, his birth and childhood, his youth and marriage, and the trust Makkah placed in him.

body: From the day he was made a prophet, his life falls into two periods: about thirteen years in Makkah and about ten in Madinah. Each passed through stages that can be traced in how the call went forward.
The years in Makkah had three stages. Each began when the one before had done its work.
sections.title: Two Periods of the Message
list: from the fourth year of prophethood until the Hijrah
from the end of the tenth year, on through the years in Madinah

body: As he neared forty, he took to long hours alone, thinking over the world around him. He would take barley porridge and water and go out to the hills around Makkah. His favourite retreat was a small cave on Mount An-Nur, two miles from Makkah: four cubits long and less than two wide.

He went there often, above all in Ramadan, to worship and reflect, and he fed the poor who came to him. The idols and wrongs of his people weighed on his heart, but no clear way to put them right had yet been shown to him.
These years of solitude, three of them before the Message, were a preparation for the trust he was about to carry.
sections.title: The Cave of Hira'

body: At forty, the age at which prophets are said to be given their message, the signs of prophethood began to appear. Stones in Makkah greeted him with peace. Every dream he saw came true, as clearly as the break of dawn. This lasted six months.
Since his prophethood lasted twenty-three years, these six months of true dreams are one forty-sixth part of it.
sections.title: True Dreams

body: In Ramadan of his third year of solitude, the revelation came. The book fixes the night as Monday, the twenty-first of Ramadan, the tenth of August 610 CE. He was forty lunar years, six months and twelve days old.

'Aishah tells it, in Al-Bukhari. The angel came to him in the cave and said, "Read!" He said, "I cannot read." The angel held him tightly until he could bear no more, then let him go and said again, "Read!" Three times this happened. Then the angel said, "Read in the name of your Lord who created..." [96:1-5]

He went home trembling and said to Khadijah, "Cover me, cover me." When his fear had passed, he told her what had happened. She comforted him and took him to her cousin Waraqah bin Nawfal, an old blind man who had become a Christian and copied the scriptures.

Waraqah said this was the angel Allah had sent to Moses, and wished he could be young when his people drove him out. "Will they drive me out?" the Prophet ﷺ asked. Waraqah said that no one had ever brought what he brought without being treated as an enemy. Waraqah died a few days later.
sections.title: "Read!"

quote.text: By Allah, Allah will never disgrace you. You keep ties of kinship, you carry the burden of the weak, you give to the poor, you honour the guest, and you help against the hardships that come to people.
quote.who: Khadijah, reported by Al-Bukhari

body: After that first revelation, it stopped for a while. The book holds, after study, that the pause lasted only days, about ten, and not the years that are commonly said. Ibn Hajar explained that the pause let his fear settle and made him long for the revelation to return.
He was deeply sad in those days. Jibreel would appear and tell him, "O Muhammad, you are truly the Messenger of Allah," and his heart would grow calm.
sections.title: The Pause

body: Jabir reports that he described what came next: "While I was walking, I heard a voice from the sky. I looked up, and there was the angel who had come to me at Hira', seated on a chair between the sky and the earth. I was afraid of him and fell to the ground. I went home and said, 'Cover me, cover me.'" Then Allah revealed the opening of Surat Al-Muddaththir [74:1-7].

These verses gave him two charges. The first was to convey and warn. The second was for himself: to magnify his Lord alone, to keep himself pure, to shun the idols, to give without seeking a return, and to be patient for his Lord's sake. They called him away from rest to a life of striving. After this, revelation came often and without a break.
sections.title: Arise and Warn

quote.text: O you wrapped in your cloak, arise and warn, and magnify your Lord.
quote.who: Al-Muddaththir 74:1-3

body: Ibn Al-Qayyim counted the ways in which the revelation came to him. In the hardest of them, he would sweat even on a cold day. If he was riding, his camel would kneel under the weight. Once his thigh rested on Zaid's when it came, and Zaid felt as if his thigh would break.
sections.title: How the Revelation Came
list: the angel unseen, the words placed in his mind
the angel speaking to him, sometimes seen by his Companions
Like the ringing of a bell
what Allah revealed to him on the night of the Mi'raj, the prayer among it

body: Makkah was the heart of idol worship in Arabia, and its people were the keepers of the idols. So the call began quietly, so as not to provoke them before it had taken root. He began at home, with those closest to him, and with those he trusted to see the truth.

Khadijah was the first to believe. Then came Zaid bin Harithah, whom Khadijah had given him and who chose to stay with him rather than go home with his own father. Then his young cousin 'Ali, who lived in his house, and his close friend Abu Bakr, all on the first day. Abu Bakr, wealthy, gentle and much visited, brought others: 'Uthman bin 'Affan, Az-Zubair bin Al-'Awwam, 'Abdur-Rahman bin 'Awf, Sa'd bin Abi Waqqas and Talhah bin 'Ubaidullah.

Others followed: Bilal, Abu 'Ubaidah bin Al-Jarrah, Abu Salamah, Al-Arqam, the three sons of Maz'un, Sa'id bin Zaid and his wife Fatimah (sister of 'Umar), Khabbab bin Al-Aratt, 'Abdullah bin Mas'ud and more. Ibn Hisham counts more than forty. They met him and learned their religion in secret.
sections.title: The First Believers
people: his wife, the first to believe
freed by him; later fell commanding the army at Mu'tah
his cousin, raised in his house
his closest friend, whose call brought many others
of Banu Umaiyah, through Abu Bakr
the Abyssinian, later the caller to prayer

body: The five daily prayers were not among the first commands. Ibn Hajar wrote that he certainly prayed before the Night Journey, and it is reported that prayer was then required twice a day, before sunrise and before sunset. It is reported that at the first revelation Jibreel taught him how to make wudu'.

When prayer was due, he and his Companions slipped away to the mountain passes to pray out of sight. Once Abu Talib came upon him praying with 'Ali. When he learned what they were doing, he told them to keep at it.

The surahs of those years were short, with strong rhythms and striking pauses. They called the soul to purity, warned against being taken in by the world, and described Paradise and the Fire as if they were in view.
sections.title: The First Prayers

body: After three years, the command came to preach openly: "And warn your nearest kin" [26:214]. He gathered the families of Banu Hashim and Banu Al-Muttalib, about forty-five men. Abu Lahab spoke first, telling him his kin could not stand against all the Arabs. He said nothing that day.

He invited them a second time and spoke. He said he praised Allah, sought His help, believed in Him and trusted Him. He bore witness that there is no god but Allah. A guide does not lie to his people, and he was the Messenger of Allah to them and to all people. They would die as they slept and rise as they woke, and they would answer for their deeds: either Paradise forever or the Fire forever.

Abu Talib answered that he would protect and defend him, though he could not leave the religion of 'Abdul-Muttalib. Abu Lahab urged him to stop his nephew before others did. Abu Talib swore he would protect him as long as he lived.
sections.title: Warn Your Nearest Kin

quote.text: I will protect him as long as I live.
quote.who: Abu Talib

body: Sure now of Abu Talib's protection, he climbed Mount As-Safa one day and called out, "Ya sabahah!", the cry raised at the sight of danger. He called the clans of Quraish one by one, and they came, or sent someone in their place. Abu Lahab came too.

"If I told you there were horsemen in the valley about to attack you, would you believe me?" They said, "Yes. We have only ever known you to tell the truth." He said, "Then I am a warner to you, ahead of a severe punishment." Abu Lahab said, "May you perish! Is this what you gathered us for?" Then Surat Al-Masad was revealed [111:1].

He called them clan by clan, down to his daughter Fatimah, to save themselves from the Fire. He told them he could not protect them from Allah at all, though he would always honour the ties between them. Then came the command: "Proclaim what you are commanded" [15:94]. He began to recite the Qur'an at their gatherings, and to pray openly in the courtyard of the Ka'bah.
sections.title: On Mount Safa

body: A few months into the open call, the pilgrimage season drew near. Quraish feared what the Arab pilgrims would hear, so they met at the house of Al-Walid bin Al-Mughirah to agree on one thing to say about him. A soothsayer? His words were not the soothsayers' rhymes. Possessed? He showed none of its signs. A poet? What he recited was nothing like poetry. A sorcerer? He used none of their spells, and his speech was sweet through and through.

At last they settled on this: his words were a magic that split son from father, brother from brother and husband from wife. The Qur'an tells how Al-Walid thought, plotted and frowned, and then called it nothing but magic [74:18-25].
At the fairs of 'Ukaz, Majannah and Dhul-Majaz, he went from camp to camp calling people to Allah, and Abu Lahab followed behind him shouting, "Don't listen to him. He is a liar."

They mocked him as a madman [15:6] and a lying sorcerer [38:4]. They laughed at the believers [83:29-33]. They called the Qur'an tales of the ancients [25:5], a lie others had helped him make [25:4], or the teaching of some man [16:103]. They asked why a messenger should eat food and walk in the markets [25:7]. An-Nadr bin Al-Harith told tales of the kings of Persia to the same crowds, and bought singing girls to draw people away [31:6].
sections.title: Sorcerer, Poet, Madman

body: When mockery could not stop the flow of people into Islam, the chiefs agreed on torture. Each clan was to deal with its own believers. If a man of standing came to Islam, Abu Jahl would shame him and threaten to ruin his trade. If he was weak, Abu Jahl beat him.

'Uthman's uncle rolled him in a mat of palm leaves and lit a fire under him. Mus'ab bin 'Umair's mother, who had kept him in luxury, starved him and threw him out. Bilal's master, Umaiyah bin Khalaf, had him dragged through the streets by boys with a rope around his neck. He laid him in the noon heat with a great rock on his chest, until Bilal would deny Muhammad or die. Bilal only said, "One, One." Abu Bakr bought him and set him free, as he freed others.

The family of Yasir were laid on the burning sand. Passing them, the Prophet ﷺ said, "Patience, family of Yasir: your meeting place is Paradise." Yasir died under the torture. His wife Sumaiyah was killed by Abu Jahl, the first martyr in Islam. Their son 'Ammar was tortured until he said what they wanted, though his heart never changed. Allah revealed that one forced to it, his heart at rest in faith, was excused [16:106].
sections.title: The Persecution
people: "One, One," under a rock in the noon heat; freed by Abu Bakr
killed by Abu Jahl, the first martyr of Islam
forced to speak against his faith; his heart never wavered
dragged over hot coals until his back was burned
laid on the scorching sand under a stone; freed by Abu Bakr

body: The chiefs of Quraish came to Abu Talib: his nephew cursed their gods and shamed their fathers, so either he must stop him or let them deal with him. He sent them away politely, and the Prophet ﷺ went on as before.

They came again with threats. Abu Talib, grieved, called his nephew and asked him not to put on him more than he could bear. The Prophet ﷺ thought his uncle meant to give him up, and he answered with the words below. He rose to leave in tears. Abu Talib called him back and said, "Go and say what you will. By Allah, I will never hand you over."

They came a third time, bringing 'Umarah bin Al-Walid, a fine young man, for Abu Talib to take as his son in exchange for his nephew, whom they would kill. "Shall I feed your son for you while you kill mine?" he said. "By Allah, that will never be."
sections.title: The Sun in My Right Hand

quote.text: O my uncle, by Allah, if they put the sun in my right hand and the moon in my left to make me leave this matter, I would not leave it until Allah makes it prevail or I perish in it.
quote.who: The Prophet ﷺ, reported by Ibn Hisham

body: His own uncle Abu Lahab led it. He threw stones at him until his ankles bled, and made his two sons divorce the Prophet's daughters, Ruqaiyah and Umm Kulthum. When one of the Prophet's sons died, Abu Lahab rejoiced and called him "the one cut off". His wife, Umm Jamil, scattered thorns on his paths, "the carrier of firewood" [111:4]. She came to the Ka'bah with a handful of stones for him, but could see only Abu Bakr beside him.

His neighbours threw filth into his house and his cooking pot. Once, as he prostrated at the Ka'bah, 'Uqbah bin Abi Mu'ait laid a camel's entrails on his back while Abu Jahl and his friends laughed. He stayed in prostration until Fatimah came and lifted it off him. Then he called on Allah against seven of them by name. Ibn Mas'ud swore he later saw them dead in the well of Badr.

Umaiyah bin Khalaf slandered him wherever he saw him [104:1]. 'Uqbah spat in his face at the urging of Ubai bin Khalaf. Abu Jahl tried to stop him praying at the Ka'bah [96:17-18]. Once he came to tread on his neck, but turned back shielding his face. He said he had seen a trench of fire between them, and wings.
sections.title: What They Did to Him
sections.when: The years of the open call

body: In the fourth year, a group of Muslims on their way to meet the Prophet ﷺ in the hills was seen and attacked. Sa'd bin Abi Waqqas struck one of the attackers and drew blood, the first blood shed in Islam's history.

To spare his weak and vulnerable followers, he told them to keep their Islam hidden. He took the house of Al-Arqam bin Abul-Arqam, at the foot of As-Safa, as a hidden meeting place where he taught them the Qur'an and the wisdom of their religion. He himself went on praying and calling to Allah in the open.
sections.title: The House of Al-Arqam

body: By the middle of the fifth year the persecution had grown unbearable. Then Allah revealed that His earth is spacious [39:10]. The Prophet ﷺ knew that Ashamah, the Negus, the king of Abyssinia, was a just king who wronged no one, so he allowed some of his followers to seek refuge there.

In Rajab of the fifth year, twelve men and four women left. Among them were 'Uthman bin 'Affan and his wife Ruqaiyah, the Prophet's daughter. He said they were the first to leave their homes for Allah since Ibrahim and Lot. They slipped out of Makkah by night and found two boats at the port of Shu'aibah sailing for Abyssinia. Quraish sent men after them, but they had already sailed. They were welcomed in Abyssinia.
sections.title: The First Hijrah, to Abyssinia

body: Quraish had a habit of drowning out the Qur'an with noise whenever it was recited [41:26]. But in Ramadan of the fifth year, he recited Surat An-Najm in the Sacred Mosque before a crowd of their chiefs. They listened in silence, held by it. At its final words, "So prostrate to Allah and worship Him" [53:62], they all fell down in prostration, believers and idolaters alike.
Those who had not been there blamed them. To excuse themselves, they put about a lie that he had spoken well of their idols.

Word reached the emigrants in Abyssinia that Quraish had all become Muslims, and they set out for home. They reached Makkah in Shawwal and learned the truth an hour from the city. Some went back to Abyssinia. Others came in secretly, or under the protection of a man of Quraish.
sections.title: The Prostration at An-Najm

body: Angered by the welcome the Muslims had found abroad, Quraish tightened their grip. The Prophet ﷺ again allowed the oppressed to leave for Abyssinia. It was harder this time, with Quraish watching every move, but they slipped away before they could be stopped.
This time eighty-three men went, and eighteen or nineteen women. Whether 'Ammar was among them is not certain.
sections.title: The Second Hijrah

body: Quraish sent 'Amr bin Al-'As and 'Abdullah bin Abi Rabi'ah, both still idolaters, with rich gifts for the king and his bishops. They asked him to hand over the refugees, who had left their fathers' religion and did not follow his either.

The Negus called the Muslims. Ja'far bin Abi Talib spoke for them. They had been an ignorant people, he said: they worshipped idols, ate dead meat, did shameful things, cut their ties of kinship, wronged their neighbours, and the strong fed on the weak. Then Allah sent them a messenger whose lineage, truthfulness, trustworthiness and purity they knew. He called them to worship Allah alone. He told them to be truthful, keep trusts, honour kinship, be good to their neighbours and spare blood. He forbade lewdness, false witness, consuming the orphan's wealth and slandering chaste women. For believing him, their people had tortured them, so they had come to his land, choosing him over all others.

Asked to recite something of what had come from Allah, Ja'far recited the beginning of Surat Maryam [19:16-26]. The Negus and his bishops wept until their beards were wet. This and what Jesus brought, he said, came from the same source of light. He would not hand them over.

The next day the envoys said the Muslims spoke ill of Jesus. Ja'far said they held what their Prophet ﷺ taught: that Jesus was Allah's servant and messenger, His spirit and His word cast into the Virgin Mary [4:171]. The Negus said Jesus was no more than that. He gave back the gifts and sent the envoys away, and the Muslims lived in peace in his land for years.
sections.title: Before the Negus
sections.place: The court of the Negus, Abyssinia

body: With every scheme failing, Quraish turned to the thought of killing him.

'Utaibah, son of Abu Lahab, came at him, tore his shirt and spat at him. The Prophet ﷺ prayed that Allah would set one of His dogs on him. Later, camped at Az-Zarqa' on the way to Syria, 'Utaibah saw a lion and cried that Muhammad's prayer had killed him though he was in Makkah. The lion took him from among his companions and crushed his head.

'Uqbah bin Abi Mu'ait once pressed his foot on the Prophet's neck as he prostrated, and once twisted his cloak around his neck and choked him hard. Abu Bakr pulled him off, crying, "Would you kill a man for saying, 'My Lord is Allah'?" They beat Abu Bakr until his hair came away in his family's hands.

One day, as they mocked him while he circled the Ka'bah, he stopped and said, "Listen, people of Quraish. By the One in whose hand my soul is, I have come to you with slaughter." The fiercest of them fell silent with fear and tried to soothe him.
sections.title: They Plot to Kill Him

body: One day Abu Jahl came upon the Prophet ﷺ at As-Safa and abused him and his religion. He said nothing in reply. Abu Jahl struck his head with a stone and drew blood, then went to sit with Quraish at the Ka'bah.

His uncle Hamzah was coming home from hunting, bow over his shoulder, when a servant girl who had seen it all told him. Furious, he strode into the Sacred Mosque, struck Abu Jahl on the head with his bow and said, "You insult him when I follow his religion and say what he says?" The men of Makhzum rose to Abu Jahl's side, but Abu Jahl stopped them: "Leave Abu 'Umarah. I did abuse his nephew badly."
It began in a man's pride at seeing his kinsman insulted, but Allah opened his heart, and Hamzah became a great strength to Islam and its people.
sections.title: Hamzah Becomes Muslim

body: Three days after Hamzah, 'Umar bin Al-Khattab became Muslim. He was the most feared man in Makkah and a fierce enemy of the new faith. The Prophet ﷺ had prayed that Allah would strengthen Islam with whichever of two men He loved more: 'Umar, or Abu Jahl.

One day 'Umar came upon him praying at the Ka'bah, reciting Surat Al-Haqqah. "A poet," he thought. "It is not the word of a poet," came the next verse. "A soothsayer," he thought. "Nor the word of a soothsayer" [69:40-43]. Islam entered his heart, he later said, but his pride held it back.

One day he set out, sword in hand, to kill the Prophet ﷺ. A man stopped him on the way: his own sister Fatimah and her husband Sa'id had become Muslims. 'Umar burst into their house, where Khabbab was teaching them Surat Ta-Ha. He struck Sa'id, then struck his sister and drew blood. They told him to do as he pleased, for they believed. Seeing his sister's blood, 'Umar softened and asked for the page. She told him to wash first. He read until "Truly I am Allah, there is no god but Me, so worship Me and establish prayer for My remembrance" [20:14]. "How beautiful this is," he said. "Take me to Muhammad."

At the house by As-Safa, a Companion saw 'Umar with his sword through the door. Hamzah said, "Let him in. If he comes for good, good. If not, we will kill him with his own sword." The Prophet ﷺ took him by his garment and asked why he had come. "To believe in Allah and His Messenger." The Companions cried "Allahu akbar" so loud it was heard at the Ka'bah. Soon the Muslims went out in two rows, Hamzah leading one and 'Umar the other, and prayed openly at the Ka'bah. From then on he was called Al-Faruq, the one who sets truth apart from falsehood.
sections.title: 'Umar Becomes Muslim

quote.text: We were never able to pray at the Ka'bah until 'Umar became Muslim.
quote.who: 'Abdullah bin Mas'ud

body: After Hamzah and 'Umar, Quraish saw that torture would not work and tried temptation. 'Utbah bin Rabi'ah, one of their chiefs, sat with him and made an offer. If he wanted wealth, they would make him the richest of them. If he wanted honour, they would make him their chief. If he wanted to be king, they would crown him. And if a spirit troubled him, they would find him the best physicians.

"Have you finished, Abul-Walid?" he asked. Then he recited the opening of Surat Fussilat [41:1-5]. 'Utbah listened, leaning back on his hands. He went on until the verse of prostration, and prostrated. In one report, when he reached the warning of a thunderbolt like the one that struck 'Ad and Thamud [41:13], 'Utbah put a hand over his mouth and begged him by their kinship to stop.

'Utbah went back to his friends with a changed face. He had never heard such words, he said: not poetry, not magic, not soothsaying. They should leave him be. If the Arabs finished him, they were spared him. If he prevailed, his glory would be theirs. They said he had been bewitched.
sections.title: The Offer of 'Utbah

quote.text: I have heard words the like of which I have never heard. By Allah, it is not poetry, nor magic, nor soothsaying.
quote.who: 'Utbah bin Rabi'ah

body: One evening the chiefs gathered behind the Ka'bah and sent for him. They made 'Utbah's offers again. He told them he wanted none of it. He was a messenger delivering his Lord's message. If they accepted it, it was good for them in this world and the next, and if not, he would be patient until Allah judged between them.

Then they demanded signs. Let his Lord move the mountains away, level their land, and bring their dead back to life. Let Him send an angel to vouch for him, and give him gardens, treasures and palaces of gold. Or let a piece of the sky fall on them. "That is for Allah," he said. "If He wills, He does it." He left them grieved.

Abu Jahl swore he would crush the Prophet's head with a rock while he prostrated. The next morning he went toward him carrying the rock, but turned back pale and shaking and let it fall. He said a monstrous camel with terrible teeth had come at him. The Prophet ﷺ said it was Jibreel, and that if Abu Jahl had come closer, he would have seized him.
sections.title: Signs on Demand

body: Some of the elders still hoped for a middle way. As he circled the Ka'bah, Al-Aswad bin Al-Muttalib, Al-Walid bin Al-Mughirah, Umaiyah bin Khalaf and Al-'As bin Wa'il came to him. Let them worship what he worshipped and he worship what they worshipped, and they would share in whichever proved better. In another report, they asked him to worship their gods for a year and they would worship his for a year.
Allah answered with Surat Al-Kafirun [109:1-6], and with the verse: "Is it other than Allah you order me to worship, O you ignorant ones?" [39:64]
sections.title: Worship Our Gods for a Year

quote.text: Say: O disbelievers, I do not worship what you worship.
quote.who: Al-Kafirun 109:1-2

body: At a loss, Quraish listened to An-Nadr bin Al-Harith. Muhammad had grown up among them, he said, the most truthful and trustworthy of them. He was no sorcerer, no soothsayer, no poet and not mad: they knew all of those. This was something serious.

They sent An-Nadr and others to the rabbis of Madinah. The rabbis gave them three questions: if he could answer them, he was a prophet. When they were put to him, Surat Al-Kahf was revealed, telling the story of the young men of the cave and of Dhul-Qarnain, and the answer about the soul came in Surat Al-Isra'. Quraish now knew he was on the truth, yet they held to their disbelief.
sections.title: Three Questions from the Rabbis
list: The young men who went away long ago
The man who travelled to the east and the west
The soul, and what it is
it is of the command of my Lord [17:85]

body: Abu Talib saw what all of this pointed to: 'Uqbah's attempt to strangle him, Abu Jahl's rock, 'Umar setting out with his sword. There was a plan to kill his nephew. He gathered Banu Hashim and Banu Al-Muttalib and called on them to protect him.
Every one of them agreed, believers and unbelievers alike, out of loyalty to their own. Only Abu Lahab sided with Quraish against him.
sections.title: His Clan Closes Ranks

body: Quraish met at Khaif Bani Kinanah, in the valley of Al-Muhassab, and swore a pact against Banu Hashim and Banu Al-Muttalib. No one would buy from them or sell to them, marry them, mix with them, visit them or speak to them, until they handed Muhammad over to be killed. They wrote it on a sheet and hung it inside the Ka'bah. Ibn Al-Qayyim says the man who wrote it was Baghid bin 'Amir, and that his hand was later paralysed after the Prophet ﷺ prayed against him.

Abu Talib withdrew with both clans, Muslim and not, into the valley of Abu Talib on the edge of Makkah. They stayed there from Muharram of the seventh year until the tenth: three years. Food was cut off. Quraish bought up whatever came into Makkah so none could reach them. They ate leaves and animal skins, and the cries of hungry children could be heard outside. Only now and then did a kind relative smuggle food in. Abu Jahl once caught Hakim bin Hizam bringing wheat to his aunt Khadijah, and only another man's intervention let it through.

At night Abu Talib had his nephew sleep in his own bed. When the rest were asleep, he moved him to another, in case of an assassin. The Prophet ﷺ still went to the Ka'bah to pray, and in the sacred months he still called the pilgrims to Allah.
sections.title: The Boycott
sections.place: The Valley of Abu Talib, Makkah

body: Not all of Quraish could stomach starving their own kin. Hisham bin 'Amr, who used to smuggle food to the valley by night, shamed Zuhair bin Abi Umaiyah into joining him. Five men came together: Hisham, Zuhair, Al-Mut'im bin 'Adi, Abul-Bukhtari and Zam'ah bin Al-Aswad.

After circling the Ka'bah, Zuhair stood before the gathering. "Do we eat and dress while Banu Hashim perish?" he asked, swearing not to rest until the unjust sheet was torn up. Abu Jahl said it never would be. One by one the other four backed Zuhair.

Abu Talib, sitting nearby, told them that Allah had revealed to his nephew that ants had eaten the sheet, all but the name of Allah. If he was wrong, Abu Talib would hand him over. If he was right, they must end the boycott. Al-Mut'im went to look, and so it was. The pact was over, and the clans came home. Even this sign, they turned away from [54:2].
sections.title: The Parchment

quote.text: Shall we eat and dress while Banu Hashim perish?
quote.who: Zuhair bin Abi Umaiyah

body: Abu Talib, past eighty, fell ill after the boycott. The chiefs feared the Arabs would call them cowards if they harmed his nephew after his death. Twenty-five of them came to Abu Talib, among them 'Utbah and Shaibah bin Rabi'ah, Abu Jahl, Umaiyah bin Khalaf and Abu Sufyan, to make terms: they would leave his religion alone if he left theirs.

The Prophet ﷺ asked for one word from them, a word by which they would rule the Arabs, and the non-Arabs would follow them. "One word?" said Abu Jahl. "By your father, we'll give you that and ten more." "Say: there is no god but Allah, and leave what you worship besides Him." They clapped their hands. "Would he make the gods one god? That is a strange thing indeed." And they left, resolved to hold on to their gods. Of them, Allah revealed the opening of Surat Sad [38:1-7].
sections.title: One Word

body: In Rajab of the tenth year, six months after the boycott ended, Abu Talib died. As he lay dying, the Prophet ﷺ came in to find Abu Jahl and 'Abdullah bin Abi Umaiyah there. "Uncle, say there is no god but Allah, a word I can plead for you with Allah." The two men kept asking, "Will you leave the religion of 'Abdul-Muttalib?" In the end he died on it.

"I will keep asking forgiveness for you until I am forbidden," the Prophet ﷺ said. Then it was revealed that a prophet and the believers should not seek forgiveness for those who join others with Allah [9:113]. And: "You cannot guide whom you love, but Allah guides whom He wills" [28:56].

Abu Talib had been a fortress around the call, shielding it from the powerful and the foolish, yet he stayed on his fathers' religion. When Al-'Abbas asked what good he had done his uncle, he said that because of him Abu Talib was in the shallowest part of the Fire.
sections.title: The Death of Abu Talib

body: Two or three months later, in Ramadan of the tenth year, Khadijah, the Mother of the Believers, died. She was sixty-five and he was fifty. For twenty-five years she had shared his life, through the hardest years of all. He grieved for her deeply.

Abu Hurairah reports that Jibreel once came and said, "Khadijah is coming to you with a dish of food. When she comes, give her greetings of peace from her Lord and from me. And give her the good news of a palace of jewels in Paradise, where there will be no noise and no weariness."
sections.title: The Death of Khadijah

quote.text: She believed in me when people disbelieved, trusted me when people called me a liar, and supported me with her wealth when people held back; and Allah gave me children by her.
quote.who: The Prophet ﷺ, reported by Ahmad

body: With Abu Talib gone, the Prophet ﷺ had lost his shield, and Quraish no longer held back. A fool threw dust on his head in the street. When his daughter washed it off, weeping, he said, "Do not weep, my daughter. Allah will protect your father." He also said that Quraish never hurt him as they did after Abu Talib died. He called that year the Year of Grief.
It was hard on his Companions too. Abu Bakr himself set out to emigrate to Abyssinia. Ibn Ad-Daghinah met him at Birk Al-Ghimad and brought him back under his protection.

In Shawwal of that year he married Sawdah, daughter of Zam'ah. She was one of the early believers and had emigrated to Abyssinia with her husband, As-Sakran bin 'Amr, who later died. She was the first woman he married after Khadijah. Years later, she gave her turn with him to 'Aishah.
sections.title: The Year of Grief

body: How did the early Muslims hold firm through such torment? The book names the roots of it.

Their enemies feared him even as they fought him. Abu Jahl admitted they did not call him a liar, only what he brought [6:33]. Wounded at Uhud, Ubai bin Khalaf remembered that he had said he would kill him. Told the Muslims would kill him, Umaiyah bin Khalaf did not want to leave Makkah. His friends loved him more than themselves. Beaten almost to death, Abu Bakr would not eat until he heard that the Prophet ﷺ was safe.

When Khabbab, worn down by torture, asked him to pray for help, he sat up, his face reddening. Believers before them had had their flesh combed from their bones with iron combs and had not turned back, he said. Allah would complete this matter until a rider could travel from San'a' to Hadramawt fearing no one but Allah. "But you are in a hurry."
sections.title: What Kept Them Firm
list: beside it every hardship was small [13:17]
the most perfect of men in character
the knowledge that what they carried could not be put down
certain they would meet their Lord, they did good in fear and hope [23:60]
it answered their enemies, and told them trials come before Paradise [2:214] [29:1-3]
that the messengers are helped [37:171-173], that the Romans would win [30:2-5], that the strongest would flee [54:45]

parts.title: The Message Comes
parts.blurb: The cave of Hira', the first words of the Qur'an, and three years of calling to Allah in secret.

body: At the end of May or the start of June 619, he set out on foot for Ta'if, about sixty kilometres from Makkah, with his freed slave Zaid bin Harithah, to call its people to Allah.

He went first to three brothers of the family of 'Umair, chiefs of Thaqif: 'Abd Yalil, Mas'ud and Habib, sons of 'Amr. One sneered that if Allah had sent him, he himself would tear down the cover of the Ka'bah. The second asked whether Allah could find no one else to send. The third said he would never speak to him: if he was a messenger, he was too great to answer, and if he was lying, he was not worth it. He rose and asked them at least to keep his visit quiet.

For ten days he went from one leading man to the next, and none would hear him. Then they set their slaves and the town's fools on him. They lined the lanes and stoned him as he went, until blood ran down both his legs. Zaid, shielding him, was cut on the head. They drove him two or three miles out of the town, until he sank down to rest against the wall of an orchard.
sections.title: The Road to Ta'if

body: Tired and wounded, with the whole world against him, he turned to his Lord in words that have been kept to this day.

He complained to Allah of his weakness, his lack of means, and how small he was in people's eyes. He called on Him as the Most Merciful of the merciful, the Lord of the weak, and asked into whose hands He was leaving him: a stranger who would frown at him, or an enemy given power over his affairs? But if Allah was not angry with him, he did not care. Allah's well-being was wider for him. He sought refuge in the light of Allah's face, by which darkness is lit and the affairs of this world and the next are set right, from Allah's anger falling on him.
sections.title: The Prayer at the Orchard Wall

quote.text: If You are not angry with me, I do not care.
quote.who: The Prophet ﷺ, at Ta'if

body: The orchard belonged to 'Utbah and Shaibah, the sons of Rabi'ah, chiefs of Makkah. Moved by kinship, they sent their Christian servant 'Addas to him with a plate of grapes. He took them, saying, "In the name of Allah."

'Addas was struck by this: the people of that land did not speak like that. The Prophet ﷺ asked where he was from, and he said Nineveh. "The town of the righteous man Yunus, son of Matta," the Prophet ﷺ said. "What do you know of Yunus?" asked 'Addas. "He is my brother. He was a prophet, and I am a prophet."

'Addas bent and kissed his head, his hands and his feet. When he came back, his masters asked what had come over him. "My masters, there is nothing on earth better than this man," he said. "He told me something only a prophet would know."
sections.title: 'Addas

quote.text: There is nothing on earth better than this man. He told me something only a prophet would know.
quote.who: 'Addas

body: 'Aishah once asked him whether he had ever known a day worse than Uhud. He said the worst of what her people had done to him was the day at Ta'if, when Ibn 'Abd Yalil would not answer him.

He walked on, overwhelmed with grief, and did not come to himself until he reached Qarn Ath-Tha'alib. There he looked up and saw a cloud shading him, and Jibreel in it. Jibreel told him that Allah had heard what his people said to him, and had sent the angel of the mountains to do whatever he commanded. The angel greeted him and said that if he wished, he would bring the two mountains of Makkah together on them.
sections.title: The Angel of the Mountains

quote.text: No. I hope that Allah will bring from their descendants people who will worship Allah alone, joining none with Him.
quote.who: The Prophet ﷺ, reported by Al-Bukhari

body: On the way back he stopped for some days in the valley of Nakhlah. There, as he recited the Qur'an at night, a company of jinn listened to him. They told each other to be silent, and went back to their people as warners [46:29-31]. Surat Al-Jinn tells it too: "We have heard a wondrous recitation" [72:1-2].

He did not know they were there until the verses were revealed. It was a sign of Allah's support: no power in the earth could stop what He had decreed. His grief lifted, and he turned back toward Makkah with new resolve.
Zaid asked how they could go back into Makkah when its people had driven him out. "Zaid, Allah will make a way out of what you see," he said, "and Allah will help His religion and His Prophet."
sections.title: The Jinn Listen

body: Near Makkah he waited in the cave of Hira' and sent a man of Khuza'ah to ask for a protector. Al-Akhnas bin Shuraiq said he was an ally of Quraish and could not. Suhail bin 'Amr also refused. Then Al-Mut'im bin 'Adi agreed. He armed his sons and his people and told the Prophet ﷺ to come in. He went straight to the Sacred Mosque, prayed two rak'ahs, and walked home between Al-Mut'im and his armed sons.
Abu Jahl asked Al-Mut'im whether this was protection or conversion. "Protection," he said. "Then we protect whom you protect," said Abu Jahl.
The Prophet ﷺ never forgot it. After Badr he said that if Al-Mut'im had been alive and asked him for the prisoners, he would have released them all to him.
sections.title: Under Al-Mut'im's Protection

body: As the pilgrimage drew near, he went back to what he had done since the fourth year, presenting himself and his message to the tribes and to men one by one. Az-Zuhri names the tribes he went to, and none of them answered.

He told Banu 'Abdullah of Kalb that Allah had given their father a good name, but they would not hear him. None of the Arabs turned him away more harshly than Banu Hanifah. A man of Banu 'Amir bin Sa'sa'ah named Bahirah bin Firas saw his chance. If they backed him and he won, would they rule after him? "The matter belongs to Allah," he said. "He gives it to whom He wills." "Then you want us to offer our necks to the Arabs for you, and give the rule to others when you win?" They refused. Back home, an old man of their tribe who had been too old to travel heard what had happened. He put his hand to his head and said that this was a true descendant of Isma'il, and asked how they could have let him go.
sections.title: To the Tribes
sections.when: Dhul-Qa'dah, 10th year of prophethood · July 619 CE
sections.place: The pilgrims' camps at Mina, 'Ukaz and Dhul-Majaz
list: would follow him only for the rule after him
no tribe turned him away more harshly
told their father's name was a good one, still would not hear
Muharib, Fazarah, Ghassan, Murrah, Sulaim, 'Abs, Banu Nasr, Banu Al-Buka', Kindah, Al-Harith bin Ka'b, 'Udhrah, Hadramawt

body: Tribes turned away, but some men answered him one by one.

Abu Dharr of Ghifar heard of a prophet in Makkah. He came and drank Zamzam for days, not daring to ask anyone, until 'Ali took him to the Prophet ﷺ. He became Muslim on the spot and was told to keep it secret. Instead he went straight to the Sacred Mosque and declared it before Quraish. They beat him almost to death. Al-'Abbas threw himself over him and reminded them that their trade road ran through the land of Ghifar. The next day he did the same again.
sections.title: Those Who Answered
people: a poet of Yathrib who had "the wisdom of Luqman"; the Qur'an, he was told, was better; killed in Yathrib's wars
a youth of the Aws, who said "this is better than what we came for"; died soon after praising Allah
declared his Islam in the Sacred Mosque and was beaten for it, twice
came with cotton in his ears so as not to hear him; heard, believed, and brought his tribe
came to cure him of madness; heard his opening words three times and said they reached the depths of the sea

body: He met the tribes by night, so Makkah could not stand in his way. One night at Al-'Aqabah in Mina, he heard men talking and found six men of the Khazraj of Yathrib. He sat with them, explained Islam and recited the Qur'an.

The men of Yathrib had long heard their Jewish neighbours say that a prophet was soon to come, and that with him they would destroy their enemies as 'Ad had been destroyed. "This is the prophet they threaten us with," the six said to one another. "Let them not get to him before us." They became Muslims and told him that no people were more torn by hatred than theirs. Perhaps Allah would unite them through him. They went home and spoke of him, and soon there was hardly a house in Yathrib where he was not talked of.
sections.title: Six Men from Yathrib
sections.when: Hajj season, 11th year of prophethood · 620 CE

body: In Shawwal of the same year, he was married to 'Aishah, the daughter of Abu Bakr. The book gives her age as six at the marriage, and nine when she came to live with him in Madinah, in Shawwal of the first year after the Hijrah.
sections.title: Marriage to 'Aishah

body: Scholars differ on its date. Some place it in the first year of his prophethood, some in the fifth, and some on the 27th of Rajab of the tenth. Others say sixteen months before the Hijrah, fourteen months before it, or one year before it. Khadijah died before the five prayers were made obligatory, and they were made obligatory that night, so the first three cannot be right. Surat Al-Isra' suggests a late date. The book inclines to a time before the first pledge of 'Aqabah, or between the two pledges.

Ibn Al-Qayyim sums it up. He was carried, in body as well as spirit, from the Sacred Mosque in Makkah to Jerusalem, riding Al-Buraq with Jibreel. There he tied it at the gate of the mosque and led the prophets in prayer [17:1].
sections.title: The Night Journey

body: From Jerusalem he was taken up through the heavens. At each, Jibreel asked for it to be opened, and in each a prophet welcomed him, returned his greeting and affirmed his prophethood. When he left Musa, Musa wept: a man sent after him would lead more of his followers into Paradise than he had.

He was taken to Sidrat Al-Muntaha, the lote tree of the furthest boundary, and shown Al-Bait Al-Ma'mur. Seventy thousand angels go round it every day, never to return. Then he was brought near, and Allah revealed to His servant what He revealed. Fifty prayers were made obligatory.

Coming down, he met Musa, who sent him back to ask for less. Again and again he went back, until the prayers were five. "I am ashamed to ask my Lord again," he said. "I accept." Then a voice called: "I have decreed My obligation and lightened it for My servants." Whether he saw Allah with his eyes, the book notes, is not established from any of the Companions. The drawing near in Surat An-Najm [53:8] is Jibreel's.
sections.title: Through the Seven Heavens
list: Adam; the souls of the blessed on his right, the wretched on his left

body: Among the things he saw that night, according to the reports:
sections.title: What He Was Shown
list: offered both, he chose the milk, and was told he had chosen the natural way (fitrah); had he taken the wine, his people would have gone astray
the Nile and the Euphrates, and two hidden rivers of Paradise
the keeper of Hell, grim and unsmiling
bellies so great they could not rise
choosing rotten meat over good meat set before them

body: When he told of it, Quraish mocked and pressed him with questions. They asked him to describe the mosque in Jerusalem, a place he had never been to, and he described it exactly. He told them of their caravans on the road, of camels gone astray, and of water he had drunk from a covered vessel while its owners slept. It only drove them further from the truth.
They went to Abu Bakr, sure that this would turn him away. He said that he believed it. From that day he was called As-Siddiq, the one who confirms the truth.

The journey was "to show him of Our signs" [17:1], as Ibrahim was shown the kingdom of the heavens and the earth to be among the certain [6:75], and as Musa was shown "of Our greater signs" [20:23]. The book reads in it the passing of leadership to a new people, holding both mosques of Ibrahim's faith.
sections.title: As-Siddiq

quote.text: Yes, I believe it.
quote.who: Abu Bakr, as the book tells it

body: The next year twelve men came from Yathrib to meet him. Five were of the six who had believed the year before. Jabir bin 'Abdullah bin Ri'ab did not come. With them were seven more: five of the Khazraj and two of the Aws.

At Al-'Aqabah they pledged allegiance to him. 'Ubadah bin As-Samit reports its terms, in Al-Bukhari: whoever kept them would have his reward from Allah. Whoever broke one and was punished for it in this world, that would be his expiation. Whoever broke one and Allah concealed it, his matter was with Allah, to forgive or to punish.
sections.title: The First Pledge of 'Aqabah
sections.when: Hajj season, 12th year of prophethood · 621 CE
list: Not to bring a slander they had invented
Not to disobey him in what is good

body: With the twelve he sent Mus'ab bin 'Umair, the first envoy of Islam, to teach them the Qur'an and the religion. He stayed with As'ad bin Zurarah, and Islam spread from house to house and clan to clan.

One day they sat by a well in the quarter of Banu Zafar. Usaid bin Hudair, a chief of Banu 'Abdul-Ashhal, came at them with his spear, cursing. "Sit and listen," said Mus'ab. "If you like it, accept it. If not, we will stop." "That is fair," said Usaid. He planted his spear in the sand, listened, heard the Qur'an, and his face lit up before he said a word. He washed, bore witness and prayed.

Then he sent Sa'd bin Mu'adh, his clan's chief, to them, and Sa'd too believed. Sa'd went back and told his people he would not speak to them until they believed. By evening, every man and woman of 'Abdul-Ashhal was Muslim except one, Al-'Usairim. He held back until the day of Uhud, then believed, fought and was killed before he had made a single prostration. "He did little and was rewarded much," the Prophet ﷺ said.
Before the next pilgrimage, Mus'ab went back to Makkah with the news: Islam had reached every house of the Helpers but one.
sections.title: Mus'ab in Yathrib

body: The next season more than seventy Muslims of Yathrib came among their people's pilgrims. "How long will we leave him to be driven around the hills of Makkah?" they said to each other. They agreed to meet him secretly in the middle nights of the days of Tashriq, at the same place.

Ka'b bin Malik tells it. They brought 'Abdullah bin 'Amr bin Haram, one of their chiefs, into Islam on the way. A third of the night gone, they slipped from their camps one by one: seventy-three men and two women. The women were Nusaibah bint Ka'b, Umm 'Umarah, and Asma' bint 'Amr, Umm Mani'.

The Prophet ﷺ came with his uncle Al-'Abbas, still not a Muslim, who wanted to be there for his nephew. Al-'Abbas spoke first. His nephew was protected and honoured among his people, he said, yet he had chosen them. If they could keep their word and defend him, the burden was theirs. If they would hand him over once he had gone with them, they should leave him now. "We have heard you," they said. "Speak, Messenger of Allah, and take for yourself and your Lord what you wish."
sections.title: The Great Pledge of 'Aqabah
sections.when: Dhul-Hijjah, 13th year of prophethood · June 622 CE

quote.text: Speak, O Messenger of Allah, and take for yourself and your Lord whatever pledge you wish.
quote.who: The men of Yathrib

body: He recited the Qur'an, called them to Allah, and set out the pledge. Al-Bara' bin Ma'rur took his hand and swore they would protect him as they protected their women: they were men of war, sons of men of war.

Abul-Haitham bin At-Taihan asked one thing. They had ties with the Jews that they would cut. If Allah gave him victory, would he leave them and go back to his own people? He smiled. "No: your blood is my blood. In life and in death I am with you and you are with me. I will fight whom you fight and make peace with whom you make peace."
sections.title: What They Pledged
list: To hear and obey, in hardship and in ease
To spend, in plenty and in want
To command good and forbid evil
To stand for Allah, fearing no one's blame
To stand by him when he comes to them, and protect him as they protect themselves, their wives and their children

body: Before the pledge, Al-'Abbas bin 'Ubadah warned them. This meant war with all comers. If they feared for their wealth and their nobles, better to leave him now than be shamed later. "And what is ours if we keep it?" they asked. "Paradise," he said. "Stretch out your hand," they said. As'ad bin Zurarah gave a last warning, and they told him to stretch out his hand, for they would never go back on it. As'ad was the first to give his hand, then man after man. The two women pledged by word, for he never took the hand of a woman not related to him.
He asked them to name twelve leaders, answerable for their people as the disciples of 'Isa were for theirs: nine of the Khazraj and three of the Aws.
sections.title: Twelve Leaders

body: As they finished, a devil cried out from the hilltop that Muhammad and his followers had gathered for war. Al-'Abbas bin 'Ubadah said that, if he wished, they would put the people of Mina to the sword the next morning. "We have not been commanded to do that," the Prophet ﷺ said. "Go back to your camps."

The next day the chiefs of Quraish came to the camp of Yathrib to complain. The idolaters of Yathrib, who knew nothing of it, swore in good faith that it was untrue, and 'Abdullah bin Ubai said his people would do nothing without him. The Muslims kept silent. Later Quraish found out the truth, but the pilgrims had gone. They caught only Sa'd bin 'Ubadah and tortured him, until Al-Mut'im bin 'Adi and Al-Harith bin Harb, with whom he traded, set him free.
sections.title: Found Out

parts.title: Beyond Makkah
parts.blurb: Stoned at Ta'if, turned away by the tribes, taken by night to Jerusalem and through the heavens, and at last answered by the men of Yathrib.

body: After the Great Pledge, he gave the believers leave to go to Yathrib. To leave meant giving up home and wealth, and the road itself was not safe. Quraish did all they could to stop them.

The first to go, a year before the Great Pledge, was Abu Salamah. His wife's people kept her back, and their little son was snatched from her, his arm wrenched out of joint. For a year Umm Salamah sat weeping each day, until her people relented and gave her back her son. She set out alone on the five-hundred-kilometre road. At At-Tan'im, 'Uthman bin Talhah met her and led her all the way to Quba', where her husband was.
