Quraish told Suhaib Ar-Rumi he had come to them a pauper and grown rich among them, so he could not leave. He offered them all his wealth, and they let him go. "Suhaib has profited," the Prophet ﷺ said. Abu Jahl tricked 'Aiyash bin Abi Rabi'ah into coming home, telling him their mother had sworn never to comb her hair or seek shade until she saw him. On the way they tied him up and brought him back to Makkah. Within two months whole quarters of Makkah stood empty. Only the Prophet ﷺ, Abu Bakr, 'Ali and those held captive remained.

He had told them he had been shown the place of their emigration in a dream: a land of date palms between two mountains. Abu Bakr was ready to go, but the Prophet ﷺ told him to wait, for he hoped to be given leave himself. So Abu Bakr waited, and fed two camels on the leaves of the samur tree for four months.
sections.title: The Believers Leave
sections.when: After the Great Pledge, 13th – 14th year of prophethood
people: the first to emigrate, a year before the Great Pledge
a year apart from husband and son, then the road alone
bought his freedom to go with everything he owned
came to Madinah with twenty of the Companions
tricked back to Makkah and held there

body: Yathrib's fighting men were known throughout Arabia. The city lay across the trade road to Syria, and Makkah's trade along it was worth around a quarter of a million gold dinars a year. If Muhammad ﷺ reached it, Quraish were in danger. Their chiefs gathered in Dar An-Nadwah: Abu Jahl, Jubair bin Mut'im, 'Utbah, Shaibah, Abu Sufyan, An-Nadr bin Al-Harith, Umaiyah bin Khalaf, Hakim bin Hizam and others.

It is reported that Iblis came to the door in the shape of an old man from Najd, asking to sit in on their counsel, and they let him in. They talked a long time, and Abu Jahl's plan won the day. Each clan would give one strong young man. Together they would strike him at once, so that his blood would be spread among all the clans and Banu 'Abd Manaf could never avenge it, only take blood money. They all agreed, and went to carry it out.
sections.title: The Council of Quraish
sections.when: Thursday, 26 Safar, 14th year of prophethood · 12 September 622 CE
list: rejected; his words would win the Arabs over, and they would come back against Makkah
rejected; his followers would grow and set him free by force
Kill him, with a young man from every clan
agreed, so that his blood could not be avenged

body: Jibreel told him of the plot, and of Allah's leave to go. 'Aishah tells it. They were sitting in Abu Bakr's house at noon, the hottest hour, when someone said, "Here is the Messenger of Allah, his head covered," at an hour he had never come before. "May my father and mother be his ransom," said Abu Bakr. "Something important brings him at this hour."

He asked that everyone else leave. "There is only your own family here," said Abu Bakr. "I have been given leave to emigrate," he said. "Your company, Messenger of Allah?" asked Abu Bakr. "Yes," he said. Then they made their plans, and he went home to wait for night.
sections.title: At Abu Bakr's Door at Noon

quote.text: I have been given leave to emigrate.
quote.who: The Prophet ﷺ, reported by Al-Bukhari

body: Eleven men waited around his house through the night. Among them were Abu Jahl, Al-Hakam bin Abil-'As, 'Uqbah bin Abi Mu'ait, An-Nadr bin Al-Harith, Umaiyah bin Khalaf, Abu Lahab, Ubai bin Khalaf, and the brothers Nabih and Munbih bin Al-Hajjaj. Through a gap in the door they watched him lying in his bed, waiting for him to come out at dawn to pray. Abu Jahl walked among them, mocking his promises.

He told 'Ali to lie in his bed under his green cloak, assuring him no harm would come to him. Then he walked out between them, throwing a handful of dust over their heads as he recited: "And We have put a barrier before them and a barrier behind them, and covered them so that they do not see" [36:9]. He went to Abu Bakr's house, and before dawn they were gone.
In the morning the watchers found 'Ali rising from the bed. He said he did not know where he had gone.
sections.title: The Night of the Hijrah
sections.when: Night of 27 Safar, 14th year of prophethood · 12 – 13 September 622 CE

quote.text: They plotted, and Allah planned, and Allah is the best of planners.
quote.who: Al-Anfal 8:30

body: Knowing Quraish would search the road north to Yathrib, he took the road south, toward Yemen, which no one would expect. They walked about five miles to Mount Thawr, a rough, rocky mountain. His sandals were worn out, and it is said he walked on his toes to leave no trail. Abu Bakr carried him up to the cave.

Abu Bakr went in first to make sure it was safe. He cleaned it and stopped up its holes with strips torn from his own clothes. The Prophet ﷺ came in, laid his head in Abu Bakr's lap and slept. Something stung Abu Bakr's foot, and the pain made his tears fall on the Prophet's face. He woke, wiped his own saliva on the sting, and the pain went.

They stayed three nights: Friday, Saturday and Sunday. Each evening Abu Bakr's son 'Abdullah came with the news from Makkah and left before dawn to be seen among Quraish. Abu Bakr's shepherd, 'Amir bin Fuhairah, grazed his flock nearby and brought them milk at night.
sections.title: The Cave of Thawr

body: Quraish dragged 'Ali to the Ka'bah, beat him and held him, but he told them nothing. They went to Abu Bakr's daughter Asma', and Abu Jahl struck her so hard her earring broke. They guarded every road out of Makkah and offered a hundred camels for each of the two men. Riders and trackers combed the country.

They came to the very mouth of the cave. "Prophet of Allah," whispered Abu Bakr, "if one of them looks down at his feet, he will see us." He was afraid for him, not for himself: if they killed Abu Bakr, it was one man, but if they killed him, the whole nation was lost. The answer is the one the Qur'an keeps: "Do not grieve; Allah is with us" [9:40].
sections.title: A Hundred Camels

quote.text: What do you think, Abu Bakr, of two when Allah is their third?
quote.who: The Prophet ﷺ, reported by Al-Bukhari

body: After three nights, when the search had slackened, their guide came to the cave as agreed with two of Abu Bakr's camels. He was 'Abdullah bin Uraiqit, not a Muslim, but trusted. Abu Bakr offered the better camel, and the Prophet ﷺ took it only on condition that he pay for it. Asma' brought their food and tied it up with half of her waistband. From then on she was called "the one with the two waistbands".

With 'Amir bin Fuhairah they set out on little-used tracks near the coast. Abu Bakr tells how they rode all that night and the next day until noon. Then he found a rock with some shade, spread a skin for the Prophet ﷺ to sleep, and kept watch. A shepherd boy came by, and Abu Bakr had him milk a ewe, cleaning its udder first. He cooled the milk with water and waited for the Prophet ﷺ to wake. "Drink, Messenger of Allah," he said, and he drank until Abu Bakr was content.
When anyone asked who the man with him was, Abu Bakr said, "A man who guides me on the way." They took him to mean the road. He meant the way of goodness.
sections.title: The Road by the Sea

body: Suraqah bin Malik heard that riders had been seen by the shore. He told the others it must be someone else, then quietly took his spear, slipped out the back of his house and rode after them for the reward.

As he drew near, his horse stumbled and threw him. He drew his divining arrows: the answer was the one he disliked. He rode on anyway. He could hear the Prophet ﷺ reciting, never turning round, while Abu Bakr kept looking back. Then his horse's forelegs sank into the ground to the knees, and when it pulled them free, dust rose like smoke. He knew then that this man would prevail. He called out to them that they were safe, told them everything Quraish had planned, and offered them provisions, which they refused. "Keep us hidden," was all the Prophet ﷺ asked. At Suraqah's request, 'Amir bin Fuhairah wrote him a promise of safety on a piece of leather.
sections.title: Suraqah

quote.text: Do not grieve; Allah is with us.
quote.who: The Prophet ﷺ to Abu Bakr, as Suraqah came [9:40]

body: They came to two tents where a generous woman of Khuza'ah, Umm Ma'bad, sat at her door for any traveller who passed. It was a year of drought, and the flock was out at pasture. The only goat left was too weak and dry to go with it.

He asked her leave, passed his hand over its udder in Allah's name and prayed, and milk poured out. He gave her to drink first, then his companions, then drank himself. He milked again and left the vessel full for her.

Her husband came home with his thin goats and could not believe the milk. She described the blessed man who had passed, and her husband knew he was the one Quraish were hunting. Her description of him became one of the best-known in all the reports. Verses praising her guest were heard in Makkah from a voice no one could see. From them Asma' learned that they were headed for Madinah.
sections.title: Umm Ma'bad's Tent

body: On the way he met Buraidah bin Al-Husaib of Aslam with about eighty men, who became Muslims and prayed the night prayer behind him. "Which people are you from?" he asked. "Aslam." "Then we are safe," he said to Abu Bakr: the name means peace. "And which clan?" "Sahm." "Then your victory has come." He liked good omens without trusting in signs.

Near Al-'Arj, Aws bin Hajar of Aslam found them with a slow camel and gave them his own, sending a boy, Mas'ud, to see them safely into Madinah. And they met Az-Zubair with a caravan of Muslims returning from Syria, who gave them white clothes.
sections.title: Met on the Way

body: Since hearing he had left Makkah, the Muslims of Madinah had gone out each morning to the stony ground of the Harrah to wait, until the noon heat drove them home. One day, just after they had gone in, a Jew on the roof of a fort saw men in white coming out of the shimmering desert. "People of the Arabs," he shouted, "here is the one you have been waiting for!"

They rushed out, crying "Allahu akbar," and met him at the Harrah. Many of the Ansar had never seen him, and at first they greeted Abu Bakr, until the sun fell on the Prophet ﷺ and Abu Bakr stood to shade him with his cloak. Then they knew. He was fifty-three.

He stayed in Quba' with Kulthum bin Al-Hadm from Monday to Thursday, and built the mosque of Quba', the first mosque built on taqwa after his prophethood [9:108]. 'Ali stayed three days in Makkah to give back the things people had left in the Prophet's keeping, then followed him and caught up with him in Quba'.
sections.title: Quba'
sections.when: Monday, 8 Rabi' al-Awwal, 1 AH · 23 September 622 CE
sections.place: Quba', on the edge of Madinah

body: On Friday he rode on, sending for Banu An-Najjar, his mother's kin, to escort him. In the valley of Banu Salim bin 'Awf he led the Friday prayer with about a hundred men. Yathrib became Madinat Ar-Rasul, the City of the Messenger: Madinah.

Every clan he passed caught his camel's rein: "Stay with us, Messenger of Allah." "Let her go," he said each time, "she is under command." The girls of Madinah sang their welcome. The camel went on with a loose rein, knelt at the site where his mosque would stand, rose, walked a little, turned and came back to kneel in the same place. It was the quarter of Banu An-Najjar, as he had wished.

"Whose house is nearest?" he asked. "Mine, Messenger of Allah," said Abu Ayyub Al-Ansari. "Here is my house and here is my door." He stayed with Abu Ayyub. A few days later his family arrived: Sawdah, his daughters Fatimah and Umm Kulthum, Usamah bin Zaid and Umm Ayman, with Abu Bakr's household, 'Aishah among them. His daughter Zainab stayed behind with her husband Abul-'As until after Badr.
sections.title: Into Madinah

quote.text: Let her go: she is under command.
quote.who: The Prophet ﷺ, of his camel

body: Madinah was known then for its fever. Abu Bakr and Bilal both fell ill. In his fever Abu Bakr would recite that every man wakes among his family while death is nearer to him than his sandal strap. Bilal, when the fever left him, would cry out in verse for one more night in a valley of sweet grass near Makkah, one more drink at Majannah, one more sight of Makkah's hills.
'Aishah told the Prophet ﷺ, and he prayed for the city.
sections.title: The Fever of Madinah

quote.text: O Allah, make it healthy, bless its measures, and take its fever away to Al-Juhfah.
quote.who: The Prophet ﷺ, reported by Al-Bukhari

parts.title: The Hijrah
parts.blurb: The believers slip away to Yathrib; Quraish resolve to kill him; three nights in a cave, the road along the sea, and a city that comes out to meet him.

body: The ten years in Madinah fall into three stages. The first was the hardest: trouble and conflict inside the city, and wave after wave from outside meant to wipe the new faith out. The second was a truce with the leaders of Quraish, in which the Prophet ﷺ wrote to the kings beyond Arabia. In the third, people came into Islam in crowds, and delegations from every corner of Arabia arrived in Madinah to give him their pledge.

The Hijrah had not been only an escape from Makkah's torment. It was a move to a safe place where a new society could be built, and every Muslim able to help was bound to help build it, with the Messenger ﷺ as its leader in everything.
sections.title: Ten Years in Madinah
list: conflict within and attack from without; it ended with the Treaty of Al-Hudaibiyah, Dhul-Qa'dah 6 AH
a truce with Quraish, and letters to kings; it ended with the conquest of Makkah, Ramadan 8 AH
people entering Islam in crowds, and delegations from all Arabia; it ended with his death, Rabi' al-Awwal 11 AH

body: In Makkah the believers had shared one aim but had been scattered and powerless. In Madinah the whole of their life was in their own hands: trade and money, government, war and peace, what was lawful and what was not. Allah gave the laws, and the Prophet ﷺ explained them, put them into practice and trained people by them [62:2]. A society like that could not be built in a month or a year.

He had three peoples to deal with, each with its own problems. Among the believers, the Helpers had land and homes but carried the old feuds of the Aws and Khazraj, while the Emigrants arrived homeless and penniless, more of them every month, as Quraish's boycott squeezed the city's trade. Among those who had not believed, some soon did; others hated the new faith but dared not show it. And there were the Jews, who had settled in the Hijaz long before.
sections.title: Three Peoples in One City
list: the Helpers, settled but divided by old feuds; the Emigrants, homeless and growing in number
'Abdullah bin Ubai had been about to be crowned over both the Aws and the Khazraj; robbed of it, he professed Islam and led the hypocrites
Banu Qainuqa', allies of the Khazraj, and Banu An-Nadir and Banu Quraizah, allies of the Aws; they held much of the city's trade and lent at interest

body: Safiyah, the daughter of Huyai bin Akhtab, later a Mother of the Believers, remembered the day he reached Quba'. She was her father's and her uncle Abu Yasir's favourite child; whenever they came home they would make a fuss of her above all the others. That day they went to see the Prophet ﷺ and came back at sunset, dragging their feet. She ran to them smiling, and neither of them even turned to her. She heard her uncle ask her father whether it was really he. It was, he said, by Allah. Had he truly recognised him? Yes, and his heart burned with enmity towards him.

'Abdullah bin Salam, the most learned of their rabbis, came the first day with questions to test whether he was a Prophet, heard the answers and became a Muslim. He knew what his people would say, so the Prophet ﷺ called some of them and asked about him first. They praised his learning and his standing. When they learned he had become a Muslim, they called him the worst of them all.
sections.title: "Is It Really He?"

quote.text: My heart is burning with enmity towards him.
quote.who: Abu Yasir bin Akhtab, as his niece Safiyah heard it

body: His first work was a mosque, on the very spot where his camel had knelt. The ground belonged to two orphan boys, and it was bought from them. It held some old graves of idolaters, which were dug up, and palm trees, which were cut down; the ground was cleared and levelled. He carried the mud bricks and stones himself with the others, and as they worked they sang that there is no life but the life of the Hereafter, and asked Allah to forgive the Helpers and the Emigrants.

Beside it were built rooms for his family, of stone and mud brick roofed with palm leaves. A place was kept at the back for believers who had no home and no family. The call to prayer began in these days, after the dream of 'Abdullah bin Zaid. The mosque was never only a place of prayer. It was a school where Islam was taught, a hall where old enemies sat down together, and the seat from which every affair of the Muslims was run.
sections.title: The Mosque
list: mud brick and stone, two beams holding up its roof
about a hundred yards a side, with doors on three sides
for the poor who had neither family nor home

body: Next he made the believers brothers. In the house of Anas bin Malik, ninety men gathered, half of them Emigrants and half Helpers, and he paired them, each Emigrant with a Helper. It was not a word but a bond binding blood and wealth: at first a man inherited from his brother in faith, until the ayah came at the time of Badr that kin by blood are closer in inheritance [8:75].

Sa'd bin Ar-Rabi' said to the man he was paired with, 'Abdur-Rahman bin 'Awf, "I am the richest of the Helpers. Half my wealth is yours, and I have two wives; choose one, I will divorce her, and when her waiting is done you can marry her." 'Abdur-Rahman prayed for blessings on him, and asked only to be shown the way to the market. He traded, prospered, and was soon married.

The Helpers asked the Prophet ﷺ to divide their palm groves between them and their brothers. He would not lay that on them; instead the Emigrants worked the groves with them, and the harvest was shared. They took only what they needed to live.
sections.title: Brothers
sections.place: The house of Anas bin Malik, Madinah

quote.text: Show me the way to the market.
quote.who: 'Abdur-Rahman bin 'Awf, offered half of his brother's wealth

body: He then wrote a charter between the Emigrants, the Helpers and those who joined them, so that nothing of the old tribal law could creep back. The believers were one nation, before all other people. The clans kept their old duties of paying blood money and ransoming their own, but under a new rule: no believer would be left alone under a debt, and none would side with a wrongdoer, even his own son.

With the Jews of Madinah he made a treaty of the same kind, which left them free in their religion and their wealth. He meant no exile, no seizing of land, no war. Madinah and its villages became one state, its capital Madinah, its head the Prophet ﷺ.
sections.title: The Charter of Madinah
list: the believers are one community, apart from all others
No one left under a debt
they pay blood money and ransom their captives together
every believer's hand is against the one who sows strife, even his own son
the protection of Allah is one; the humblest believer may give it
whoever shelters or helps one bears Allah's curse
one community with the believers, each with its own religion; each helps the other if attacked
those under it boycott Quraish and give them no help
whatever they differ in goes to Allah and to Muhammad ﷺ

body: On these foundations he built people. He taught them to purify their souls, to keep good manners and good relations, to worship, and above all to obey Allah and His Messenger. He would remind them of the reward of each deed and tie what he asked of them to the Revelation.

'Abdullah bin Salam said that when he first saw the Prophet's face he knew it was not the face of a liar, and the first words he heard from him were these: spread the greeting of peace, feed people, keep the ties of kinship, and pray at night while others sleep, and you will enter Paradise in peace. Ibn Mas'ud said of the Companions raised this way that they were the best of this nation, the purest in heart, the deepest in knowledge and the least given to show.
sections.title: What He Taught Them
list: Feed people, and greet those you know and those you do not
None of you truly believes until he loves for his brother what he loves for himself
The Muslim is the one from whose tongue and hand the Muslims are safe
He will not enter Paradise whose neighbour is not safe from his harm
The believers in their love for each other are like one body
when one part aches, the whole body feels it
Be merciful to those on earth, and the One in the heaven will be merciful to you
Charity puts out sin as water puts out fire
Guard yourselves from the Fire even with half a date; and if you cannot, with a good word

body: Quraish kept watch over the Muslims left in Makkah and tormented them. To 'Abdullah bin Ubai and the idolaters of Madinah they sent an ultimatum: fight Muhammad or drive him out, or they would come in force, kill their fighting men and take their women. Ibn Ubai's men gathered to fight. The Prophet ﷺ went to them and asked if they would really fight their own sons and brothers, and they broke up. Ibn Ubai went along outwardly, and went on plotting.

Sa'd bin Mu'adh went to Makkah for 'Umrah and stayed with Umaiyah bin Khalaf, who took him round the Ka'bah at noon when it was empty. Abu Jahl found them and told Sa'd that had he not been under Umaiyah's protection he would not have gone home alive. Sa'd answered that if Abu Jahl stopped him from this, he would stop Abu Jahl from something dearer to him: his road through Madinah.

The danger was real. Guards stood watch around the Prophet's house. One night he wished aloud for a righteous man to keep watch over him, and there was a clatter of weapons outside: it was Sa'd bin Abi Waqqas, come to guard him. So it went on until the ayah came that Allah would protect him from the people [5:67], and he put his head out and sent his guards home.
sections.title: Quraish Write to Ibn Ubai

quote.text: O people, go away, for Allah has protected me.
quote.who: The Prophet ﷺ, when the ayah came

body: In Makkah the believers had been told to be patient. Now, in Madinah, with Quraish set on destroying them, Allah gave them leave to fight [22:39-40]: leave for those who were fought against, because they had been wronged. It came with its purpose: those who, if given power in the land, establish prayer, give zakah, enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong [22:41]. That it came after the Hijrah is certain; its exact date is not.

The wisest course was to take control of the trade road from Makkah to Syria, which ran close to Madinah. There were two ways to do it. One was treaties with the tribes along the road and between it and Madinah; the charter and the pacts with the neighbouring tribes had begun that. The other was to send armed patrols along the road, to show the Jews, the Bedouin and Quraish that the believers were no longer afraid, and that Quraish's trade would not pass in peace while they persecuted the believers left behind in Makkah.
sections.title: Leave to Fight
sections.when: After the Hijrah, its date not certain

quote.text: Permission is given to those who are fought against, because they have been wronged; and Allah is able to give them victory.
quote.who: Al-Hajj 22:39

body: Eight such marches came before Badr, four sent out and four led by the Prophet ﷺ himself. Their flags were white. In the first seven no one was killed and nothing was plundered; the only raid on property was Kurz bin Jabir Al-Fihri's, on Madinah's pastures. Quraish learned that the Muslims now watched three hundred miles of their road.

On the march to Waddan he made a pact with Banu Damrah: they were safe in their lives and wealth, and would help him when he called on them. On the march to Dhul-'Ushairah he made one with Banu Mudlij. It was there that he had set out to catch the caravan returning from Syria, the caravan that would lead to Badr.
sections.title: The First Patrols
sections.place: The road between Makkah and Syria
list: Hamzah with thirty Emigrants met Abu Jahl's caravan of three hundred; Majdi bin 'Amr, friend to both sides, kept them apart; the first flag, carried by Abu Marthad Kannaz
'Ubaidah bin Al-Harith with sixty riders met Abu Sufyan with two hundred; a few arrows flew; Al-Miqdad and 'Utbah bin Ghazwan crossed over from Quraish to the Muslims
Sa'd bin Abi Waqqas with twenty riders, five days out; the caravan had passed the day before
the first he led himself, seventy men, fifteen days; a pact with Banu Damrah
two hundred men after Umaiyah bin Khalaf's caravan of 2,500 camels; it had gone
after Kurz bin Jabir, who had raided Madinah's pastures; he escaped; it was called the first Badr
up to two hundred men on thirty camels, turn by turn; the Syria caravan had passed days before; a pact with Banu Mudlij

body: He sent 'Abdullah bin Jahsh with twelve Emigrants and a sealed letter, not to be opened for two days. When he opened it, it told him to go on to Nakhlah, between Makkah and Ta'if, watch for a caravan of Quraish and bring back news. He read it to his men, and every one of them went on with him.

A caravan came by with raisins, food and other goods, 'Amr bin Al-Hadrami among its men. It was Rajab, a sacred month. They argued among themselves, and decided to attack. 'Amr bin Al-Hadrami was killed by an arrow, two men were taken and one escaped. They brought back the caravan and set aside a fifth of it.

The Prophet ﷺ was displeased that they had fought in the sacred month, and touched neither the goods nor the captives. Quraish made the most of it: Muhammad had broken the sacred months. Then the ayah came [2:217]: fighting in it is grave, but graver still with Allah is to bar people from His way, to disbelieve in Him, to keep them from the Sacred Mosque and drive out its people, and persecution is worse than killing. The two captives were later freed and blood money paid for the man killed.
sections.title: The Letter Opened After Two Days
facts: 'Abdullah bin Jahsh and twelve Emigrants, six camels
a letter, to be read after two days on the road

body: In Sha'ban of the second year the command to fight came plainly [2:190-193]: fight in Allah's way those who fight you, and do not transgress. More ayahs followed teaching them how to fight and how to treat captives [47:4-7], and rebuking the hypocrites who looked at him like a man fainting at death when fighting was mentioned [47:20].

In the same month came the command to turn the qiblah from Jerusalem to the Sacred Mosque in Makkah [2:144]. It sifted the ranks: hypocrites, and the weak of faith among the Jews and others, showed what they were, and the Muslims were rid of them. And it pointed to a task ahead. The believers' qiblah could not be left in the hands of idolaters for ever.
sections.title: Facing the Ka'bah

quote.text: So turn your face towards the Sacred Mosque; and wherever you are, turn your faces towards it.
quote.who: Al-Baqarah 2:144

parts.title: A New Society
parts.blurb: A mosque of palm trunks, brothers who shared their wealth, a charter for the whole city, and the first patrols on the road to Syria.

body: The caravan he had missed at Dhul-'Ushairah was on its way home from Syria. He sent Talhah bin 'Ubaidullah and Sa'id bin Zaid north to watch for it; at Al-Hawra' they saw Abu Sufyan pass, and hurried back. It carried fifty thousand gold dinars and was guarded by about forty men: a blow at it would shake Makkah's whole standing.

He urged the Muslims to go out and win back something of what they had been made to leave in Makkah, but he bound no one: whoever wished could stay. It seemed a small affair. So they went out ill-equipped: two horses, seventy camels ridden in turns by two or three men each. He himself shared a camel with 'Ali and Marthad bin Abi Marthad.
sections.title: The Caravan from Syria
facts: between 300 and 317, about 82 to 86 Emigrants, 61 of the Aws, 170 of the Khazraj
the Emigrants' with 'Ali, the Helpers' with Sa'd bin Mu'adh
Az-Zubair on the right, Al-Miqdad on the left, Qais bin Abi Sa'sa'ah at the rear
left with Ibn Umm Maktum, then Abu Lubabah

body: Abu Sufyan travelled on edge, asking after Muhammad's movements at every stop. When his scouts told him the Muslims were waiting for him, he hired Damdam bin 'Amr Al-Ghifari to ride to Makkah for help. Damdam came into Makkah like a madman. He stood before the Ka'bah, cut off his camel's nose and ears, turned its saddle upside down, tore his shirt front and back, and screamed.

Makkah rose at once, its pride still stung by Nakhlah. Every man of standing went or sent someone in his place; only Abu Lahab stayed, sending a man who owed him money. Every clan of Quraish joined but Banu 'Adi. Soon thirteen hundred men were marching, a hundred of them on horses and six hundred in mail, slaughtering nine or ten camels a day to feed themselves.

They feared that Banu Bakr, their old enemies, would fall on Makkah behind them. Then Iblis came to them in the form of Suraqah bin Malik, a chief of Kinanah, and promised that no harm would reach them from behind.
sections.title: "Your Merchandise!"

quote.text: O Quraish! Your merchandise! It is with Abu Sufyan, and Muhammad and his companions are after it. Help! Help!
quote.who: Damdam bin 'Amr Al-Ghifari, before the Ka'bah

body: They marched north boastfully, to be seen of men [8:47], past 'Usfan and Qudaid to Al-Juhfah. There another message reached them from Abu Sufyan: the caravan was safe, go home. He had turned off the main road towards the sea and slipped past.

Many wanted to turn back. Abu Jahl would not have it. They would go on to Badr, he said, and stay three nights there feasting, so that the Muslims would learn their lesson and the Arabs would know Quraish still ruled the land. Al-Akhnas bin Shuraiq took Banu Zahrah home anyway, and ever after they obeyed him in everything. Banu Hashim wanted to leave too, but Abu Jahl's threats kept them. A thousand men went on, and camped behind a dune at the far side of the valley of Badr.
The Prophet ﷺ had marched out on the main road towards Makkah, then turned left for Badr. At As-Safra' he sent two men of Juhainah ahead for news of the caravan. What came back was news of an army.
sections.title: The Caravan Slips Away

body: Now the choice was hard. If they turned away, Quraish could march on to Madinah itself. Some of the believers were afraid, as if they were being driven to their death with their eyes open [8:5-6]. He told them how things stood and asked their counsel. Abu Bakr spoke well, and 'Umar after him.

Then Al-Miqdad bin 'Amr stood: they would not say, as the Children of Israel said to Musa, "Go, you and your Lord, and fight; we will sit here" [5:24]. They would say, "Go, you and your Lord, and fight, and we will fight with you." If he led them as far as Birk Al-Ghimad, they would fight beside him until he reached it.

He thanked him and prayed for him, and asked again, "Advise me, people." The three who had spoken were Emigrants; he meant the Helpers, the greater part of the army, whose pledge at Al-'Aqabah bound them only to defend him in their own city. Sa'd bin Mu'adh understood. "It seems you mean us." "Yes." Then Sa'd answered for them all.
"Go on, and be glad," he told them. "Allah has promised me one of the two parties. By Allah, it is as if I can see the places where they will fall."
sections.title: "Advise Me"

quote.text: If you took us into this sea and plunged into it, we would plunge in with you; not one man of us would stay behind. Lead us on, with the blessing of Allah.
quote.who: Sa'd bin Mu'adh, for the Helpers

body: He rode out with Abu Bakr to scout, and from an old Bedouin they had out of him, without giving themselves away, where Quraish were camped. That evening he sent 'Ali, Az-Zubair and Sa'd bin Abi Waqqas to the wells of Badr. They caught two boys drawing water for Quraish and brought them back.

The boys said they were Quraish's water carriers. Some of the men wanted them to belong to the caravan, and beat them; so they said they were Abu Sufyan's, and were let alone. The Prophet ﷺ, who had been praying, finished and was angry. He spoke with them a little, and learned from them how many Quraish were, where they were camped, and which of their chiefs had come. "Here is Makkah," he told his men, "sending you the dearest of its lives."
sections.title: The Water Carriers

quote.text: When they told you the truth you beat them, and when they lied you let them be. By Allah, they told the truth: they are Quraish's.
quote.who: The Prophet ﷺ

body: That night it rained on both camps. For Quraish it was a hindrance that held them back. For the Muslims it was a blessing that washed them, firmed the ground beneath their feet and steadied their hearts [8:11].

They moved up and stopped at the nearest well of Badr. Al-Hubab bin Al-Mundhir asked whether Allah had put him in this place, so that they could not move from it, or whether it was a matter of war and planning. War and planning, he said. Then this was no place to stop, said Al-Hubab: let them camp at the well nearest the enemy, build a cistern there, and stop up the wells behind it, so that they would have water and Quraish would have none. He agreed, and it was done in the night.

Sa'd bin Mu'adh asked that a shelter be built for him, to command the army from: if Allah gave them victory, all was well; if not, he could go back to the many in Madinah who loved him and would have come had they known. Sa'd stood guard over it with a band of the Helpers. The Prophet ﷺ walked over the ground, pointing: here so-and-so will be tomorrow, if Allah wills, and here so-and-so. Then he spent the night in prayer beside a tree, while the army slept the deep sleep Allah sent over them as a security from Him.
sections.title: Rain in the Night
sections.when: The night before Friday, 17 Ramadan 2 AH
list: a hindrance to Quraish, a mercy to the Muslims
taken on Al-Hubab bin Al-Mundhir's advice
proposed by Sa'd bin Mu'adh, guarded by the Helpers
sent by Allah over the Muslims, as a security from Him

body: Quraish took their place on the far side of the valley. A few of them came down to draw water at the Muslims' wells; all were shot down but Hakim bin Hizam, who would one day be a devoted Muslim. 'Umair bin Wahb rode round the Muslim camp and came back: about three hundred men, no reinforcements behind them and no ambush, men who would not surrender and would take many with them before they fell. That, and the ties of kin between the two sides, took the heart out of some. 'Utbah bin Rabi'ah spoke for turning back. Abu Jahl answered with a cry for revenge for the man killed at Nakhlah, and carried the rest with him.

The Prophet ﷺ told them not to begin until he gave the word, to spend their arrows sparingly, and not to draw swords until the enemy was close. Abu Jahl prayed that whichever side cut the ties of kin and brought what was not known be destroyed that day. The answer had already come [8:19].

The first of Quraish to come forward was Al-Aswad bin 'Abdul-Asad Al-Makhzumi, a hot-tempered man who swore he would drink from the Muslims' cistern or destroy it or die for it. Hamzah met him, cut through his leg, and finished him at the cistern's edge.
sections.title: Face to Face

quote.text: O Allah, here are Quraish, come in their pride and arrogance, defying You and belying Your Messenger. O Allah, Your help, which You promised me.
quote.who: The Prophet ﷺ, as the armies came in sight

body: 'Utbah bin Rabi'ah stepped out between his brother Shaibah and his son Al-Walid and called for single combat. Three young men of the Helpers went out: 'Awf and Mu'awwidh, the sons of Al-Harith, and 'Abdullah bin Rawahah. Quraish wanted none of them: they wanted their own cousins. So the Prophet ﷺ called on 'Ubaidah bin Al-Harith, on his uncle Hamzah and on his cousin 'Ali.

It was quickly over. Hamzah killed Shaibah, and 'Ali killed Al-Walid. 'Ubaidah was badly wounded, and before he fell Hamzah turned on 'Utbah and killed him. 'Ali and Hamzah carried 'Ubaidah back, his leg cut off. He died four or five days later. 'Ali used to swear that the ayah about the two opposing parties who disputed over their Lord [22:19] was revealed about them.
sections.title: The Duels
people: fought 'Utbah bin Rabi'ah; his leg was cut off, and he died four or five days later
the chief who had spoken for turning back; killed by Hamzah

body: The duels had cost Quraish some of their best, and in fury they came on all together. The Muslims held their ground as he had told them, and the charge broke on them.

In the shelter he turned to the qiblah, raised his hands and called on his Lord, again and again, until his cloak slipped from his shoulders. Abu Bakr picked it up and put it back on his shoulders. "Enough, Prophet of Allah. You have pleaded with your Lord enough. He will keep what He promised you."

The answer came: Allah inspired the angels that He was with them, so let them make the believers firm, and He would cast terror into the hearts of the disbelievers [8:12]; He would help them with a thousand angels, rank upon rank [8:9].
sections.title: His Cloak Fell

quote.text: O Allah, if this band perishes today, You will not be worshipped.
quote.who: The Prophet ﷺ, in the shelter at Badr

body: He dozed a moment, then raised his head. "Good news, Abu Bakr. Allah's help has come. There is Jibreel on his horse, in the thick of the dust." He came out of the shelter reciting that the host would be routed and turn their backs [54:45], took a handful of pebbles at Jibreel's word, threw it towards Quraish and said, "Confusion seize their faces!" A storm of dust blew into their eyes. You did not throw when you threw, but Allah threw [8:17].

Only now did he give the order to charge, telling them of a Paradise as wide as the heavens and the earth [3:133]. A boy of sixteen named 'Umair was eating some dates. "These are holding me back from Paradise," he cried, threw them away, ran into the fighting and was killed.

The Companions told of what they saw. A man chasing an idolater heard a whip crack above him and a voice cry, "Forward, Haizum!", and saw the man fall dead before him; "That was help from the third heaven," the Prophet ﷺ told him. Al-'Abbas, brought in a prisoner by a man of the Helpers, said it was not this man who had taken him, but a bald rider with the most handsome face, on a piebald horse, whom he could not see among them. "Be quiet," the Prophet ﷺ told the Helper. "Allah strengthened you with a noble angel."
sections.title: Jibreel in the Dust

quote.text: Good news, Abu Bakr: Allah's help has come. There is Jibreel on his horse, in the thick of the dust.
quote.who: The Prophet ﷺ

body: Iblis, in Suraqah's form, saw the angels and fled, saying he saw what they did not see [8:48]; though Quraish begged him to stay, he ran and threw himself into the sea. Quraish's ranks began to break. Retreat became flight; they threw away their armour and left their camp and their camels, while the Muslims pursued, killing and taking captives.

Abu Jahl stood his ground, begging them by Al-Lat and Al-'Uzza to hold, until only a knot of men stood round him. 'Abdur-Rahman bin 'Awf was in the ranks between two boys of the Helpers. One whispered to him to show him Abu Jahl: he wanted to fight him until one of them was dead. The other whispered the same. 'Abdur-Rahman could hardly believe it. He pointed him out, and they ran at him together and struck him down. Each came back claiming to have killed him. The Prophet ﷺ looked at their swords. "You both killed him."

When it was over, 'Abdullah bin Mas'ud found him with his last breath in him, and put his foot on his neck: had Allah disgraced him now? "Disgraced? I am only a man killed by his own people. Tell me, who won?" "Allah and His Messenger." "You have climbed a hard road, little shepherd," said Abu Jahl, for Ibn Mas'ud had once herded the flocks of Makkah's nobles. Ibn Mas'ud brought his head to the Prophet ﷺ, who praised Allah, Who had kept His promise, helped His servant and routed the parties alone.
sections.title: The Pharaoh of This Nation

quote.text: This is the Pharaoh of this nation.
quote.who: The Prophet ﷺ, over Abu Jahl's body

people: one of the two boys; Abu Jahl's spoils were given to him
the other; killed later the same day

body: Badr set kin against kin, and the Companions' hearts were laid bare. Before the battle he had told them to spare some men of Banu Hashim and others who had come out unwillingly, among them his uncle Al-'Abbas and Abul-Bukhtari bin Hisham, who had never harmed him in Makkah and had worked to end the boycott.

Abu Hudhaifah bin 'Utbah cried out: they were to kill their fathers, sons and brothers, and spare Al-'Abbas? If he met him he would put his sword in him. The Prophet ﷺ turned to 'Umar: "Should the face of the Messenger's uncle be struck with a sword?" Abu Hudhaifah never stopped fearing what he had said, until he was killed a martyr at Al-Yamamah.

When the dead of Quraish were dragged to the well, the Prophet ﷺ saw Abu Hudhaifah's face fall as his father 'Utbah was carried past. He had never doubted his father deserved his end, Abu Hudhaifah said; he had only hoped he would be guided. The Prophet ﷺ prayed for him and spoke kindly to him.
sections.title: Fathers, Sons and Brothers
list: offered his life, he would not take it unless his companion was spared too, and fought until he was killed

'Abdur-Rahman bin 'Awf, his old friend, was leading him and his son away as captives when Bilal saw the man who had tortured him, and swore he would not escape; the Muslims closed in and killed them both
killed his own maternal uncle, Al-'As bin Hisham
called to his son 'Abdur-Rahman, still among Quraish, "Where is my wealth, you wretch?"
saw a Helper tying up his brother Abu 'Aziz and told him to tie him tight, for their mother was rich; "This is how you treat your brother?" "He is my brother, not you."
his sword broke, and the Prophet ﷺ gave him a stick of wood which became in his hand a long, bright sword; he fought with it for years after
when captives were taken, he said he would sooner have seen the idolaters killed in this first battle than spared

body: Fourteen Muslims were killed at Badr, six Emigrants and eight Helpers. Of Quraish seventy were killed and seventy taken captive, and among the dead lay many of their leaders and the bitterest of his enemies, Abu Jahl first among them.

He had the bodies of twenty-four of the leaders of Quraish thrown into an old well. On the third day he went and stood at its edge and called them by their names and their fathers' names. You were an evil kin to your Prophet, he said: you called me a liar when others believed me, you abandoned me when others helped me, you drove me out when others took me in. Would it not have been better had you obeyed Allah and His Messenger? We have found what our Lord promised us to be true; have you found what your Lord promised you to be true?
"Messenger of Allah," said 'Umar, "why speak to bodies without souls?"
sections.title: Speaking to the Well

quote.text: By Him in Whose hand is Muhammad's soul, you do not hear what I say any better than they do.
quote.who: The Prophet ﷺ, at the well of Badr

body: Quraish fled home in scattered groups, too ashamed to face their people. The first to reach Makkah was Al-Haisuman bin 'Abdullah Al-Khuza'i, naming the dead chief by chief; at first they thought he had gone mad.

Abu Lahab heard the whole story from Abu Sufyan bin Al-Harith, who told him of the angels' part in it. Abu Lahab flew into a rage and fell to beating Abu Rafi', a Muslim, who was there. Umm Al-Fadl, a Muslim woman, took a stick and split his head open. Seven days later he died of a foul ulcer; his sons left him three days unburied for fear of it, then took him to a pit and threw stones and earth over him from a distance. In Makkah there was hardly a house without its dead or its captive, and Quraish forbade weeping aloud, so that the Muslims would not rejoice to hear it.

To Madinah he sent 'Abdullah bin Rawahah and Zaid bin Harithah with the good news. The Jews and hypocrites had spread word that he was dead, for Zaid was riding his camel Al-Qaswa'. The news reached the city as they finished burying Ruqaiyah, his daughter. 'Uthman, her husband, had stayed behind at the Prophet's word to nurse her.
sections.title: The News Comes Home
list: wailing forbidden, so the Muslims would not hear it
struck down by Umm Al-Fadl; dead in seven days
rumours of his death, then 'Abdullah bin Rawahah and Zaid with the truth
buried the day the news came; 'Uthman had stayed to nurse her

body: The spoils caused the first quarrel. Those who had gathered them, those who had chased the enemy and those who had guarded the Prophet ﷺ each claimed them, for no rule had yet been given. He held them back until the ayah came: the spoils belong to Allah and the Messenger, so fear Allah and set things right between you [8:1]. On the way home he divided them equally, after the fifth. At As-Safra' he had An-Nadr bin Al-Harith put to death, and at 'Irq Az-Zabyah 'Uqbah bin Abi Mu'ait, the man who had laid an animal's entrails on him as he prayed. "And who will look after my children?" 'Uqbah asked. "The Fire."

At Ar-Rawha' the people of Madinah came out to meet him, and many there became Muslims after it. He told them to treat the captives well, and they gave them their bread and ate the dates themselves. He asked Abu Bakr and 'Umar about them. Abu Bakr said to take ransom: they were kin, the money would strengthen the Muslims, and Allah might guide them. 'Umar said to kill their leaders. He took Abu Bakr's advice. The next day 'Umar found the two of them weeping: an ayah had come rebuking them for taking ransom before the enemy was crushed in the land [8:67-68]; but Allah had already allowed ransom [47:4], so no punishment came.
sections.title: The Spoils and the Captives
list: from a thousand to four thousand dirhams, by what each man could pay
a captive who could not pay, but could read and write, would teach ten children of Madinah, and go free
some poor men were released for nothing
sent her necklace for her husband Abul-'As; they gave it back and freed him, on condition he let her come to Madinah, and he did
'Umar wanted his front teeth pulled so he could not speak against Islam; the Prophet ﷺ refused
held in Makkah, exchanged for Abu Sufyan's son 'Amr

body: Surat Al-Anfal came down about Badr, a commentary on the battle: on the help Allah sent, on the faults still left in the believers' hearts, on what Allah wanted the believers to be in war and in peace, unlike the Arabs of the Ignorance.

The fast of Ramadan had been made obligatory that same year, and zakat to ease the poverty of the Emigrants. Days after the victory came the first 'Eid al-Fitr. The Muslims went out of their houses praising Allah aloud, glorifying Him for His favour and the help He had sent them.
sections.title: The First 'Eid

quote.text: Remember when you were few and weak in the land, afraid that people would snatch you away; but He sheltered you, strengthened you with His help and provided you with good things, so that you might be grateful.
quote.who: Al-Anfal 8:26

parts.title: Badr
parts.blurb: A caravan that got away, an army that would not turn back, a night of rain, and the Day of the Criterion, when three hundred met a thousand.

body: Badr was a victory all Arabia heard of, and it made the new faith four kinds of enemy. Quraish burned for revenge. The Jews of Madinah saw every Muslim victory as a blow to themselves [5:82]. The hypocrites, led by 'Abdullah bin Ubai, raged in secret. And the Bedouin around Madinah, who lived by raiding, feared a strong state would put an end to their raids.

The first news after Badr was that Banu Sulaim were gathering men to attack. The Prophet ﷺ struck first, at their own watering place, Al-Kudr. They fled before he arrived. He stayed three days, and the Muslims came home with five hundred camels, two for each man after the fifth was set aside. It was a week after Badr.
sections.title: Enemies on Every Side
list: open calls for revenge, and every resource gathered to silence Islam
Islam on their tongues, plots in their hearts
indifferent to belief, afraid for their raiding

body: In Makkah, 'Umair bin Wahb sat alone with Safwan bin Umaiyah, mourning the dead of Badr. 'Umair's son was a captive in Madinah. Were it not for his debts and his family, he said, he would go and kill Muhammad. Safwan took his debts and his family on himself, and asked him to keep it secret. 'Umair dipped his sword in poison and rode to Madinah.

'Umar saw him at the door of the mosque, knew he meant harm, and brought him in by his sword belt. 'Umair greeted the Prophet ﷺ in the old way of the Ignorance; Allah had given them a better greeting, he was told, the greeting of the people of Paradise: peace. Why had he come? To see that his captive son was treated well. And the sword? What good had swords done them? Then the Prophet ﷺ told him what had passed between him and Safwan when they sat alone. 'Umair stood amazed and bore witness that he was the Messenger of Allah, praising Allah for guiding him.

The Prophet ﷺ told his Companions to teach him the faith and the Qur'an, and to free his son. In Makkah, Safwan waited daily for news that would bury the shame of Badr. What came was word that 'Umair was a Muslim. 'Umair went back to Makkah and called people to Islam, and many believed through him.
sections.title: A Poisoned Sword
sections.place: Makkah and the mosque in Madinah

quote.text: Teach your brother his religion and the Qur'an, and free his captive for him.
quote.who: The Prophet ﷺ, of 'Umair bin Wahb

body: The Muslims kept every word of the treaty with the Jews. Before Badr, an old man named Shas bin Qais, seeing the Aws and Khazraj sitting together as friends, sent a youth to sit among them and recite the poems of the War of Bu'ath, until the old hostility flared up between them. The Prophet ﷺ came with some Emigrants. Would they go back to the ways of the Ignorance, he asked them, while he was still among them, after Allah had joined their hearts? They saw it was a trick of their enemies, embraced each other and went home.

After Badr, Banu Qainuqa', goldsmiths and smiths with seven hundred fighting men, the boldest of the Jews of Arabia, were the first to break the treaty. He gathered them in their market and urged them to accept Islam before what befell Quraish befell them. They answered that he had only beaten a people who knew nothing of war; if he fought them, he would learn what men were [3:12-13]. He held back.

Then an Arab woman sat at a goldsmith's in their market, and the goldsmith secretly fastened the hem of her garment, so that when she stood she was uncovered, and they laughed. A Muslim killed the goldsmith; the Jews killed the Muslim. On 15 Shawwal he besieged their forts for fifteen days, Hamzah carrying the standard, until they surrendered to his judgment. 'Abdullah bin Ubai, their old ally, pleaded for them. He spared their lives. They gave up their wealth and weapons and were sent out of Arabia to Syria.
sections.title: The Market of Banu Qainuqa'
sections.place: The quarter of Banu Qainuqa', Madinah

quote.text: Would you go back to the ways of the Ignorance while I am among you, after Allah has guided you to Islam and joined your hearts?
quote.who: The Prophet ﷺ, to the Aws and Khazraj

body: Abu Sufyan swore after Badr that he would not wash until he had his revenge. He came with two hundred men, but dared not attack by day. He slipped into Madinah by night and went to the Jews: Huyai bin Akhtab would not open his door, but Sallam bin Mishkam, a chief of Banu An-Nadir, took him in, fed him and told him all he knew. Late that night his men raided Al-'Uraid on the edge of Madinah, burned some palms and killed two Muslims, then ran. The Prophet ﷺ chased them; to lighten their camels they threw away their sacks of sawiq, barley meal, and the Muslims picked them up. So it was called the raid of the barley meal.
sections.title: Raids and Marches
list: Abu Sufyan's night raid on Al-'Uraid; he escaped, dropping his provisions

Banu Tha'labah and Banu Muharib gathered to raid Madinah; he came with four hundred and fifty men, his largest march before Uhud, and they fled to the mountains; he stayed the whole of Safar, so the Bedouin would know the Muslims' strength
three hundred men to Buhran in the region of Al-Furu'; no fighting

body: Ka'b bin Al-Ashraf, a poet, rich and handsome, of Tai' by his father and Banu An-Nadir by his mother, hated Islam more than any of the Jews. When the news of Badr came he swore that if it were true, death was better than life. When it was confirmed he wrote verses against the Prophet ﷺ and in praise of Quraish, and rode to Makkah to stir them to revenge. When Abu Sufyan asked him whose religion was better guided, theirs or Muhammad's, he said theirs [4:51]. Back in Madinah he made obscene verses about the Muslim women.

"Who will deal with Ka'b bin Al-Ashraf?" the Prophet ﷺ asked. "He has spoken evil of Allah and His Messenger." Muhammad bin Maslamah offered, with 'Abbad bin Bishr, Al-Harith bin Aws, Abu 'Abs bin Jabr and Abu Na'ilah, Ka'b's foster brother, and was given leave to say what he must. He went to Ka'b complaining that this man had brought them only hardship, and asked for a loan. Ka'b asked for their women and sons as pledges; they offered their weapons instead, which gave them reason to come armed.

On the night of 14 Rabi' al-Awwal they came to his fort under the moon. His wife told him she heard the sound of murder in their voices; he said a man of honour answers a call even at night. They walked and talked, and Abu Na'ilah praised the perfume in his hair and asked to smell it, once, and then again; the second time he held his head fast, and they killed him. Al-Harith bin Aws was wounded by his own companions' swords. At Baqi' Al-Gharqad they cried "Allahu akbar," and the Prophet ﷺ, who had stayed behind praying for them, knew. He put his saliva on Al-Harith's wound, and it healed. The Jews were afraid after that, and kept to their treaties outwardly.
sections.title: Ka'b bin Al-Ashraf

quote.text: Cheerful be your faces.
quote.who: The Prophet ﷺ, as they returned; and they answered, "And yours, Messenger of Allah."

body: Quraish lived by their caravans, to Syria in summer and to Abyssinia in winter, and the coast road was now closed to them. With summer coming they met to find another way, and chose the long road through Najd to Iraq, with Safwan bin Umaiyah to lead and Furat bin Haiyan to guide.

Nu'aim bin Mas'ud let the plan slip while drinking, and Sulait bin An-Nu'man carried it to Madinah. The Prophet ﷺ sent Zaid bin Harithah with a hundred riders. They came upon the caravan at Al-Qaradah and took it by surprise; Safwan and his guards fled without a fight. It carried silver and goods worth a hundred thousand dirhams. Furat, captured, became a Muslim.

It was the most successful march before Uhud. Quraish's last road was closed, and Makkah's trade faced ruin. They had two choices: make peace with the new state, or crush it in one great war. They chose war.
sections.title: The Iraq Road

body: Makkah had forbidden weeping for its dead and ransoming its captives, so the Muslims would not see its grief. Now 'Ikrimah bin Abi Jahl, Safwan bin Umaiyah, Abu Sufyan and 'Abdullah bin Abi Rabi'ah led the cry for war. They sent to Kinanah and the tribes of Tihamah for allies, and set aside the whole profit of the caravan that had escaped at Badr, a thousand camels and fifty thousand dinars, to arm the army [8:36]. Safwan hired the poet Abu 'Azzah to rouse the tribes, the same Abu 'Azzah the Prophet ﷺ had freed without ransom at Badr on his word never to fight him again.
At the turn of the year they marched, and took their women with them to spur the men on.

Al-'Abbas, still in Makkah, sent word of every preparation. The letter reached the Prophet ﷺ at Quba', where Ubai bin Ka'b read it to him. He asked him to keep it quiet, and hurried back to Madinah to take counsel.
sections.title: Three Thousand
facts: three thousand, seven hundred in mail
Abu Sufyan; the horse under Khalid bin Al-Walid, with 'Ikrimah

body: Madinah went on alert. Men carried their weapons even at prayer. Sa'd bin Mu'adh, Usaid bin Hudair and Sa'd bin 'Ubadah kept watch through the night at his door, and armed men guarded the roads. At Al-Abwa', Hind wanted to dig up the grave of the Prophet's mother; the leaders of Quraish refused, fearing what would follow. The army came by Wadi Al-'Aqiq and camped at 'Ainain, below Mount Uhud, on Friday 6 Shawwal.

He called a council and told them his dream. Some of his Companions would be killed; one of his household would be hurt; and the armour was Madinah. His view was to stay within the city: let Quraish sit in the open, and if they came in, the men would fight them in the lanes and the women from the rooftops. 'Abdullah bin Ubai agreed, not for the plan's sake but because he did not want to fight.

But many of the best men, who had missed Badr, begged him to go out and meet them, so that Quraish would not think them afraid. Hamzah swore he would not eat until he had fought them with his sword outside Madinah. After weighing it, it was decided to go out to Uhud.
sections.title: The Dream of the Cows

quote.text: I saw cows being slaughtered, and a notch in the edge of my sword, and I put my hand into a strong coat of mail.
quote.who: The Prophet ﷺ, of his dream before Uhud

body: In the Friday sermon he urged them to fight and be steadfast. After 'Asr he went into his house with Abu Bakr and 'Umar, who helped him arm: his helmet, his sword, and two coats of mail, one over the other. Sa'd bin Mu'adh and Usaid bin Hudair told the people they had forced him out against his view, and when he came out they said they were sorry: if he wished to stay, they would stay.

He divided the army into three: the Emigrants under Mus'ab bin 'Umair, the Aws under Usaid bin Hudair, the Khazraj under Al-Hubab bin Al-Mundhir. A thousand men, a hundred in mail, and no horsemen. Ibn Umm Maktum stayed to lead the prayer in Madinah. On the road a well-armed troop was seen apart from the army: Jews, allies of the Khazraj. Had they accepted Islam? No. He would not seek the help of disbelievers against the idolaters, and sent them back.

At Ash-Shaikhan he reviewed the army and sent home the boys too young to fight: 'Abdullah bin 'Umar, Usamah bin Zaid, Zaid bin Thabit, Zaid bin Arqam, Abu Sa'id Al-Khudri, Al-Bara' bin 'Azib and others. Rafi' bin Khadij was allowed to stay because he was a good archer. Samurah bin Jundub protested that he could throw Rafi', so they wrestled, Samurah won, and he stayed too. Fifty men under Muhammad bin Maslamah guarded the camp that night.
sections.title: His Armour

quote.text: It is not right for a Prophet who has put on his armour to take it off until Allah has judged between him and his enemy.
quote.who: The Prophet ﷺ

body: Before dawn he broke camp and prayed Fajr at Ash-Shawt, within sight of the enemy. There 'Abdullah bin Ubai turned back with three hundred men, a third of the army. They had taken his advice and not his, he said, so why should they get themselves killed? His real aim was to shake the army in front of the enemy. Two clans, Banu Harithah and Banu Salamah, nearly lost heart and went with him, but Allah held them firm [3:122].

'Abdullah bin 'Amr bin Haram, father of Jabir, followed the deserters and pleaded with them to come back and fight in Allah's way, or at least defend their homes. Had they known there would be fighting, they said, they would have come [3:167]. "May Allah drive you away, enemies of Allah," he said. "Allah will suffice His Prophet without you."

Seven hundred remained. Quraish's camp blocked the ways to Uhud, so Abu Khaithamah led them by a short path across the lava field of Banu Harithah. As they passed the garden of Mirba' bin Qaizi, a blind hypocrite, he threw dust in their faces. They rushed to kill him. "Do not kill him," the Prophet ﷺ said. "He is blind of heart as well as of eye."
sections.title: Three Hundred Turn Back

quote.text: Come, fight in the way of Allah, or at least defend yourselves.
quote.who: 'Abdullah bin 'Amr bin Haram, to those who turned back

body: He camped with Mount Uhud at his back and his face towards Madinah, with Quraish between him and the city. Fifty archers he set under 'Abdullah bin Jubair on a low hill across the Qanat valley, about a hundred and fifty metres south-east of the army, guarding the one way round to the Muslims' rear. It was called after that day the Hill of the Archers.

His orders to them were plain: keep the horses off us with your arrows. Win or lose, do not leave this place. Even if you see the birds snatching at us, do not move until I send for you; and if you see us beat them and take the spoils, do not come down to share in them.

Al-Mundhir bin 'Amr led the right, Az-Zubair the left, with Al-Miqdad beside him, to hold off Khalid bin Al-Walid's horse. The bravest men stood in the front rank. Though he came after Quraish, he had taken the better ground: the mountain guarded his back, the archers his flank, and the enemy was left on the low ground below.
sections.title: The Hill of the Archers
sections.when: Saturday morning, 7 Shawwal 3 AH · 23 March 625 CE

quote.text: Even if you see the birds snatching at us, do not leave your place until I send for you.
quote.who: The Prophet ﷺ, to the archers

body: He held up a sword and asked who would take it and give it its due. 'Ali, Az-Zubair, 'Umar and others reached out for it, and he gave it to none of them. Abu Dujanah Simak bin Kharashah asked what its due was. "To strike the enemy's faces with it until it bends." "I will take it, with its due." Abu Dujanah was a proud fighter; when he tied on his red band, everyone knew he meant to fight to the death. He tied it on and strutted between the ranks. "That is a walk Allah dislikes," said the Prophet ﷺ, "except in a place like this."

Quraish drew up in ranks: Abu Sufyan in the centre, Khalid on the right, 'Ikrimah on the left, Safwan with the foot, 'Abdullah bin Abi Rabi'ah with the archers, and the standard with Banu 'Abdud-Dar, as it had been since Qusai. Abu Sufyan goaded them: their bearer had been taken at Badr; if they could not keep it, let them hand it over. They nearly fell on him, and swore he would see what they would do.

He sent word to the Helpers to stand aside and let Quraish fight their cousins; they would not fight them. The Helpers' answer was not what he hoped. Then Abu 'Amir, once a chief of the Aws, who had left Madinah in hatred and whom the Prophet ﷺ called Al-Fasiq, the corrupt, called out to his people, sure they would come over to him. "May Allah give no comfort to your eyes, Fasiq," they answered. Behind Quraish's lines Hind and the women beat their drums and sang that they would welcome the men who fought and abandon those who fled.
sections.title: Who Will Give This Sword Its Due?

quote.text: To strike the enemy's faces with it until it bends.
quote.who: The Prophet ﷺ, asked what the sword's due was

body: The first out was Quraish's standard-bearer, Talhah bin Abi Talhah, called the Ram of the Battalion, on a camel, calling for single combat. Az-Zubair leapt at him like a lion onto the camel's back, pulled him to the ground and killed him. The Prophet ﷺ cried "Allahu akbar!" and the Muslims with him, and he said every Prophet has a disciple, and his disciple was Az-Zubair.

Then the battle closed, and the fiercest fighting was round the standard. One after another the men of Banu 'Abdud-Dar took it up and fell: five of the house of Abu Talhah, brothers and sons, then others, ten in all. Then their Abyssinian slave, Sawab, raised it, braver than his masters. When his hands were cut off he knelt and held it against his chest and neck so it would not fall, until he was killed. Then it lay on the ground, and no one dared lift it.
sections.title: The Standard of Quraish
people: the Ram of the Battalion; killed by Az-Zubair
another brother; killed by 'Asim bin Thabit
his other son; killed by Talhah bin 'Ubaidullah, or by 'Asim
their Abyssinian slave; held it to his chest when his hands were gone

body: The faith of the Muslims swept over Quraish like a flood; "Martyrdom!" was their cry that day. Abu Dujanah cut through their ranks with the Prophet's sword. Az-Zubair, stung not to have been given it, followed him to watch, and saw him kill every man in his way. Once he raised it over someone urging Quraish on, who shrieked: it was Hind bint 'Utbah. He lowered it. He honoured the Prophet's sword too much, he said, to strike a woman with it.

Hamzah fought like a man possessed, the strongest men scattering from him like leaves. He was not killed face to face. Wahshi, an Abyssinian slave of Jubair bin Mut'im, had been promised his freedom if he killed Muhammad's uncle, to avenge Jubair's uncle killed at Badr. Wahshi tells it himself: he hid behind trees and rocks, watching Hamzah cut men down like a dappled camel, no one able to stand before him. When Hamzah struck down Siba' bin 'Abdul-'Uzza, Wahshi balanced his spear and threw it. It went into his belly and came out between his legs. Hamzah tried to come at him and fell. Wahshi went back to the camp and sat there; he had come for no one else. In Makkah he was freed.
Years later, after Ta'if, Wahshi became a Muslim, and with the same spear he killed Musailimah the liar.
sections.title: The Lion of Allah

quote.text: I killed him only to free myself.
quote.who: Wahshi bin Harb, of Hamzah

body: Hanzalah, son of Abu 'Amir Al-Fasiq, had married the night before. He heard the call and left his bride's side to join the army. He cut his way through Quraish to Abu Sufyan himself and was about to kill him when Shaddad bin Al-Aswad killed him.

Three times Khalid bin Al-Walid led the Makkan horse against the Muslims' left flank, to break it and get round behind them, and three times the archers drove him back. Quraish's ranks began to give way. Their standard lay in the dust and no one would go near it; to them, it seemed they were fighting thirty thousand, not seven hundred. Az-Zubair saw Hind's maidservants running with their skirts gathered up, and nothing to stop the Muslims taking them. Allah had kept His promise [3:152], and it was a rout.
sections.title: From His Wedding Night

body: Then, with a second Badr almost won, the archers made the mistake that turned the day. Seeing Quraish flee and the camp open, forty of them went down for the spoils, though 'Abdullah bin Jubair reminded them of the Prophet's order. He and nine others stayed.

Khalid saw the hill nearly empty and wheeled round behind it. He killed 'Abdullah bin Jubair and those with him and fell on the Muslims from the rear, his horsemen shouting. 'Amrah bint 'Alqamah snatched up the fallen standard, and Quraish rallied round it. The Muslims were caught between two armies.

The Prophet ﷺ was at the rear with only nine men. He could have saved himself. Instead he called out, "Servants of Allah, to me!", knowing Quraish would hear him before the Muslims did. They did. The Muslims broke into three: some fled, as far as Madinah or up the mountain; some, mixed in among the enemy, fought on in confusion; and some cared for nothing but to reach him.
sections.title: Forty Left the Hill

quote.text: Servants of Allah, to me!
quote.who: The Prophet ﷺ, calling his scattered army, though it gave his place away

body: In the confusion the Muslims struck at each other. Hudhaifah saw his father Al-Yaman about to be killed by Muslims and cried out that he was his father, but they did not hear, and killed him. "May Allah forgive you," said Hudhaifah, and he gave away the blood money in charity.

Then a cry went up that Muhammad had been killed. Some sat down and threw away their weapons; some spoke of asking 'Abdullah bin Ubai to get them a pledge of safety from Abu Sufyan. Anas bin An-Nadr came on them sitting. Why? "The Messenger of Allah has been killed." "Then what will you do with life after him? Get up and die for what he died for." He asked Allah's pardon for what the Muslims had done and declared himself free of what the idolaters had done. Meeting Sa'd bin Mu'adh, he said he could smell the scent of Paradise this side of Uhud. He fought until he was killed. His body had more than eighty wounds, and only his sister knew him, by his fingertips.

Thabit bin Ad-Dahdah called to the Helpers that if Muhammad was dead, Allah lived and would never die, and led them against Khalid's horse until they were all killed. A Helper covered in blood, told that Muhammad had been killed, answered that then he had delivered his message, so fight for your religion. Slowly they came back to themselves, and fought on, and the rumour was found to be false.
sections.title: "Muhammad Has Been Killed"

quote.text: How sweet is the scent of Paradise; I can smell it this side of Uhud.
quote.who: Anas bin An-Nadr

body: When Quraish heard his voice and came for him, he had with him seven men of the Helpers and two of Quraish. "Whoever drives them off from us will have Paradise," he said, or, "will be my companion in Paradise." One of the Helpers went forward and fought until he was killed. They came on again, and another went, and another, until all seven had fallen. The last of them was 'Umarah bin Yazid bin As-Sakan, who fought until his wounds brought him down.
Then he said to the two of Quraish who were left with him that they had not been fair to their companions.
sections.title: The Seven Helpers

quote.text: We have not done justice to our companions.
quote.who: The Prophet ﷺ, when the seven Helpers had fallen

body: For a moment only Talhah bin 'Ubaidullah and Sa'd bin Abi Waqqas were left with him, and Quraish closed in to kill him. 'Utbah bin Abi Waqqas threw a stone that broke his lower right tooth and cut his lip. 'Abdullah bin Shihab Az-Zuhri wounded his forehead. 'Abdullah bin Qami'ah struck his shoulder with a blow that his two coats of mail turned, but which pained him for more than a month, then struck his cheek so that two rings of his helmet were driven into it. "Take that, I am Ibn Qami'ah." Wiping the blood from his face, he answered, "May Allah humiliate you."

"How can a people prosper who wound their Prophet's face and break his tooth, while he calls them to Allah?" The ayah came: the matter is not yours; Allah may turn to them in mercy or punish them [3:128]. Then he said, "O Allah, forgive my people, for they do not know."

Sa'd shot arrow after arrow at them. "Shoot, Sa'd, may my father and mother be your ransom," he said, words he never said to any other. Talhah fought like eleven men; he caught a blow aimed at him with his hand, and his fingers were cut through. He had thirty-five or thirty-nine wounds that day, and his hand stayed lame. "Whoever would see a martyr walking on the earth, let him look at Talhah," the Prophet ﷺ said later, and whenever Uhud was mentioned, Abu Bakr said, "That day was all Talhah's." Sa'd saw two men in white fighting for him as he had never seen men fight, before or after; it is said they were Jibreel and Mika'il.
sections.title: His Face Was Wounded

quote.text: O Allah, forgive my people, for they do not know.
quote.who: The Prophet ﷺ, with the blood on his face, at Uhud

body: The first to reach him was Abu Bakr, then Abu 'Ubaidah bin Al-Jarrah, running like a bird. "See to your brother," he said, pointing to Talhah. Abu 'Ubaidah begged to be the one to draw the helmet rings from his cheek. He drew them with his teeth, slowly so as not to hurt him, and lost a front tooth doing it. Then they came to Talhah and found some ten wounds on him.

More came, and stood round him with their bodies and their weapons. Quraish pressed harder. He fell into one of the pits Abu 'Amir had dug as traps, and grazed his knee; 'Ali took his hand and Talhah lifted him. Arrows flew at him from every side and none struck him. 'Abdullah bin Shihab swore he would kill him or not live, and walked right past him without seeing him.
sections.title: A Shield of Bodies
list: shielded him with his own chest and broke two or three bows shooting; "Do not look out, lest an arrow strike you"
stood over him and took the arrows on his back
caught 'Utbah bin Abi Waqqas, who had broken the Prophet's tooth, and killed him
his eye was struck out onto his cheek; the Prophet ﷺ put it back with his hand, and it was the better of his two eyes
sucked the blood from the Prophet's wound and would not spit it out; he went back to the fighting and was killed
fought Ibn Qami'ah and took twelve wounds
more than twenty wounds; lame in one leg ever after

carried the standard; when both his hands were cut off he held it with his chest until Ibn Qami'ah killed him, and, thinking he had killed the Prophet, for Mus'ab looked like him, cried that Muhammad was dead

body: He gave the standard to 'Ali. Ka'b bin Malik was the first to recognise him, and shouted the good news; the Prophet ﷺ signed to him to be quiet, but the Muslims had heard, and some thirty gathered round him. He began to draw them back up the mountain in good order. 'Uthman bin 'Abdullah bin Al-Mughirah rode at him, swearing to kill him or die; his horse stumbled into a pit, and Al-Harith bin As-Simmah killed him. Then a drowsiness came over the Muslims, a peace from Allah [3:154]; Abu Talhah's sword fell from his hand again and again.

Ubai bin Khalaf came up after him, crying, "Where is Muhammad? Let me kill him or be killed." The Companions asked to deal with him. "Leave him." He took a spear from Al-Harith bin As-Simmah and struck Ubai through a gap in his armour by the collarbone, and Ubai rolled from his horse. It was only a scratch, Quraish told him. "He told me in Makkah he would kill me," said Ubai. "By Allah, if he had spat on me it would have killed me." He died at Sarif, on the way home.

A rock barred the way; weighed down by his armour and his wounds, he could not climb it, so Talhah crouched for him to stand on and lifted him up. Then Khalid and Abu Sufyan led a band of Quraish up the mountain. "O Allah, they must not be above us," he prayed, and 'Umar and some Emigrants drove them down. Sa'd shot one with an arrow, picked it up and shot another, and a third with the same arrow, and kept it all his life.
sections.title: Up the Mountain

quote.text: Talhah has earned it.
quote.who: The Prophet ﷺ, of Paradise, when Talhah lifted him onto the rock

body: Sure he was dead, Quraish went back to their camp to make ready to leave. Some of them and their women went among the Muslim dead, cutting off ears and noses and slitting open bellies. Hind cut out Hamzah's liver and chewed it, could not swallow it and spat it out, and made anklets and necklaces of the ears and noses she had cut.

Ka'b bin Malik, passing the dead, saw an armoured idolater going among the Muslims saying, "Gather them like sheep for slaughter," and a Muslim waiting for him. The idolater was bigger and better armed; the Muslim's sword split him to the hip. Then he uncovered his face: "What do you think of that, Ka'b? I am Abu Dujanah."
sections.title: Hind and the Dead
list: ran to and fro with waterskins on their backs, pouring water into the mouths of the wounded
carried water to the fighters, 'Umar remembered

threw dust in the faces of men fleeing into Madinah, told them to take a spindle and leave the swords, then went to give water to the wounded; Hibban bin Al-'Araqah shot her down and laughed, and the Prophet ﷺ gave Sa'd a headless arrow; Sa'd's shot struck Hibban in the throat

body: 'Ali brought water from Al-Mihras; it smelt, so he would not drink it, but washed the blood from his face, saying Allah's anger was great at those who had bloodied His Prophet's face. Fatimah washed the wound while 'Ali poured; when the blood would not stop she burned a piece of straw mat and pressed the ashes into it. Weak from his wounds, he led the Dhuhr prayer sitting, and they prayed sitting behind him.

As Quraish made ready to go, Abu Sufyan came up the mountain and called, "Is Muhammad among you?" No answer; he had told them not to answer. "Is Ibn Abi Quhafah among you? Is 'Umar?" No answer. "Then those three are finished." 'Umar could not hold back: they were all alive, enemy of Allah. "Hubal, be exalted!" cried Abu Sufyan. "Answer him," said the Prophet ﷺ. "Allah is higher and more majestic." "We have Al-'Uzza and you have none." "Allah is our protector, and you have none." "This day for the day of Badr. War goes by turns." "Not the same," said 'Umar. "Our dead are in Paradise, and yours in the Fire."

Abu Sufyan called 'Umar over and asked him, by Allah, had they killed Muhammad? "By Allah, no; he is listening to you now." "You are more truthful to me than Ibn Qami'ah." As he left he called out that they would meet again at Badr next year. "Say: yes, it is an appointment between us." Then 'Ali followed them: if they rode their camels and led their horses they were going home; if they rode their horses, they were going to Madinah, and he would fight them there. They rode their camels, towards Makkah.
sections.title: "Hubal, Be Exalted!"
sections.when: The end of the day, 7 Shawwal 3 AH
sections.place: Below the Muslims on Mount Uhud

quote.text: Allah is our Protector, and you have no protector.
quote.who: The answer the Prophet ﷺ gave Abu Sufyan

body: They went out among the dead and wounded. He sent Zaid bin Thabit to look for Sa'd bin Ar-Rabi' with his greeting and a question: how was he? Zaid found him dying, with seventy wounds. Sa'd returned the greeting: tell the Messenger of Allah he could smell the scent of Paradise, and tell the Helpers they would have no excuse before Allah if any harm reached the Prophet ﷺ while an eye of theirs still blinked. Then he died.

Al-Usairim, 'Amr bin Thabit, had always refused Islam; they found him among the dying and asked what had brought him. Islam, he said; he believed in Allah and His Messenger, and had fought with him until this befell him. He died. "He is of the people of Paradise," the Prophet ﷺ said, and he had never prayed a single prayer. Quzman fought bravely and killed seven or eight, but when told of Paradise he said he had fought only for his people; and when his wounds grew worse he killed himself. Of him the Prophet ﷺ had always said he was of the people of the Fire. And Mukhairiq, a Jew of Banu Tha'labah, told his people they knew it was their duty to help Muhammad; it was the Sabbath, they said. There is no Sabbath for you, he said, left his wealth to the Prophet ﷺ and fought until he was killed. "Mukhairiq is the best of the Jews."
sections.title: Seventy
facts: seventy; sixty-five of them Helpers, forty-one of the Khazraj and twenty-four of the Aws, with four Emigrants and one Jew

body: Some had carried their dead towards Madinah; he had them brought back and buried where they fell, unwashed, in their wounds, their armour taken off. He buried two and three to a grave, sometimes two men in one cloth, asking which of them knew more of the Qur'an and laying him first. 'Abdullah bin 'Amr bin Haram and 'Amr bin Al-Jamuh, who had loved each other, he buried together.
