Hanzalah's body was found apart, water dripping from it: the angels were washing him, he said; ask his wife. She told them he had gone out to the battle without time to wash. He was called Hanzalah, washed by the angels.

The sight of Hamzah grieved him beyond anything. His aunt Safiyah came to see her brother, and he told her son Az-Zubair to turn her back. Why, she asked, when she knew what had been done to him, and it was in Allah's way? She would be patient. She looked at him, said, "To Allah we belong and to Him we return," and prayed for him. He was buried with 'Abdullah bin Jahsh, his nephew. Ibn Mas'ud never saw the Prophet ﷺ weep as he wept for Hamzah.

There was nothing to shroud Hamzah in but a striped cloak too short for him: cover his head, and his feet showed; cover his feet, and his head showed. They covered his head and put idhkhir grass over his feet. So it was with Mus'ab bin 'Umair too.
sections.title: Buried Where They Fell

quote.text: I will bear witness for these on the Day of Resurrection.
quote.who: The Prophet ﷺ, at the graves of Uhud

body: Before they left he had them stand in rows behind him while he praised his Lord: none can hold back what You give or give what You hold back, none guide whom You leave astray or lead astray whom You guide. Make faith beloved to us and beautiful in our hearts; let us live as Muslims and die as Muslims.

On the road Hamnah bint Jahsh met him. He told her of her brother 'Abdullah, and she said, "To Allah we belong and to Him we return," and asked forgiveness for him; of her uncle Hamzah, and she said the same; then of her husband Mus'ab, and she cried out and wept. "A husband has a place in a woman's heart like nothing else," he said. A woman of Banu Dinar, told her husband, father and brother had all been killed, asked only how the Messenger of Allah was, and would not rest until she saw him. Sa'd bin Mu'adh's mother came running, her son 'Amr killed; he waited for her and gave her his condolence, and she said her loss was nothing while he was safe. He prayed for the families of the dead: their dead were companions together in Paradise.
At home he handed his sword to Fatimah to wash the blood from it. 'Ali gave her his too: it had served him well. "If you fought well," said the Prophet ﷺ, "so did Sahl bin Hunaif and Abu Dujanah."
sections.title: "So Long As You Are Safe"

quote.text: Every misfortune is small so long as you are safe.
quote.who: A woman of Banu Dinar, who had lost her husband, father and brother

body: That night Madinah kept watch at every way in. He lay awake thinking that Quraish, finding they had gained nothing, might turn back on the city. In the morning he called the Muslims out to pursue them: only those who had fought at Uhud. 'Abdullah bin Ubai offered to come; no. Jabir bin 'Abdullah, kept at home on the day to look after his sisters, asked to go and was allowed. Wounded and exhausted, they marched eight miles to Hamra' Al-Asad and camped.

Ma'bad bin Abi Ma'bad of Khuza'ah came to him there, a friend if not yet a Muslim, and he sent him to Abu Sufyan. At Ar-Rawha', Quraish were blaming each other for leaving the Muslims standing, and wanted to go back and finish them; Safwan bin Umaiyah warned them to go home while they were winners. Ma'bad told them Muhammad was coming with an army such as he had never seen, all those who had stayed home now burning to avenge Uhud. Their resolve broke and they made for Makkah, paying a passing caravan of 'Abdul-Qais in raisins to tell the Muslims they were coming back to destroy them. The message only increased the believers in faith [3:173-174].

He stayed three days and returned. On the way he took Abu 'Azzah, the poet freed at Badr on his oath never to fight him again, who begged for mercy a second time. A believer is not stung twice from the same hole, he said, and Abu 'Azzah was put to death.
sections.title: Hamra' Al-Asad
sections.place: Hamra' Al-Asad, eight miles from Madinah

quote.text: Allah is sufficient for us, and He is the best disposer of affairs.
quote.who: The believers, at Hamra' Al-Asad (Al 'Imran 3:173)

body: Was Uhud a defeat? In its second half Quraish had the upper hand and dealt the Muslims heavy losses. But they never took the Muslims' camp, took no captives and no spoils, did not pursue the army up the mountain, and left the field first; Madinah lay open a few miles away, and they dared not march on it. The next day the beaten army chased the victors, and the victors ran. Both sides had suffered, and both had hope; but the believers hoped from Allah what the others did not [4:104].

Some sixty ayahs of Surat Al 'Imran came down about it, from the morning he set out to place the believers at their posts [3:121] to its end: Allah would not leave the believers as they were until He had told the bad from the good [3:179].
sections.title: Defeat, or Victory?
list: the archers' leaving their post turned a victory into loss
so that those who follow them for victory alone are told apart from those who believe
their withdrawal and their talk showed the Muslims the enemy within
it humbles the soul; the believers are patient where the hypocrites are not
a rank Allah grants to those He loves, and a means by which His enemies earn their end

parts.title: Uhud
parts.blurb: Enemies on every side after Badr; then three thousand men at the foot of Uhud, fifty archers on a hill, an order broken, and a day of martyrs.

body: Uhud had cost the Muslims their name for strength, and enemies inside and outside Madinah grew bold. Two months after it, Banu Asad were gathering to raid the city. In Safar of the fourth year 'Adi and Qarah betrayed ten Companions, and Banu 'Amir seventy at the Well of Ma'unah. Banu An-Nadir plotted to kill the Prophet ﷺ, and Ghatafan made ready to attack. He met each in turn. His march to Hamra' Al-Asad had already begun to win back their standing.
sections.title: The Year of Betrayals
list: Abu Salamah with a hundred and fifty men fell on them in their own land, scattered them and brought back their cattle; on the way home he died of his wound from Uhud, which had flared up again
Khalid bin Sufyan Al-Hudhali, Muharram 4 AH

gathering men against Madinah; 'Abdullah bin Unais was sent against him, was gone eighteen days and killed him; the Prophet ﷺ gave him a staff, "a sign between me and you on the Day of Resurrection," and it was buried with him in his shroud
Banu 'Amir and Banu Sulaim, Safar 4 AH
the betrayal at the Well of Ma'unah
a stone to be dropped on his head

body: Men of 'Adi and Qarah came to Madinah saying some of their people had become Muslims, and asked for teachers. He sent six of his Companions, or ten, under Marthad bin Abi Marthad, or, in Al-Bukhari's report, 'Asim bin Thabit. At Ar-Raji', between Rabigh and Jeddah, a hundred archers of Banu Lihyan surrounded them. The Companions climbed a hill. Come down, they were told, and you will not be killed.

'Asim refused to come down. He fought until he and six others were killed. Three came down on the promise: Khubaib, Zaid bin Ad-Dathinah and one more. At once they were bound. The third cried treachery, resisted and was killed. Khubaib and Zaid had killed chiefs of Quraish at Badr, so they were taken to Makkah and sold.

Quraish sent men to bring back some part of 'Asim's body, for he had killed one of their nobles. They could not get near it: a great swarm of hornets covered it. 'Asim had vowed to Allah that no idolater would ever touch him, nor he them.
sections.title: Ar-Raji'
sections.place: Ar-Raji', on the road towards Makkah

quote.text: Allah guards His believing servant after his death, as He guarded him in his life.
quote.who: 'Umar, hearing of 'Asim and the hornets

body: Khubaib was kept prisoner until Quraish agreed to crucify him. He was seen in his bonds eating a bunch of grapes when there was not a single date to be had in Makkah: provision from Allah.

They led him out of the Sanctuary to At-Tan'im. He asked to pray two rak'ahs, and prayed them. Then he turned to them: had he not feared they would think he was afraid of death, he would have prayed longer. He was the first to make two rak'ahs a custom before being put to death. He asked Allah to count them one by one and destroy them to the last. He spoke verses: the parties had gathered their tribes around him, their women and children, while he was bound to a tall trunk; to Allah alone he complained; he did not care, if he died a Muslim, on which side he fell for Allah.

Abu Sufyan asked him whether he would not rather Muhammad were here in his place, to be beheaded, while he sat safe with his family. 'Uqbah bin Al-Harith, whose father Khubaib had killed, crucified him, and guards were set over his body; 'Amr bin Umaiyah Ad-Damri came by night, took it down and buried it. Zaid bin Ad-Dathinah was bought by Safwan bin Umaiyah and killed for his father.
sections.title: Two Rak'ahs at At-Tan'im
sections.place: At-Tan'im, outside the Sanctuary of Makkah

quote.text: By Allah, I would not wish Muhammad to be where I am now, nor that even a thorn should hurt him, while I sat safe among my family.
quote.who: Khubaib, to Abu Sufyan

body: Abu Bara' 'Amir bin Malik, called the Spear Player, came to Madinah and would neither accept Islam nor reject it. If the Prophet ﷺ sent some of his Companions to Najd to call its people, he said, he hoped they would accept. "I fear the people of Najd will kill them." "They are under my protection." He sent seventy, or forty, under Al-Mundhir bin 'Amr. They were the best of the Companions in the Qur'an. By day they gathered firewood and sold it to feed the poor of the mosque; by night they prayed and studied the Qur'an.

They camped at the Well of Ma'unah and sent Haram bin Milhan with the Prophet's letter to 'Amir bin At-Tufail. 'Amir did not even look at it; he signed to a man, who drove a spear into Haram's back. Haram saw his own blood and cried, "Allahu akbar! By the Lord of the Ka'bah, I have won!" 'Amir called on Banu 'Amir to kill the rest; they would not break Abu Bara''s protection. So he called on 'Usaiyah, Ri'l and Dhakwan of Banu Sulaim, and they surrounded the Companions and killed them all. Only Ka'b bin Zaid was carried out wounded from among the dead; he was killed later, at the Trench.

'Amr bin Umaiyah and Al-Mundhir bin 'Uqbah, out with the camels, saw birds circling and came back. Al-Mundhir fought and was killed; 'Amr was taken, his head shaved, and freed to fulfil a vow of 'Amir's mother. On his way home 'Amr killed two men of Bani Kilab as they slept, not knowing the Prophet ﷺ had given them his protection. "You have killed two men whose blood money I must pay," he told him.

He grieved for Ma'unah and Ar-Raji' as for nothing else. For a month, in every Fajr prayer, he called on Allah against Ri'l, Dhakwan, Lihyan and 'Usaiyah, who had disobeyed Allah and His Messenger, until words came down that they recited for a time, before they were lifted from the Qur'an.
sections.title: The Well of Ma'unah
sections.place: The Well of Ma'unah, in Najd

quote.text: Tell our people that we have met our Lord; He is pleased with us, and has made us pleased.
quote.who: words revealed of the martyrs of Ma'unah, recited for a time and then lifted

body: By their treaty, Banu An-Nadir were bound to share the blood money of the two men 'Amr bin Umaiyah had killed. The Prophet ﷺ went to ask them for it with Abu Bakr, 'Umar, 'Ali and a few others. They agreed, and asked him to sit and wait beside a wall of their houses. Then they met apart. 'Amr bin Jahsh offered to climb up and drop a great stone on his head. Sallam bin Mishkam warned them that Allah would tell him, and that it would break the treaty. Jibreel did tell him. He rose at once and hurried back to Madinah with his Companions, and told them on the way.

He sent Muhammad bin Maslamah to them: leave Madinah within ten days, or be killed. 'Abdullah bin Ubai sent to say stay, he had two thousand men to help them, and Quraizah and Ghatafan would come too [59:11]. Huyai bin Akhtab believed him and answered, "We will not leave our homes. Do what you will." "Allahu akbar," said the Prophet ﷺ, and the Muslims with him.

He besieged them for six nights, or fifteen, 'Ali carrying the standard. They shot from their forts behind their palm groves, and he had palms cut down and burned [59:5]. Quraizah stayed out of it, and neither Ibn Ubai nor Ghatafan came, like Satan, who tells man to disbelieve and then disowns him [59:16]. Fear entered their hearts, and they asked to be let go. They could take all their camels could carry, but no weapons. They loaded six hundred camels, even with their doors and roof beams, wrecking their houses as they went. Surat Al-Hashr came down about them.
sections.title: Banu An-Nadir
sections.place: The quarter of Banu An-Nadir, Madinah
list: Huyai bin Akhtab and Sallam bin Abul-Huqaiq to Khaibar; others to Syria
Yamin bin 'Amr and Abu Sa'd bin Wahb kept their wealth
fifty coats of mail, fifty helmets, three hundred and forty swords, their land and houses
so it was the Prophet's to give; he gave it to the first Emigrants and to two poor Helpers, Abu Dujanah and Sahl bin Hunaif, kept his family's provision for a year from it, and spent the rest on arms

body: A year had passed since Uhud, and the appointment Abu Sufyan had called out from the mountain came due. The Prophet ﷺ marched to Badr with fifteen hundred men and ten horses, 'Ali with the standard and 'Abdullah bin Rawahah over Madinah, and waited.

Abu Sufyan set out with two thousand men and fifty horses. At Majannah, near Marr Az-Zahran, a little way from Makkah, his nerve failed. He told Quraish that only a green year would do for them, a year when their animals grazed and gave milk; this was a year of drought, so he was going home, and so should they. They turned back without a word.

The Muslims stayed eight days at Badr and traded there, and came home with good profit. The balance turned back their way, and all Arabia knew it. It is called Badr the Appointment, the Second Badr, the Last Badr and the Lesser Badr.
sections.title: Badr, the Appointment

quote.text: This is a year of drought. I am going back, and I bid you go back with me.
quote.who: Abu Sufyan, at Majannah

body: After six quiet months, word came that the tribes around Dumat al-Jandal, on the edge of Syria, were robbing travellers and gathering to attack Madinah. It lay fifteen days' march from Madinah, and five from Damascus. He left Siba' bin 'Arfatah Al-Ghifari over the city and set out with a thousand men, with a guide of Banu 'Udhrah named Madhkur, marching by night and hiding by day so the enemy would not hear of them.

They fled before he came, leaving their herds, and the people of Dumah scattered. He stayed five days, sending out parties to find them, and found no one. On the way home he made a treaty with 'Uyainah bin Hisn. The hypocrites were quieter now, one Jewish tribe was gone and the others kept their treaties outwardly, the Bedouin were subdued, and Quraish showed no wish to fight. It was the calm before the greatest storm of all.
sections.title: Dumat al-Jandal
sections.when: End of Rabi' al-Awwal 5 AH · August 626 CE

body: The Jews of Banu An-Nadir, now in Khaibar, watched for the Muslims to fall, and the Muslims did not fall. So twenty of their chiefs went to Makkah and offered Quraish their full support if they would attack Muhammad, and Quraish, who had not dared to come to Badr, took it. Then the same men went to Ghatafan, and to tribe after tribe, until all Arabia that hated Islam was joined against it.

They came from the south and the east at an agreed time and met outside Madinah. They were more than all the people of Madinah together, women, children and old men included. Had they come by surprise, they might have destroyed them all. But the city was watching, and word of the march came in time.
sections.title: The Confederates Gather
facts: Quraish, Kinanah and the people of Tihamah, four thousand under Abu Sufyan
Banu Sulaim and Ghatafan, with Fazarah under 'Uyainah bin Hisn, Murrah under Al-Harith bin 'Awf and Ashja' under Mis'ar bin Rakhilah

body: He called a council, and after long talk they took the advice of Salman Al-Farisi. In Persia, Salman said, when they were besieged they dug a trench. Nothing like it had been seen in Arabia. Madinah was walled on the other sides by lava fields, hills and palm groves; only the north lay open, and that was the way the army would come. So the trench was dug there.

The work was shared out: forty yards to each ten men. He dug with them, carried earth with them, and kept their hearts on the Hereafter. Sahl bin Sa'd remembered them digging while others carried the earth away on their backs. They were so hungry they were near starving, and still they worked, by day, going home at night, until it was done.
sections.title: Salman's Trench
facts: about five and a half kilometres
about four and a half metres
everyone, the Prophet ﷺ with them

body: Jabir bin 'Abdullah saw how hungry the Prophet ﷺ was, and killed a lamb and had a little barley ground, and quietly invited him with a few men. He called out all the diggers, thousands of them, and they ate until they were full, while the pot still bubbled with meat and the dough was still being baked. A woman brought a handful of dates; he spread them on his cloak and called the Companions to eat, and the dates went on increasing until they spilled over its edge.

A great rock stopped the digging, and their picks would not break it. He took the pick, said "In the name of Allah," and struck. "Allahu akbar! I have been given the keys of Syria. By Allah, I can see its red palaces from here." He struck again: "Allahu akbar! I have been given Persia. By Allah, I can see the white palace of Al-Mada'in." The third blow broke the rest of it: "Allahu akbar! I have been given the keys of Yemen. By Allah, I can see the gates of San'a' from where I stand."
sections.title: The Rock and the Meal

quote.text: Allahu akbar! I have been given the keys of Syria; by Allah, I can see its red palaces from here.
quote.who: The Prophet ﷺ, striking the rock in the trench

body: Quraish camped at Majma' Al-Asyal, Ghatafan near Uhud. The believers saw them and said, this is what Allah and His Messenger promised us [33:22]; the hypocrites said Allah and His Messenger had promised them nothing but delusion [33:12]. Three thousand Muslims took their stand with their backs to Mount Sala' and the trench before them. Quraish came up to it and stopped, amazed. They had never seen such a thing.

So they laid siege, riding up and down it looking for a weak place, while the Muslims kept them off with arrows. Then 'Amr bin 'Abd Wudd, 'Ikrimah bin Abi Jahl and Dirar bin Al-Khattab found a narrow place and spurred their horses across it, and 'Amr called for single combat. 'Ali went out, and killed him, and the others fled back over the trench.

It was so hard that prayers were missed. 'Umar came cursing Quraish: the sun had set and he had not prayed 'Asr. "By Allah, nor have I," said the Prophet ﷺ, and went down to Buthan, made wudu' and prayed 'Asr after sunset, then Maghrib, and prayed against them. The fighting was mostly arrows across the trench; six Muslims were killed and ten idolaters. An arrow cut an artery of Sa'd bin Mu'adh.
sections.title: Ten Thousand at the Trench

quote.text: O Allah, if any fighting with Quraish remains, keep me alive for it; and if You have ended it, let this wound open and let my death be in it; and do not let me die until my heart is at rest about Banu Quraizah.
quote.who: Sa'd bin Mu'adh, wounded at the Trench

body: Huyai bin Akhtab went to Ka'b bin Asad, chief of Banu Quraizah, who were bound by treaty to help the Muslims. Ka'b would not listen at first. Huyai talked of the chiefs of Quraish at Al-Asyal and Ghatafan at Uhud, sworn to finish Muhammad, and promised that if they went home he would come into Ka'b's fort and share his fate. Ka'b gave way, and broke the treaty. The Muslims' women and children were now open behind them.

Safiyah bint 'Abdul-Muttalib was in a fort with Hassan bin Thabit and the women and children when she saw a Jew circling it. Hassan said he was not the man for it. She took a tent pole, went down and killed the Jew with it, and Quraizah thought after that the forts were guarded. The Prophet ﷺ sent the two Sa'ds, 'Abdullah bin Rawahah and Khawwat bin Jubair to learn the truth, telling them not to spread it among the people if it was true, so as not to frighten them, and to say so openly if it was false. It was true, and Quraizah told them to their faces there was no treaty any more. The eyes grew wild and hearts rose to the throats [33:10-11], and some asked leave to go home, saying their houses lay open, when they did not [33:12-13].

He lay wrapped in his cloak a long while. Then he rose: "Allahu akbar! Good news, Muslims, of Allah's victory and help." He sent men back to guard the families, and thought of offering Ghatafan a third of Madinah's dates to go home. He asked the two Sa'ds. It was only for their sake, he told them, when he saw all the Arabs shooting at them from a single bow.
sections.title: Quraizah Break Their Word

quote.text: If this is Allah's command, we obey. If it is something you do for our sake, we do not need it. We knew these people in our days of idols: it is not our dates they want, but our end. Now that Allah has honoured us with Islam, we will give them nothing but the sword.
quote.who: Sa'd bin Mu'adh and Sa'd bin 'Ubadah

body: Nu'aim bin Mas'ud of Ghatafan came to the Prophet ﷺ by night: he had become a Muslim, and his people did not know it. Let him do whatever he could, he was told.

He went to Banu Quraizah as an old friend: Quraish and Ghatafan were not like them, he said; this was not their land, and if things went badly they would go home and leave Quraizah alone with Muhammad. Let them fight only if Quraish gave them some of their nobles as hostages. Then he went to Quraish: Quraizah regretted breaking with Muhammad, he said, and had promised to hand him nobles of Quraish to be killed; give them no hostages. And he told Ghatafan the same.

On a Saturday night Quraish and Ghatafan sent to Quraizah: attack tomorrow. Quraizah answered that they did not fight on the Sabbath, and would not fight at all without hostages. Then Nu'aim was right, said Quraish and Ghatafan, and refused; then Nu'aim was right, said Quraizah. Each side now trusted the other no more. And the Prophet ﷺ prayed.
sections.title: Nu'aim's Stratagem

quote.text: O Allah, Revealer of the Book, swift in reckoning, defeat the Confederates.
quote.who: The Prophet ﷺ, at the Trench

body: Then Allah sent a wind, with rain and bitter cold, that tore up their tents and overturned their pots. That freezing night the Prophet ﷺ sent Hudhaifah bin Al-Yaman across to bring news of them. He found them packing to leave, with nothing to show for a month.

The siege had begun in Shawwal and ended in Dhul-Qa'dah, more than a month. It was a battle of nerves more than of blood, but it settled one thing: no army, however great, would wipe out the power growing in Madinah. Allah had turned back the disbelievers in their rage, and spared the believers the fighting [33:25].
sections.title: The Wind

quote.text: Now we will march against them, and they will not march against us.
quote.who: The Prophet ﷺ, as the Confederates left

body: The very day he came home, as he was washing in Umm Salamah's house, Jibreel came to him: this was no time to put away his sword. Let him go to Banu Quraizah; Jibreel would go ahead with the angels to shake their forts and cast fear into their hearts. He had it called out: no one is to pray 'Asr except at Banu Quraizah. On the way the time for 'Asr came. Some prayed on the road; others would not pray until they arrived. He blamed neither.

He set out with three thousand men on foot and thirty horses, Ibn Umm Maktum over Madinah, 'Ali ahead with the standard, close enough to hear Quraizah reviling the Prophet ﷺ. They were besieged twenty-five days. Their chief, Ka'b bin Asad, put three choices to them: accept Islam, which their own books told them was true; kill their women and children and fight to the death; or attack on the Sabbath, when they would not be expected. They would take none of them.

They asked for Abu Lubabah, their old ally, to advise them. The men pleaded with him and the women and children wept round him, and when they asked his advice, he pointed to his throat: death was waiting for them. At once he knew he had betrayed his trust. He went straight to the Prophet's mosque, tied himself to a pillar, and swore no one should untie him but the Messenger of Allah. "Had he come to me, I would have asked forgiveness for him," the Prophet ﷺ said; "now it is for Allah to turn to him." When 'Ali and Az-Zubair came forward, 'Ali swearing he would take their fort or die as Hamzah had died, they surrendered to the Prophet's judgment.
sections.title: Banu Quraizah

quote.text: If he had come to me, I would have asked Allah to forgive him; but since he has tied himself of his own will, it is for Allah to turn to him.
quote.who: The Prophet ﷺ, of Abu Lubabah

body: The men were bound and the women and children kept apart. The Aws, their old allies, begged him to be lenient with them. Would they accept one of their own as judge? They would; and he named Sa'd bin Mu'adh, who lay wounded in Madinah. Sa'd was brought on a donkey, his people pleading with him all the way to be kind to his old allies. He said nothing, until at last he said that the time had come for Sa'd not to care for anyone's blame in Allah's cause.

He asked whether his judgment would bind everyone there, and was told it would. He judged that their fighting men be put to death, their women and children be taken captive, and their wealth be divided among the Muslims. "You have judged with the judgment of Allah," the Prophet ﷺ said. They had gathered fifteen hundred swords, two thousand spears, three hundred coats of mail and five hundred shields, for the war they had joined against Madinah.

Huyai bin Akhtab, who had brought them to it, was brought in with his hands tied to his neck. He declared his enmity to the Prophet ﷺ to the last, but said that Allah's will was done and he submitted to it, and he was put to death. Of their women only one was killed: she had dropped a millstone on a Muslim, Khallad bin Suwaid, and killed him. A few accepted Islam and kept their lives, families and wealth.
sections.title: Sa'd's Judgment

quote.text: You have judged among them with the judgment of Allah.
quote.who: The Prophet ﷺ, to Sa'd bin Mu'adh

body: Sa'd bin Mu'adh had asked not to die until his heart was at rest about Banu Quraizah. Now it was. The Prophet ﷺ had pitched a tent for him in the mosque, to visit him often. His wound opened, and the blood ran out of the tent towards the tent of Banu Ghifar beside it, and they called out to ask what was coming to them. It was Sa'd's wound; and of it he died.
His bier, the hypocrites said, was strangely light. "The angels are carrying him," the Prophet ﷺ said.

Abu Lubabah stayed tied to his pillar six nights; his wife untied him at each prayer and bound him again after it. Then, one dawn, forgiveness for him came down. The people ran to free him, but he would let no one but the Prophet ﷺ do it, and he did, as he came out for Fajr. Surat Al-Ahzab came down about the Confederates, the believers and the hypocrites, and the treaty broken.
sections.title: The Throne Shook

quote.text: The Throne of the Most Merciful shook at the death of Sa'd bin Mu'adh.
quote.who: The Prophet ﷺ

body: Sallam bin Abul-Huqaiq, called Abu Rafi', had gathered the Confederates and paid for their army. The Aws had rid the Muslims of Ka'b bin Al-Ashraf; the Khazraj asked leave to match them, and were given it, so long as no woman or child was harmed.

Five men under 'Abdullah bin 'Atik went to his fort at Khaibar. At sunset, as the herds came in, 'Abdullah wrapped himself in his cloak by the gate as if answering a call of nature; the gatekeeper called him in, and he hid. When the castle slept he took the keys from their peg, and went up through the house, locking every door behind him. In the dark he called "Abu Rafi'!", struck at the voice and failed to kill him, came back as if to help, and killed him.

Going down, he thought he had reached the ground and stepped out, and fell, and broke his leg in the moonlight. He bound it with his turban and sat by the gate until the cock crowed and a voice on the wall announced the death of Abu Rafi', the merchant of the Hijaz. Then he went home to the Prophet ﷺ, who passed his hand over the leg, and it was as if it had never been hurt.
sections.title: The Merchant of the Hijaz

quote.text: Stretch out your leg.
quote.who: The Prophet ﷺ, to 'Abdullah bin 'Atik; he passed his hand over it, and it healed

body: Muhammad bin Maslamah went with thirty men against Banu Bakr bin Kilab in Najd, scattered them and came back with spoils, and with a prisoner they had come upon: Thumamah bin Uthal, chief of Banu Hanifah of Al-Yamamah. They tied him to a pillar of the mosque.

"What have you to say, Thumamah?" the Prophet ﷺ asked him. "Good, Muhammad. If you kill, you kill a man whose blood will be avenged. If you are generous, you are generous to one who will be grateful. If you want wealth, ask, and you will have what you wish." Three days he asked, and three days Thumamah said the same. On the third he set him free. Thumamah went a little way off, washed, came back, and bore witness that there is no god but Allah and that Muhammad is His Messenger.

He went on to Makkah for 'Umrah. Quraish said he had left his religion. He had become a Muslim, he said, and by Allah, not one grain of wheat would reach them from Al-Yamamah until the Prophet ﷺ allowed it. He kept his word, until the Prophet ﷺ himself asked him to let the grain go.
sections.title: Thumamah

quote.text: By Allah, there was no face on earth I hated more than yours, and now yours is the dearest of all faces to me.
quote.who: Thumamah bin Uthal

body: Banu Lihyan had betrayed his Companions at Ar-Raji'. While Quraish and the Arabs still sought his blood, he had not wanted to go so deep towards Makkah. Now, with the Confederates broken, he set out with two hundred men, giving out that he was going towards Syria, then turned south to Batn Gharran, where his Companions had been killed, and prayed for Allah's mercy on them.

Banu Lihyan had heard and fled into the mountains. He sent ten horsemen on to Kura' Al-Ghamim, near enough to Makkah for Quraish to hear of it, and came home after fourteen days. Then the small marches went on, one after another, into the lands of those who still made war on Madinah.
sections.title: Batn Gharran
sections.when: Rabi' al-Awwal or Jumada al-Ula 6 AH · 627 CE

parts.title: The Trench
parts.blurb: Betrayals at Ar-Raji' and the Well of Ma'unah, the exile of Banu An-Nadir, and ten thousand men stopped by a trench and a wind.

body: With the Confederates broken, small columns went out one after another against the tribes still at war with Madinah. Most ended without hard fighting; they were meant to show the enemies of Islam that they could no longer stop it.
sections.title: The Marches of the Sixth Year
sections.place: Najd, the Hijaz and the north
list: 'Ukashah bin Mihsan against Banu Asad; they fled and left two hundred camels
Muhammad bin Maslamah against Banu Tha'labah; a hundred of them fell on his men in their sleep and killed all but him, and he escaped badly wounded
Abu 'Ubaidah bin Al-Jarrah with forty men, marching all night; the enemy fled to the mountains but for one, wounded, who later became a Muslim; much was taken
Zaid bin Harithah against Banu Sulaim, guided by a woman of Muzainah, whom the Prophet ﷺ later freed and married to one of his Companions
Zaid with fifteen men against Banu Tha'labah; twenty camels taken, the people fled
Zaid with twelve men to scout; they were attacked and nine were killed

body: Zaid bin Harithah went out with a hundred and seventy riders to Al-'Is and took a caravan of Quraish. Its leader escaped: Abul-'As, the husband of the Prophet's daughter Zainab, freed after Badr on his promise to let her go to Madinah. He took refuge with Zainab in Madinah, and begged her to ask her father for his goods back.

The Prophet ﷺ did not order it. He asked the people, and they gave back everything. Abul-'As went to Makkah, returned to every man what had been entrusted to him, accepted Islam and emigrated to Madinah. After three and a half years apart, the Prophet ﷺ gave Zainab back to him on their first marriage, for the ayah forbidding believers to marry disbelievers had not yet come down.
sections.title: Abul-'As Comes Home

body: Abu 'Ubaidah bin Al-Jarrah led three hundred riders to watch for a caravan of Quraish. Their food ran out, and they were so hungry they ate the leaves of trees, so they were called the Army of the Leaves. One man slaughtered camels for them three at a time, nine in all, until Abu 'Ubaidah stopped him.

Then the sea threw up a great whale, rich with fat, and they lived on it for half a month. When they came home and told the Prophet ﷺ, he said it was provision Allah had brought out for them, and asked if they had any of it left, so that he might eat some too.
sections.title: The Army of Leaves
sections.place: The coast of the Red Sea

quote.text: It is provision Allah brought out for you. Have you any of its meat with you, to give us some?
quote.who: The Prophet ﷺ, to the Army of the Leaves

body: On 2 Sha'ban word came that Al-Harith bin Dirar, chief of Banu Al-Mustaliq, was gathering his men and other Arabs to attack Madinah. Buraidah bin Al-Husaib Al-Aslami went to see for himself, spoke with Al-Harith and heard it from his own mouth. A spy they sent towards the Muslims was caught and killed. The Prophet ﷺ left Zaid bin Harithah over Madinah and marched; the Arabs who had joined Al-Harith heard and ran for their lives.

Abu Bakr carried the standard of the Emigrants and Sa'd bin 'Ubadah that of the Helpers. They met at the well of Al-Muraisi'. Arrows flew for an hour, then the Muslims charged, and it was over. Some of the enemy were killed, their women and children taken, and much was won. One Muslim died, killed by mistake by a Helper.

Among the captives was Juwairiyah, the daughter of Al-Harith their chief, and the Prophet ﷺ married her. At once the Muslims set free a hundred of her people's captives who had become Muslims: they were now the Prophet's in-laws.
sections.title: Al-Muraisi'

quote.text: They are the in-laws of the Messenger of Allah.
quote.who: the Muslims, freeing the captives of Banu Al-Mustaliq

body: 'Abdullah bin Ubai had never forgiven the Prophet ﷺ for the crown he had lost. Each Friday he would stand before the sermon and tell the people to honour and obey this Messenger, as a mockery; after Uhud they pulled him down by his cloak, and he walked out saying he wanted no one's forgiveness. When the Prophet ﷺ married Zainab bint Jahsh, after Zaid his adopted son had divorced her, the hypocrites spread that it was a great sin, until ayahs came down to settle it [33:1].

At Al-Muraisi', 'Umar's hired man Jahjah and Sinan Al-Juhani pushed at the well. One shouted "Helpers!", the other "Emigrants!" "The calls of the Ignorance, while I am among you? Leave them: they are rotten." Ibn Ubai heard of it and burst out: they had brought this on themselves, sheltering these men and sharing their wealth with them; when they got back to Madinah, the more honourable would drive out the meaner. A boy, Zaid bin Arqam, heard him and told his uncle, who told the Prophet ﷺ. 'Umar wanted 'Abbad bin Bishr to kill him. "And have people say Muhammad kills his companions?" Instead he ordered a march at an hour no one marched, all that day and night, until they dropped asleep and forgot.

Ibn Ubai swore he had never said it, and some of the Helpers said the boy must have heard wrong. Zaid sat at home in shame, until Surat Al-Munafiqun came down with the very words: it is they who say, do not spend on those with the Messenger until they leave him, and the more honourable will drive out the meaner [63:7-8]. "Allah has confirmed what you said," the Prophet ﷺ told him. At the gate of Madinah stood Ibn Ubai's own son, 'Abdullah, a believer, with his sword drawn: his father would not enter until the Messenger of Allah gave him leave, for he was the mighty and his father the humbled.
sections.title: "The More Honourable Will Drive Out the Meaner"

quote.text: By Allah, you shall not enter until the Messenger of Allah gives you leave; for he is the mighty one, and you the humbled.
quote.who: 'Abdullah, the son of 'Abdullah bin Ubai, to his father

body: 'Aishah was with him on this march. Near Madinah the army stopped for the night, and she went a little way off for a need. Coming back she found she had lost her necklace, a borrowed one, and went back to look for it. When she returned the army had gone; the men had lifted her litter onto the camel without noticing she was not in it, for she was young and light. She sat down alone and wept until sleep took her.

Safwan bin Al-Mu'attal, riding at the rear, knew her, for he had seen her before the veil was commanded. He set her on his camel and walked, leading it, all the way to Madinah. 'Abdullah bin Ubai and the hypocrites made a scandal of it, and some Muslims were drawn in. The Prophet ﷺ took counsel; the Aws and Khazraj almost came to blows over it, until he calmed them.

'Aishah, knowing nothing, fell ill for a month. When she heard, she went to her parents and wept for two days and a night without sleep, until she thought her heart would burst. He came to her: if she was innocent, Allah would clear her; if not, let her ask His forgiveness. Her tears stopped. She asked her parents to answer for her; they did not know what to say. So she answered herself: if she said she was innocent, and Allah knew she was, they would not believe her; if she confessed to what Allah knew she had not done, they would. She could only say what the father of Yusuf said [12:18]. Then she lay down. And at that moment the revelation came that cleared her [24:11].

Mistah bin Athathah, Hassan bin Thabit and Hamnah bint Jahsh, who had spread it, were flogged eighty lashes. 'Abdullah bin Ubai was not; but from then on his own people despised him. "Do you see, 'Umar?" the Prophet ﷺ said a month later. "Had I had him killed that day, noses would have quivered for him; now, if I ordered it, they would kill him themselves."
sections.title: The Necklace
sections.when: On the way home from Al-Muraisi', 6 AH
sections.place: The road to Madinah, and Madinah

quote.text: Patience is most fitting, and it is Allah whose help is sought against what you describe.
quote.who: 'Aishah, in the words of the father of Yusuf

body: More columns went out in the months after Al-Muraisi'. The Prophet ﷺ wound a turban on 'Abdur-Rahman bin 'Awf's head with his own hands and sent him to Banu Kalb at Dumat al-Jandal: if they obeyed, let him marry their king's daughter. He called them for three days; they accepted Islam, and he married Tamadur bint Al-Asbagh.
sections.title: Turbans and Raids
sections.place: Dumat al-Jandal, Fadak and Wadi Al-Qura
list: 'Ali against Banu Sa'd bin Bakr, who were raising men for the Jews of Khaibar; travelling by day and hiding their camp by night, they caught one of their messengers, found their camp and took five hundred camels and two thousand sheep

Abu Bakr, or Zaid, against Fazarah, after their attempt on the Prophet's life; Salamah bin Al-Akwa' turned back their women with an arrow between them and the mountain; Umm Qirfah's daughter was later exchanged for Muslim captives in Makkah

men of 'Ukl and 'Urainah who had professed Islam were sent to the pastures to recover their health; they killed the Prophet's herdsman, drove off the camels and left Islam; Kurz bin Jabir brought them back, and they were put to death for what they had done

body: He dreamed that he and his Companions entered the Sacred Mosque in safety and did 'Umrah, their heads shaved and their hair cut. He told them, and they were overjoyed.

He washed his clothes and mounted his camel Al-Qaswa'. With Ibn Umm Maktum over Madinah, or Numailah Al-Laithi, he set out on a Monday early in Dhul-Qa'dah with fourteen or fifteen hundred men, and Umm Salamah. Many of the Bedouin stayed home. They carried no arms but a traveller's sheathed sword. At Dhul-Hulaifah the sacrificial camels were garlanded and they all put on ihram, so that everyone could see they had come as pilgrims.

A scout brought word that Quraish had gathered their allies and blocked the road. He asked his Companions; they would fight no one unless they were stopped from the House. Quraish sent Khalid bin Al-Walid with two hundred horsemen to catch them at their noon prayer; the ayahs of the prayer of fear came down, and the Muslims turned off by a rough, rocky track, and Khalid rode back to tell Quraish.
sections.title: A Dream of the Ka'bah
sections.when: Monday, beginning of Dhul-Qa'dah 6 AH · March 628 CE

quote.text: We would fight no one, unless they stop us from the House.
quote.who: The Companions, asked what they should do

body: At Thaniyat Al-Murar his camel knelt and would not get up. He swore that whatever plan Quraish offered him that honoured the sanctity of Allah's House, he would accept. Then he urged her on, and she leapt up.

They camped at the far edge of Al-Hudaibiyah by a well with only a little water in it, and soon the men were complaining of thirst. He took an arrow from his quiver and had it set in the well, and the water welled up until they had all drunk their fill.
sections.title: Al-Qaswa' Kneels

body: Budail bin Warqa' of Khuza'ah came to ask what he wanted. Only to visit the House, he said. If Quraish would accept the faith, as others had, they were welcome; but if they barred the way, he would fight them to the last, and Allah's command would be done. Budail took the message to Quraish, who did not want to hear it. They sent Mikraz bin Hafs: "a treacherous man," the Prophet ﷺ said as he came, and gave him the same message.

Next came Al-Hulais bin 'Alqamah, an ally of theirs. He was so moved by the Muslims' reverence for the House that he went back and warned Quraish he would break with them if they barred people come to honour it. Then came 'Urwah bin Mas'ud Ath-Thaqafi. "Muhammad, you have gathered a rabble to set against your own kin. By Allah, I think they will desert you tomorrow." Abu Bakr answered him sharply. As 'Urwah talked he took hold of the Prophet's beard, and Al-Mughirah bin Shu'bah, standing over him in a helmet with his sword, struck his hand with the scabbard.
'Urwah watched them closely, and went back to Quraish.
sections.title: "Never Have I Seen a King So Loved"

quote.text: I have been to Chosroes, to Caesar and to the Negus in their kingdoms, and never have I seen a king among his people as Muhammad is among his Companions. When he makes wudu' they will not let its water fall to the ground; when he speaks they lower their voices. They will never give him up. He has offered you a fair plan: take it.
quote.who: 'Urwah bin Mas'ud, to Quraish

body: Seeing their elders lean towards peace, some hot-headed young men of Quraish planned to slip into the Muslim camp and start a fight that would end all talk of it. Seventy or eighty of them came down by night from the mountain of At-Tan'im. Muhammad bin Maslamah, captain of the guard, took them all. The Prophet ﷺ, for the sake of what was coming, let them go.
sections.title: Seventy by Night

quote.text: It is He who held back their hands from you and your hands from them in the valley of Makkah, after He had given you the upper hand over them.
quote.who: Al-Fath 48:24

body: He asked 'Umar to go to Quraish. 'Umar asked to be excused: Quraish hated him, and he had no strong kin in Makkah to protect him. Send 'Uthman, he said, whose family was among the most powerful there. 'Uthman went to Abu Sufyan and the chiefs: they had come only to visit the House and worship there, and would leave in peace. He was to call them to Islam, and to give the believers hidden in Makkah the good news that victory was near. Quraish would not move. But they told 'Uthman he could go round the House himself. "How could I, when the Messenger of Allah has been kept from it?"

He was gone long, and word spread that he had been killed. The Muslims gave the Prophet ﷺ their pledge that they would not run, some that they would die. Abu Sinan Al-Asadi was the first; Salamah bin Al-Akwa' pledged three times, at the beginning, the middle and the end. Then he held out his own hand: "This is for 'Uthman." He took the pledge under a tree, 'Umar holding his hand and Ma'qil bin Yasar holding back a branch from his face. Every man there pledged but one hypocrite, Jadd bin Qais. Then 'Uthman came back, and pledged too.
sections.title: The Pledge Under the Tree

quote.text: Allah was pleased with the believers when they pledged themselves to you under the tree.
quote.who: Al-Fath 48:18

body: Seeing the Muslims ready to die, Quraish sent Suhail bin 'Amr to make peace. 'Ali wrote. "In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Kind," the Prophet ﷺ dictated. "I do not know Ar-Rahman," said Suhail; "write: In Your name, O Allah." The Muslims muttered; he agreed. "This is what Muhammad, the Messenger of Allah, has agreed with Suhail bin 'Amr." "If we believed you were the Messenger of Allah, we would not have kept you from the House or fought you. Write your name and your father's." The Muslims would not; so he rubbed the words out with his own hand, and dictated, "Muhammad, the son of 'Abdullah." Khuza'ah, the old allies of Banu Hashim, at once joined his side of the treaty.
sections.title: The Treaty
list: The Muslims go home this year, and come back next year for three days, with no arms but sheathed swords in their bags
No war for ten years; each side safe from the other
Any tribe may join Muhammad's side or Quraish's
Any man of Quraish who comes to Muhammad without his guardian's leave is sent back; any of Muhammad's who goes to Quraish is not

body: As the treaty was being written, Abu Jandal, Suhail's own son, stumbled into the camp in chains, worn out from the torture. "This is the first test of your word," said Suhail. The treaty was not yet signed when he came, said the Prophet ﷺ. "But its terms were agreed." Abu Jandal cried out, "Muslims, will I be sent back to the idolaters to be turned from my religion?"
His heart went out to him, but he would keep his word.

'Umar could not hold back his anger and grief. He spoke bitterly, and brought his sword close, so that Abu Jandal could seize it and strike his father. Abu Jandal spared his father, and was led away in his chains.
sections.title: Abu Jandal in Chains

quote.text: Be patient, Abu Jandal, and hope for Allah's reward. Allah will make for you and the weak with you relief and a way out. We have made a peace with them and given them our word before Allah, and we will not break it.
quote.who: The Prophet ﷺ

body: When the treaty was done he told them to slaughter their sacrificial animals and shave. No one moved; they were too heartbroken. Three times he said it. He went in to Umm Salamah and told her. She told him to go out and slaughter his own camel first, and have his head shaved.

He did, and when they saw it they rose, in their grief, and slaughtered, and shaved one another's heads. He prayed three times for those who shaved, and once for those who cut their hair short. A camel or a cow was sacrificed for each seven men. His own was a camel that had been Abu Jahl's, taken at Badr, to anger the idolaters. Ka'b bin 'Ujrah, ill and in ihram, was allowed to shave his head, paying for it by a sheep, three days' fast or feeding six poor men, as the ayah came [2:196].
sections.title: Umm Salamah's Counsel

quote.text: Go out yourself, slaughter your camel and have your head shaved.
quote.who: Umm Salamah's counsel to the Prophet ﷺ

body: Believing women escaped from Makkah to Madinah and asked for refuge. When their families demanded them back, he would not return them, for the ayah came: test them, and if you know them to be believers, do not send them back to the disbelievers; they are not lawful to them, nor they to them; give the husbands what they spent on them [60:10]. Either the treaty had spoken only of men, or the Qur'an set that part of it aside. Muslim men were told likewise to let go of wives who remained idolaters; 'Umar divorced two wives he had married before Islam.
sections.title: The Believing Women

quote.text: When believing women come to you as emigrants, test them; Allah knows best their faith.
quote.who: Al-Mumtahanah 60:10

body: To many Muslims it felt like defeat: no 'Umrah this year, and a peace that seemed to bow to the idolaters. 'Umar could not bear it. "Are you not truly the Messenger of Allah?" "Yes." "Are we not in the right and they in the wrong?" "Yes." "Then why accept humiliation in our religion?" "I am the Messenger of Allah. I do not disobey Him, and He will help me." "Did you not tell us we would go to the House?" "Did I tell you it would be this year?" 'Umar went to Abu Bakr and said the same, and Abu Bakr answered as the Prophet ﷺ had.

Then Surat Al-Fath came down: We have given you a manifest victory [48:1]. He sent for 'Umar and told him. 'Umar was overjoyed, and full of regret; to atone for what he had said, he gave in charity, fasted, prayed and freed slaves.

And it was a victory. Quraish had recognised the Muslims as equals and given up their claim to stand between Arabia and its faith; the war they had led for years was over. With peace, people met and talked, and no one heard of Islam with an open mind but he entered it. Fourteen hundred went to Al-Hudaibiyah; two years later ten thousand marched on Makkah.
sections.title: A Manifest Victory
sections.when: On the road home, Dhul-Qa'dah 6 AH

quote.text: We have given you a manifest victory.
quote.who: Al-Fath 48:1

body: Back in Madinah, Abu Basir, a Muslim who had escaped from Quraish, came to him. Quraish sent two men to fetch him, and the Prophet ﷺ handed him over. On the road Abu Basir killed one of them, and the other ran back to Madinah with Abu Basir behind him. "You have kept your word," Abu Basir said; "you gave me up, and Allah has saved me." "Woe to his mother," said the Prophet ﷺ, "he would light a war, if he had men with him."

Abu Basir understood he would be sent back again, and went off to the coast at Saif Al-Bahr. One by one the oppressed Muslims of Makkah escaped and joined him, Abu Jandal among them, until they were a band that preyed on Quraish's caravans. At last Quraish begged the Prophet ﷺ, by Allah and by their kinship, to take them in: whoever came to him from now on would be safe. The clause that had so grieved the Muslims fell away.
sections.title: Abu Basir by the Sea
sections.place: Madinah, and the coast at Saif Al-Bahr

quote.text: Woe to his mother: he would kindle a war, if only he had men with him.
quote.who: The Prophet ﷺ, of Abu Basir

body: In the early part of the seventh year three of the foremost men of Makkah came to Madinah and accepted Islam: 'Amr bin Al-'As, Khalid bin Al-Walid, who had turned the day at Uhud, and 'Uthman bin Talhah.
sections.title: "Quraish Have Given Us Their Own Blood"

quote.text: Quraish have given us their own blood.
quote.who: The Prophet ﷺ, as 'Amr, Khalid and 'Uthman bin Talhah came to him

parts.title: Al-Hudaibiyah
parts.blurb: A raid that ended in a slander, a dream of the Ka'bah, a pledge under a tree, and a treaty that looked like defeat and was called a manifest victory.

body: Back from Al-Hudaibiyah, at peace with Quraish, he decided to write to the kings beyond Arabia and call them to Islam. To vouch for his envoys, a silver seal was made, engraved with three words, one above another: Allah, Messenger, Muhammad. He chose envoys for their knowledge and experience, and in Muharram of the seventh year, a few days before he marched on Khaibar, they set out.
sections.title: A Silver Seal
sections.when: End of 6 AH – Muharram 7 AH · 628 CE
facts: To Al-Mundhir bin Sawa, governor of Bahrain
To Haudhah bin 'Ali, governor of Al-Yamamah
To Al-Harith bin Abi Shimr Al-Ghassani, at Damascus
To Jaifar and 'Abd, sons of Al-Julanda, in Oman

body: 'Amr bin Umaiyah carried the letter to Ashamah, the Negus. It greeted him with peace for whoever follows guidance, bore witness that Allah has no partner, no wife and no son, and that Muhammad is His servant and Messenger, called him to Islam, and ended with the ayah calling the People of the Book to a word just between them [3:64].

The Negus took the letter and laid it on his eyes. He came down from his throne to the ground, declared his Islam, and wrote back: by the Lord of heaven and earth, 'Isa is no more than what you say of him; he had taken in Ja'far and his companions, and he bore witness that Muhammad was the Messenger of Allah, and gave his pledge to Allah through Ja'far.

At the Prophet's request he sent Ja'far and the emigrants home; they reached him at Khaibar. The Negus died in Rajab of the ninth year, and the Prophet ﷺ told the Muslims of his death and prayed the funeral prayer for him from afar.
sections.title: The Negus Answers

quote.text: By the Lord of the heavens and the earth, 'Isa is no more than what you say of him.
quote.who: The Negus, in his reply

body: Hatib bin Abi Balta'ah took the letter to Al-Muqawqis, ruler of Egypt and leader of the Copts. Before he handed it over he spoke to him: there had been one before you who called himself the supreme lord, and Allah made an example of him; take warning from others, not let others take warning from you. We will not leave our religion, said the Muqawqis, except for a better one. Hatib answered that Islam was enough in place of everything else; that as Musa foretold 'Isa, 'Isa foretold Muhammad; and that they were calling him to Islam as he called the people of the Torah to the Gospel.

The Muqawqis thought on it. This prophet, he said, called to nothing hateful, nor was he a wandering sorcerer or a lying soothsayer; he had the marks of prophethood. He had the letter put in an ivory casket and wrote back that he knew a prophet was still to come, but had thought he would rise in Syria. He sent gifts: two maids of noble Coptic families, clothing, and a mount to ride, named Duldul, which lived on into the days of Mu'awiyah.
He did not accept Islam. One of the maids, Mariyah, stayed with the Prophet ﷺ and bore him his son Ibrahim; the other, Sirin, he gave to Hassan bin Thabit.
sections.title: The Ruler of Egypt

quote.text: This prophet calls to nothing hateful; he is no wandering sorcerer and no lying soothsayer, and he has the marks of prophethood.
quote.who: Al-Muqawqis

body: 'Abdullah bin Hudhafah As-Sahmi took the letter towards Chosroes by way of the governor of Bahrain. The king of Persia was enraged that the Prophet's name was written above his own. He tore the letter to pieces, and ordered his governor in Yemen, Badhan, to send two men to bring this Arab to him.

Badhan's two men came to Madinah. The Prophet ﷺ told them that he had learned by revelation that Chosroes Parvez had been killed by his own son, and that Islam would reach as far as the kingdom of Chosroes. They hurried back to Badhan; soon after, a letter from the new king, Sherweh, confirmed it and told Badhan to do nothing more about the Arab. Badhan, and the Persians with him in Yemen, accepted Islam.
sections.title: Chosroes Tears the Letter

quote.text: Tell your new king that my religion will reach as far as the kingdom of Chosroes.
quote.who: The Prophet ﷺ, to Badhan's two men

body: Dihyah Al-Kalbi carried the letter to the governor of Busra, to send on to Heraclius. It happened that Abu Sufyan was trading in Syria with some men of Quraish, and Heraclius, at Iliya', sent for them. Who was nearest of kin to this man who called himself a prophet? Abu Sufyan was, so he was seated in front, his companions behind him, told to call out if he lied. "By Allah," Abu Sufyan said later, "had I not feared they would call me a liar, I would have lied about him."

So he told the truth: of noble lineage; no king among his forefathers; followed by the weak, more of them every day; no one had ever caught him in a lie or a betrayal; the war between them went by turns; he told people to worship Allah alone and leave what their fathers worshipped, and to pray, to be truthful, chaste and keep the ties of kinship. Heraclius weighed each answer: Prophets come from noble lines; a man who will not lie about people would not lie about Allah; the weak follow prophets; faith, once its sweetness enters the heart, is not abandoned. If this was true, the man would rule the ground beneath his feet. He had known a prophet was coming, but never thought he would be an Arab. If he could, he would go to him and wash his feet.

Then the letter was read, and the court was in uproar, and the Arabs were put out. "Ibn Abi Kabshah's affair has grown so great," Abu Sufyan said to his friends, "that the king of the Romans fears him." From then on he was sure Muhammad would win, until Allah brought him to Islam. Heraclius did not believe. On his way home Dihyah was robbed by men of Judham at Hisma; Zaid bin Harithah went against them with five hundred men, and when a chief of Judham who was a Muslim complained, the Prophet ﷺ had everything taken given back.
sections.title: Heraclius Questions Abu Sufyan

quote.text: If what you say is true, he will rule the very ground beneath these feet of mine. If I could reach him, I would wash his feet.
quote.who: Heraclius, to Abu Sufyan

body: The answers were as different as the men. Some believed; some held on to what they had. But all of them now had to think about Islam, and a new prophet.

In Oman, 'Amr bin Al-'As went first to 'Abd, the gentler of the brothers. What had his father thought of this faith? He had died before it, said 'Amr; he wished he had believed, and he himself had been the same until Allah guided him, at the court of the Negus, who had believed too, and his bishops and monks with him. "Beware of lying, 'Amr; nothing shames a man more." "I do not lie, and our religion forbids it." What did his Prophet command? To obey Allah, keep faith with kin, and leave wrongdoing, adultery, wine and the worship of idols and the cross. "These are fair things he calls to." His brother Jaifar was harder, and kept 'Amr waiting days; but after the two brothers talked alone, both accepted Islam.
sections.title: Bahrain, Al-Yamamah, Damascus and Oman
list: some of his people accepted Islam and some did not, and he asked what to do about the Magians and Jews of his land; let him stay in his post, he was told, and let those who keep their religion pay the jizyah

a famous poet and orator, he would follow if given a share in the rule; the Prophet ﷺ refused, for the land is Allah's to give. Haudhah died soon after, and the Prophet ﷺ said a liar claiming prophethood would come out of Al-Yamamah, and be killed
Al-Harith bin Abi Shimr Al-Ghassani at Damascus
threw the letter down in a rage: who would take his kingdom from him? He would march on him
both accepted Islam; the letter seems to have gone later, after the conquest of Makkah

body: At dawn 'Abdur-Rahman Al-Fazari raided the Prophet's camels at their pasture, killed the man watching them and drove them off. Salamah bin Al-Akwa', who was there with Talhah's horse, sent the Prophet's servant Rabah galloping to Madinah, climbed a hill, shouted three times towards the city for help, and set off after the raiders alone on foot.

He shot at them as he ran, chanting, "I am the son of Al-Akwa'; today the mean will meet their end." When a horseman turned on him he hid at the foot of a tree and shot his horse. When they went into a narrow pass he climbed above them and rolled down stones. He chased them until every camel was free, and they threw away more than thirty cloaks and thirty spears to lighten themselves; he marked each with a stone for the Muslims to find. Then the Prophet's horsemen came through the trees. Akhram fought 'Abdur-Rahman and was killed by him; Abu Qatadah killed 'Abdur-Rahman. Salamah drove the rest from the water of Dhu Qarad before they could drink.

He begged for a hundred men to finish them. "Ibn Al-Akwa', you have had your fill; now be gentle. They are already feasting among Ghatafan." He gave Salamah two shares, a rider's and a footman's, and had him ride home behind him on his camel Al-'Adba'.
sections.title: The Son of Al-Akwa'
sections.place: Dhu Qarad, a day's ride from Madinah

quote.text: Our best horseman today is Abu Qatadah, and our best footman Salamah.
quote.who: The Prophet ﷺ

body: Quraish were at peace with him now. The Jews of Khaibar, sixty to eighty miles north of Madinah, were not: they had stirred Quraizah to betray him, stayed in league with Ghatafan and plotted against his life. He took with him only those who had pledged at Al-Hudaibiyah, about fourteen hundred men, and Allah had promised them gains [48:20]; those who had hung back before now asked to come, and were refused [48:15]. Siba' bin 'Arfatah stayed over Madinah. It was then that Abu Hurairah came and accepted Islam.

'Abdullah bin Ubai sent word to Khaibar: you outnumber them, and are better armed. They sent to Ghatafan, promising half Khaibar's dates for their help. So he camped at Ar-Raji', between Ghatafan and Khaibar, to cut them off.

They marched by night. 'Amir bin Al-Akwa' sang to urge the camels on: O Allah, without You we would not have been guided, nor given charity, nor prayed. "Who is this driver?" "'Amir." "May Allah have mercy on him." The men knew what that meant when he said it of a Companion on the march. At As-Sahba' he called for their food, and what little they brought increased in his hands until all had eaten. Then, as Khaibar came in sight below, he stopped and prayed for the good of this town and its people, and refuge from its evil.
At dawn the people of Khaibar came out with their spades and baskets to their fields, saw the army and ran back shouting, "Muhammad and his army!"
sections.title: The Road to Khaibar

quote.text: Allahu akbar, Khaibar is ruined. When we come down into a people's land, evil is the morning of those who were warned.
quote.who: The Prophet ﷺ, at dawn below Khaibar

body: Khaibar was two districts of forts. In the first, An-Natah and Ash-Shiqq, stood Na'im, As-Sa'b bin Mu'adh, Az-Zubair, Ubai and An-Nizar; in the second, Al-Katibah, stood Al-Qamus, the fort of the family of Abul-Huqaiq, Al-Watih and As-Sulalim. Al-Hubab bin Al-Mundhir advised moving the camp, and he moved it.

"Tomorrow I will give the banner to a man who loves Allah and His Messenger, and whom Allah and His Messenger love." All night they wondered who it would be. In the morning he called for 'Ali, whose eyes were sore; he prayed for him, and they were healed. 'Ali said he would fight them until they became Muslims. "Go gently until you reach them; call them to Islam and tell them their duty to Allah. By Allah, that Allah should guide one man through you is better for you than the finest camels."

At Na'im, Marhab the Jew called for combat. 'Amir bin Al-Akwa' answered; his own sword rebounded and cut his knee, and he died of it. "He has a double reward," the Prophet ﷺ said, holding two fingers together. 'Ali killed Marhab, and Az-Zubair killed his brother Yasir. Fort by fort they fell: As-Sa'b to Al-Hubab after three days; Az-Zubair after a Jew showed them the spring beneath it and it was cut; Ubai to Abu Dujanah; An-Nizar, high and strong, to the catapults. Hungry, some men cooked the flesh of tame donkeys; he had the pots overturned and forbade it. Then he besieged Al-Katibah fourteen days, and as the catapults were readied they asked for terms.
sections.title: "A Man Who Loves Allah and His Messenger"

quote.text: That Allah should guide one man through you is better for you than the finest camels.
quote.who: The Prophet ﷺ, giving 'Ali the banner at Khaibar

body: Ibn Abul-Huqaiq came to make terms: their lives would be spared if they left Khaibar and its lands and left their gold and silver behind, and the treaty would hold only if they hid nothing. But the sons of Abul-Huqaiq hid a leather bag of jewels and money that Huyai bin Akhtab had carried out of Madinah. Kinanah bin Ar-Rabi' denied it to the last, and when it was found where he had hidden it, he and the two sons were put to death for breaking the treaty.

The Jews asked to stay and work their land, which they knew better than anyone, for half its harvest, and he agreed. Of the land he set half aside for the needs of the Muslims and for guests and delegations, and half went to those who had been at Al-Hudaibiyah, whether at Khaibar or not.

Some sixteen to eighteen Muslims were killed at Khaibar, and ninety-three of the Jews. As the conquest ended, Ja'far bin Abi Talib arrived from Abyssinia with his companions, and with Abu Musa Al-Ash'ari and some fifty of his people, whose ship from Yemen had carried them to Abyssinia, where they had stayed with Ja'far. He gave them a share of the spoils.
sections.title: Half the Harvest
list: thirty-six; a horseman got three portions, a man on foot one
we never ate our fill until we took Khaibar
now we can eat our fill of dates
home in Madinah, they gave back to the Helpers all the gifts they had been given

body: Among the captives was Safiyah, daughter of Huyai bin Akhtab, chief of Banu An-Nadir, whose husband Kinanah had been put to death. Dihyah Al-Kalbi asked leave to take a captive and chose her. The Companions told the Prophet ﷺ that the daughter of the chief of Quraizah and An-Nadir was fit only for him. He called her to Islam, freed her, and married her when she accepted. The wedding feast, of dates, fat and barley, was held on the way home at Sadd As-Sahba'.

A Jewish woman, Zainab bint Al-Harith, sent him a roast sheep, poisoned. He took a mouthful, did not like it and spat it out. She confessed: if he was a king, she would be rid of him; if a prophet, he would be told. He let it pass, until Bishr bin Al-Bara' died of the poison; then she was put to death for it.
sections.title: Safiyah, and the Poisoned Sheep

quote.text: If he were a king, I would be rid of him; and if he were a prophet, he would be told.
quote.who: Zainab bint Al-Harith, of the poisoned sheep

body: The rest of the Jews of the north made their peace. While he was away, Aban bin Sa'id had kept the Bedouin off Madinah, and he joined him at Khaibar after its fall. The Prophet ﷺ came home late in Safar or early in Rabi' al-Awwal of the seventh year.
sections.title: Fadak, Wadi Al-Qura and Taima'
list: Allah cast fear into its people, and they asked for peace on the same terms as Khaibar; it was taken without a fight, so it was the Prophet's own
he called them to Islam and they refused; eleven of them fell one by one, with a fresh call to Islam after each; after two days they surrendered, and he stayed four days and gave them Khaibar's terms
hearing of all this, its people offered a treaty and tribute without a fight

body: With Quraish at peace and the Jews subdued, there remained the Bedouin of Najd, scattered in the desert, raiding and running. Word came that Banu Muharib and Banu Tha'labah of Ghatafan were gathering. He set out with four to seven hundred men, leaving Abu Dharr, or 'Uthman, over Madinah, and went deep into their land to Nakhlah. They met the Bedouin there but no one fought, and he led the prayer of fear. Abu Musa Al-Ash'ari remembered six of them sharing one camel by turns, their feet so torn that their nails came off and they bound them in rags.

Jabir told how they rested at noon under the trees, and the Prophet ﷺ hung his sword on a branch and slept. He woke to find a Bedouin standing over him with the sword drawn. "Who will protect you from me?" "Allah." The sword fell from the man's hand, and the Prophet ﷺ took it up: "And who will protect you from me?" "You are the better one to hold a sword." He would not fight him again, he said, nor join anyone against him, and was let go, and told his people he had come from the best of men.

A captive woman's husband swore to have a Muslim's blood. By night he found 'Abbad bin Bishr standing guard in prayer and shot him. 'Abbad pulled the arrow out and prayed on, and again, and again, three arrows, before he finished and woke his companion 'Ammar. Why had he not woken him at the first? He was in the middle of a surah, he said, and did not want to cut it short.
sections.title: The Expedition of Rags

quote.text: Allah.
quote.who: The Prophet ﷺ, when the Bedouin asked who would protect him

body: The Confederates' three parties had been met one by one: Quraish at peace, the Jews subdued, the Bedouin humbled. Some of the Bedouin now accepted Islam and later rode with him to Makkah and Hunain. Small columns went out against the last pockets of trouble.
sections.title: The Marches of the Seventh Year
sections.place: Najd, Hawazin's lands and the north
list: Ghalib bin 'Abdullah Al-Laithi; a flood kept the pursuers from them on the way home
'Umar with thirty men against Hawazin; they fled before him
Bani Murrah near Fadak, Sha'ban 7 AH
Bashir bin Sa'd with thirty; caught by night on the way back, all were killed but Bashir, who healed among the Jews of Fadak
Ghalib with a hundred and thirty; Usamah bin Zaid killed Mirdas bin Nahik after he had said there is no god but Allah. "Did you open his heart, to see if he spoke the truth?"
'Abdullah bin Rawahah with thirty brought him from Khaibar, where he was stirring up Ghatafan; a quarrel on the road ended in his death and his thirty men's
Bashir bin Sa'd with three hundred, marching by night; the enemy fled
Abu Hadrad and two men broke up Jusham bin Mu'awiyah's gathering of Qais by a stratagem

body: A year after Al-Hudaibiyah he went to make the 'Umrah the treaty allowed, with all who had been at Al-Hudaibiyah: two thousand men, some women and children, and sixty camels for sacrifice. 'Uwaif bin Al-Adbat, or Abu Ruhm, stayed over Madinah. Fearing a trick, they took their weapons, but left them with two hundred men eight miles out, and went in with sheathed swords, he riding Al-Qaswa', the Companions all round him calling, "Here I am, O Allah, at Your service!"

Quraish had left the town for the hills and watched from Mount Qu'aiqi'an. They had said the fever of Yathrib had worn the Muslims out, so he told them to run the first three rounds of the tawaf and walk the rest, to show their strength. 'Abdullah bin Rawahah walked before him chanting verses. They went between As-Safa and Al-Marwah, sacrificed at Al-Marwah and shaved, and then those who had kept the weapons came in and did the same.

On the fourth morning the chiefs of Quraish sent 'Ali to tell him his three days were over. He kept the treaty and left, and stopped at Sarif. On this visit his uncle Al-'Abbas offered him Maimunah bint Al-Harith, his wife's sister, in marriage, and the wedding was at Sarif. It is called the 'Umrah of the treaty, or the 'Umrah made good. After it a few more columns went out: fifty under Ibn Abul-'Awja' to Banu Sulaim, two hundred under Ghalib to Fadak, fifteen under Ka'b bin 'Umair against Quda'ah, all killed but one, and twenty-five under Shuja' bin Wahb against Hawazin.
sections.title: The 'Umrah of the Treaty

quote.text: Here I am, O Allah, here I am, at Your service.
quote.who: The Muslims, entering Makkah for the 'Umrah

body: He had sent Al-Harith bin 'Umair Al-Azdi with a letter to the ruler of Busra. On the way Shurahbil bin 'Amr Al-Ghassani, governor of Al-Balqa' for Caesar, had him bound and beheaded. To kill an envoy was to declare war. He raised three thousand men, the largest army the Muslims had yet sent out but for the Trench, and gave a white banner to Zaid bin Harithah: if Zaid fell, Ja'far bin Abi Talib; if Ja'far fell, 'Abdullah bin Rawahah. At the place of Al-Harith's murder they were first to call the people to Islam.

Madinah came out to see them off. 'Abdullah bin Rawahah wept: not for love of this world, he said, but for the ayah he had heard the Prophet ﷺ recite, that every one of us will come to the Fire [19:71]. He told them to fight in Allah's name; not to steal from the spoils; not to kill women, children, old men or hermits; and not to cut down trees or pull down houses. The Prophet ﷺ walked with them as far as Ath-Thaniyah, and prayed for them.

At Ma'an, on the edge of Syria, they learned that Heraclius had come with a hundred thousand men, and a hundred thousand more of the Arab tribes who served Rome. They had never imagined such an army. For two nights they talked of writing to the Prophet ﷺ for help or orders. Then 'Abdullah bin Rawahah stood up.
sections.title: Mu'tah

quote.text: By Allah, what you are shrinking from is the very thing you came out to seek: martyrdom. We do not fight by number or strength, but by this religion Allah has honoured us with. Go on: it is one of two good things, victory or martyrdom.
quote.who: 'Abdullah bin Rawahah, at Ma'an

body: They met the enemy near Masharif and drew back to Mu'tah to fight: three thousand against fifty times as many. Zaid bin Harithah, dearest of men to the Prophet's heart, led them in and fought until the spears brought him down. Ja'far took the banner. He jumped down from his horse and killed it, and fought until his right hand was cut off; he held the banner in his left, until that was cut off too; then he held it in his arms, until a Roman struck him and cut him in two. There were fifty wounds on him, and not one in his back. Allah gave him two wings in Paradise in place of his hands, to fly where he wishes there, and he is called Ja'far of the Two Wings.

'Abdullah bin Rawahah took the banner, urged himself on in verse, and fought until he was killed. Thabit bin Al-Arqam lifted it and called on the Muslims to choose a leader, and they chose Khalid bin Al-Walid. Nine swords broke in Khalid's hand that day. He changed his ranks, right to left and rear to front, so that the Romans thought fresh men had come; and he drew the army back slowly, skirmishing, until the Romans, fearing a trap in the desert, stopped following. Only twelve Muslims were killed.

Al-Harith was not avenged, but no one had thought three thousand men could stand against two hundred thousand of the greatest power on earth, and come home. Banu Sulaim, Ashja', Ghatafan, Dhubyan, Fazarah and other tribes accepted Islam after it.
sections.title: Zaid, Ja'far and 'Abdullah

quote.text: He fought until his right hand was cut off, then his left; then he held the banner in his arms, until he was killed.
quote.who: of Ja'far bin Abi Talib, at Mu'tah

body: The Arab tribes on the Syrian border had stood with Rome; now Quda'ah were gathering. He sent 'Amr bin Al-'As, whose grandmother was of Bali, one of the tribes there, with three hundred Emigrants and Helpers and thirty horse, under a white flag and a black banner, to win over Bali, 'Udhrah and Balqain and strike at Quda'ah. 'Amr marched by night and hid by day. Finding the enemy many, he sent back for help, and two hundred came under Abu 'Ubaidah bin Al-Jarrah, Abu Bakr and 'Umar among them, told to work together and never to quarrel.

At noon Abu 'Ubaidah went to lead the prayer. 'Amr would not have it: he had come only to help; the command was 'Amr's. Abu 'Ubaidah gave way. They went deep into Quda'ah's land and scattered them, and sent a rider home with the news. In Sha'ban, Abu Qatadah with fifteen men was out fifteen days against Ghatafan at Khadrah, and came home victorious.
sections.title: Dhat As-Salasil

quote.text: You have come only to reinforce me; the command is mine.
quote.who: 'Amr bin Al-'As, to Abu 'Ubaidah; who let him lead

parts.title: Letters to Kings
parts.blurb: A silver seal and eight envoys to the kings of the world; the forts of Khaibar; the 'Umrah of the treaty; and three commanders falling one after another at Mu'tah.

body: Under the treaty of Al-Hudaibiyah every tribe could join either side, and Banu Bakr joined Quraish while Khuza'ah joined the Prophet ﷺ. The old blood between them had never cooled. In Sha'ban of the eighth year Banu Bakr fell on Khuza'ah by night at the water of Al-Watir, and Quraish helped them in the dark with men and weapons. Khuza'ah fled into the Sanctuary, and even there Nawfal, chief of Banu Bakr, followed and killed them, where blood was never shed.
It was a plain breach of the treaty. Quraish knew at once what they had done, and met in alarm, and sent Abu Sufyan himself to Madinah to renew it.
sections.title: The Treaty Broken

body: He went first to his daughter Umm Habibah, the Prophet's wife. As he went to sit on the Prophet's bedding she folded it away. Was the bed too good for him, he asked, or he too good for the bed? It was the bed of the Messenger of Allah, she said, and he was an idolater, unclean.

He went to the Prophet ﷺ, who gave him no word of assurance. He went to Abu Bakr, who would not speak for him, and to 'Umar, who refused him flatly, and at last to 'Ali, pleading humbly and hinting that he might be master of the Arabs if he helped; 'Ali too refused. He went home to Makkah with nothing, and reported his daughter's words, his friends' refusals, and the Prophet's silence.
sections.title: Abu Sufyan in Madinah

quote.text: It is the bed of the Messenger of Allah, and you are an idolater, unclean.
quote.who: Umm Habibah, to her father

body: Three days before the news came, he had told 'Aishah to make ready for a march. Abu Bakr found her at it and asked; she did not know where. Then 'Amr bin Salim Al-Khuza'i rode in with forty horsemen to ask for help, and Madinah learned of the breach; Budail came after him, and then Abu Sufyan. To keep the march hidden he sent Abu Qatadah with eight men towards Idam, as if that were the way.

Hatib bin Abi Balta'ah, one of the most trusted of his Companions, sent a woman to Makkah with a letter warning Quraish. The revelation told him, and he sent 'Ali, Al-Miqdad, Az-Zubair and Abu Marthad after her. They caught her, and after a long search found the letter hidden in her hair.

Why had he done it? He had no kin in Quraish, said Hatib, only friends; his family was in Makkah with no tribe to protect them, unlike the other Emigrants'. He had wanted Quraish to owe him a favour, for his children's sake; he had not left Islam. 'Umar asked leave to strike off the hypocrite's head.
sections.title: Hatib's Letter
sections.place: Madinah, and the road to Makkah

quote.text: He was at Badr. And what do you know, 'Umar? Perhaps Allah looked at the people of Badr and said, "Do as you will, for I have forgiven you."
quote.who: The Prophet ﷺ, pardoning Hatib

body: On the tenth of Ramadan he marched with ten thousand men, leaving Abu Ruhm Al-Ghifari over Madinah. At Al-Juhfah his uncle Al-'Abbas met him with his family, coming to join him. At Al-Abwa' they came on his cousins Abu Sufyan bin Al-Harith and 'Abdullah bin Abi Umaiyah, who had mocked and harmed the believers for years, and he would not receive them. 'Ali told Abu Sufyan to come to him as Yusuf's brothers came: by Allah, Allah has preferred you above us, and we were sinners [12:91]. He did, and the Prophet ﷺ answered with Yusuf's words: no blame on you today [12:92]. Abu Sufyan bin Al-Harith became a Muslim, and a good one.
