They had set out fasting. At Al-Kadid, between 'Usfan and Qudaid, he broke his fast and the army with him. They camped in the valley of Fatimah at Marr Az-Zahran, and that night he had every man light a fire: ten thousand fires, with 'Umar over the watch.
sections.title: Ten Thousand Fires

quote.text: No blame on you today; Allah will forgive you, and He is the most merciful of those who show mercy.
quote.who: The Prophet ﷺ, to his cousin Abu Sufyan bin Al-Harith

body: Abu Sufyan came out from Makkah to look, with Hakim bin Hizam and Budail bin Warqa'. Before they reached the camp they met Al-'Abbas, who told him how things stood: let him accept Islam and bring his people to surrender, or he would be killed. He brought Abu Sufyan in under his protection. The Muslims wanted to kill him on the spot, and only with difficulty did they reach the Prophet ﷺ, who told them to come back in the morning.

"Woe to you, Abu Sufyan, is it not time you bore witness that there is no god but Allah, and that I am His Messenger?" Abu Sufyan, praising his kindness and patience, bore witness. Al-'Abbas reminded him that Abu Sufyan loved to be honoured, and the Prophet ﷺ gave him a share in the amnesty he now proclaimed.
sections.title: Abu Sufyan Comes In

quote.text: Whoever enters Abu Sufyan's house is safe; whoever shuts himself in his own house is safe; and whoever enters the Sacred Mosque is safe.
quote.who: The Prophet ﷺ

body: In the morning he left Marr Az-Zahran, and told Al-'Abbas to hold Abu Sufyan at a place where he could see the whole army go by. Tribe after tribe passed under its banners, and he asked of each who they were, until at last came the Prophet ﷺ in his battalion of Emigrants and Helpers, clad in iron. "Who are these?" "Muhammad and his Companions." No one could stand against them, said Abu Sufyan: "By Allah, your brother's son's kingdom has grown mighty." "It is prophethood," said Al-'Abbas. "Yes, then," said Abu Sufyan.

Sa'd bin 'Ubadah carried the Helpers' banner. Passing Abu Sufyan he cried that today was the day of slaughter, the day the Sanctuary would not protect them, the day Quraish would be humbled. Abu Sufyan complained of it, and the Prophet ﷺ was angry, took the banner from Sa'd and gave it to his son Qais, or to Az-Zubair.

Al-'Abbas sent Abu Sufyan ahead to Makkah, and there he shouted to Quraish not to resist, and to take refuge in his house. His wife seized his moustache and cursed him for a coward. The people scattered into their houses and into the Sanctuary, but a band under 'Ikrimah bin Abi Jahl, Safwan bin Umaiyah and Suhail bin 'Amr gathered at Al-Khandamah, meaning to fight.
sections.title: The Army Passes By
sections.place: The road from Marr Az-Zahran to Makkah

quote.text: No, today is the day the Ka'bah will be honoured, and the day Allah will honour Quraish.
quote.who: The Prophet ﷺ, when Sa'd called it the day of slaughter

body: He sent the army in from every side. Khalid bin Al-Walid led the right, with Aslam, Sulaim, Ghifar, Muzainah and Juhainah, into the lower town; Az-Zubair the left, with the Prophet's banner, into the upper town; Abu 'Ubaidah the men on foot through a valley between. They were to fight no one who did not fight them, and to crush anyone who did.

Only Khalid's column met resistance. He broke through; twelve of the idolaters were killed and two of the Muslims. Az-Zubair planted the banner where the Mosque of the Conquest now stands, and waited. A tent was pitched for the Prophet ﷺ there, and when he came he prayed in thanks to Allah, who had given him so great a victory.
sections.title: Into Makkah

body: He did not rest, but went straight to the Ka'bah with the Emigrants and Helpers around him. Three hundred and sixty idols stood round the House. He struck them one by one with his bow, reciting that truth has come and falsehood has vanished, for falsehood is bound to vanish [17:81], and that falsehood can neither begin anything nor bring it back [34:49]. Then he went round the House on his camel; he was not in ihram that day.

He called for 'Uthman bin Talhah, keeper of its key, and took the key from him. Inside were pictures, among them Ibrahim and Isma'il casting divining arrows, and he condemned what Quraish had done and had every idol broken and every picture erased. He went in with Usamah and Bilal, prayed facing the wall opposite the door, and went round inside saying "Allahu akbar" and declaring Allah's oneness.
sections.title: "Truth Has Come"

quote.text: Truth has come, and falsehood has vanished; falsehood is bound to vanish.
quote.who: Al-Isra' 17:81

body: Then he stood on the step of the Ka'bah's door and looked down at Quraish crowding the Sanctuary below. There is no god but Allah alone, he said: He has kept His promise, helped His servant and alone defeated the parties. Every claim of privilege, of blood or of wealth, was beneath his feet, but the keeping of the House and the giving of water to pilgrims. The blood money for a man killed by a whip or a stick, even half by intent, was heavy: a hundred camels, forty of them in calf.

Allah had taken from them the pride of the Ignorance and its boasting of fathers: all people were from Adam, and Adam from dust. And he recited: We created you from a male and a female and made you nations and tribes that you might know one another; the noblest of you with Allah is the most mindful of Him [49:13].

"People of Quraish, what do you think I will do with you?" "Good: you are a noble brother, the son of a noble brother." He gave the key back to 'Uthman bin Talhah, and the water of the pilgrims to Al-'Abbas.
sections.title: "Go, You Are Free"

quote.text: I say to you what Yusuf said to his brothers: no blame on you today. Go, you are free.
quote.who: The Prophet ﷺ, to Quraish

body: When the time for prayer came, Bilal climbed onto the roof of the Ka'bah and gave the call. Abu Sufyan, 'Attab bin Asid and Al-Harith bin Hisham sat in the courtyard. 'Attab said Allah had honoured his father Asid by taking him before he heard this. The Prophet ﷺ came up and told them, by revelation, what they had said. Al-Harith and 'Attab were astounded: by Allah, no one had been with them to tell him. They bore witness that he was the Messenger of Allah.

That day he went into the house of his cousin Umm Hani', washed, and prayed the prayer of victory. She had given refuge to two Makkan relatives of hers, and he upheld it: whomever she had protected was protected.
sections.title: Bilal on the Ka'bah

quote.text: We bear witness that you are the Messenger of Allah; by Allah, no one was with us to tell you.
quote.who: Al-Harith bin Hisham and 'Attab bin Asid

body: Nine of the worst criminals were named whose blood was lawful even if found clinging to the curtains of the Ka'bah. Some of them were pardoned. Ibn Khatal was found holding the curtains, and killed. Miqyas bin Sababah, who had taken blood money for his brother, killed the Helper anyway and fled to Makkah an apostate, was killed, and so were Al-Huwairith and a singing girl. But every effort went into pardoning.
sections.title: The Pardons
list: who had driven his spear at the Prophet's daughter Zainab as she left Makkah, so that she died of it in the end; forgiven
chief of Quraish; forgiven, and later a Muslim
who had meant to kill the Prophet ﷺ as he went round the House; forgiven, and became a devoted believer

body: On the second day he stood and praised Allah, and declared Makkah sacred until the Day of Judgment. No blood was to be shed in it. If anyone claimed leave to fight there because the Messenger had fought, let him know that leave had been given to the Messenger alone, for an hour of one day. Its thorn trees were not to be cut nor its game disturbed, nor its lost things picked up except by one who would announce them. "Except the idhkhir grass," said Al-'Abbas, "for our smiths and our houses." "Except the idhkhir."

Men of Khuza'ah killed a man of Laith in revenge for the old days. He told them to stop the ways of the Ignorance: the family of anyone killed could take blood money or retribution. A man from Yemen, Abu Shah, asked to have it written for him. "Write it for Abu Shah."

Then he went up As-Safa and, facing the House, raised his hands in prayer. The Helpers round him whispered that now Allah had given him his own city, he would stay. He asked what they were saying, and they told him.
sections.title: The Sanctity of Makkah

quote.text: I lived with you, and I will die with you.
quote.who: The Prophet ﷺ, to the Helpers, at As-Safa

body: Makkah saw that its way now lay through Islam, and its people came to give their pledge: first the men, then the women, 'Umar beside him to take their words. Hind bint 'Utbah came veiled among the women, afraid he would know her. They pledged not to associate anything with Allah. Not to steal: Abu Sufyan was a mean man, Hind said. Abu Sufyan, standing by, said whatever she had taken was hers. The Prophet ﷺ laughed and knew her, and she asked his forgiveness for all that was past. Not to commit adultery, not to kill their children, not to bring forth slander. She swore she would not have come to pledge if she had any wish left to disobey him. At home she broke her idol: what a fool she had been about it.

He stayed nineteen days in Makkah teaching the people. He had Abu Usaid Al-Khuza'i renew the stones that mark the bounds of the Sanctuary, sent callers to every quarter, and had the idols round Makkah broken.
sections.title: The Women's Pledge

quote.text: Whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day should not leave an idol in his house without breaking it.
quote.who: The Prophet ﷺ, at Makkah

body: One by one the great idols of the Arabs fell.
sections.title: Al-'Uzza, Suwa' and Manat
sections.place: Nakhlah, the land of Hudhail, and Al-Mushallal
list: goddess of Quraish and Kinanah. Khalid bin Al-Walid went with thirty horsemen and pulled it down. Had he seen anything? No. Then it had not been destroyed, go back. The second time a black woman ran out, naked, with wild hair, and Khalid cut her in two. Now, the Prophet ﷺ said, it was done
the idol of Hudhail. Its keeper told 'Amr bin Al-'As he would not be able to destroy it; 'Amr was amazed at him, broke it and its treasure house, and found nothing; and the keeper became a Muslim
the idol the Aws and Khazraj once honoured. Sa'd bin Zaid Al-Ashhali went; a black woman with wild hair came out wailing and beating her breast, and he killed her and broke the idol

body: He sent Khalid bin Al-Walid with three hundred and fifty riders of the Emigrants, Helpers and Banu Sulaim to call Banu Jadhimah to Islam, and told him to go in peace. They could not find the words to say they had become Muslims, and in the confusion Khalid had his men kill some and take the rest captive. He meant to kill the captives too, but some of the Companions refused.

When the news came, the Prophet ﷺ raised his hands to the sky and said twice that he was free before Allah of what Khalid had done. He sent 'Ali, who looked into every loss and paid blood money for all of it, and gave what was left over to the tribe to ease their grief. When Khalid quarrelled over it with 'Abdur-Rahman bin 'Awf, the Prophet ﷺ was angry: let him leave his Companions alone, they were above such quarrels.
sections.title: "I Am Free of What Khalid Has Done"

quote.text: O Allah, I am free before You of what Khalid has done.
quote.who: The Prophet ﷺ, twice

body: The conquest of Makkah stunned Arabia, but the proud tribes of Hawazin and Thaqif would not bow. Nasr, Jusham, Sa'd bin Bakr and Banu Hilal rallied to Malik bin 'Awf An-Nasri, and he made them bring their wives, children and herds with them to Awtas, a valley in their land near Hunain, so that they would fight to the death for them.

Old Duraid bin As-Simmah, famous for his wisdom in war, asked which valley they were in. Awtas: good ground for horses, he said, neither rocky nor soft; but why did he hear camels groaning, donkeys braying, children crying and sheep bleating? Malik explained. "You are nothing but a shepherd," said Duraid. Can anything stop a beaten man from running? If you win, all that helps you is a man with his sword and spear; if you lose, you shame your people and lose your wealth. Send the families back to safety. Malik would not: let Hawazin obey him, or he would fall on his sword. Hawazin said they would obey.

His spies came back from the Muslim camp with their limbs trembling. They had seen men of distinction on piebald horses, they said, and could not help what had come over them. The Prophet ﷺ sent Abu Hadrad Al-Aslami to live among Hawazin and bring back word.
sections.title: Hawazin Gather
sections.place: Awtas, in the land of Hawazin

quote.text: This is a day I have not missed, and yet I will not be sorry to miss it.
quote.who: Duraid bin As-Simmah, at Awtas

body: Nineteen days after he entered Makkah he marched out with twelve thousand men: the ten thousand of the conquest, and two thousand more, most of them Makkans newly Muslim. He borrowed a hundred coats of mail from Safwan bin Umaiyah, and made 'Attab bin Asid governor of Makkah. That evening a rider came: he had climbed such and such a mountain and seen all Hawazin gathered with their camels, cattle and sheep. The Prophet ﷺ smiled: they would all be the Muslims' spoils tomorrow, if Allah willed. Anas bin Abi Marthad stood guard that night.

On the way they passed a great green lote tree called Dhat Anwat, where the Arabs hung their weapons and slaughtered beneath. Some of the new men asked him to make them a Dhat Anwat like theirs. And seeing how many they were, some said they would not be beaten today; it weighed on him to hear it.
sections.title: Twelve Thousand
sections.when: Shawwal 8 AH, nineteen days after he entered Makkah
sections.place: The road from Makkah to Hunain

quote.text: Allahu akbar! By Him in whose hand is my soul, you have said what the people of Musa said to him: make us a god as they have gods. You will follow the ways of those before you.
quote.who: The Prophet ﷺ, at Dhat Anwat

body: Malik bin 'Awf had gone into the valley by night and hidden his men in its ravines and narrow places, with orders to rain stones and arrows on the Muslims the moment they came in sight, and then charge together. Before dawn the Prophet ﷺ set out his ranks and banners, and in the half-dark the army began to go down into the valley, knowing nothing. As they were making camp the arrows came, and then Hawazin, and the Muslims turned and ran in confusion.

The rout was so complete that Abu Sufyan bin Harb, newly Muslim, said they would not stop running until they reached the sea, and Kaladah bin Al-Junaid said the magic had failed today. The Prophet ﷺ turned to the right and called, "Come, people! I am the Messenger of Allah; I am Muhammad, son of 'Abdullah." Only a few Emigrants and some of his kin stood by him. He urged his mule towards the enemy, calling out in verse, and his cousin Abu Sufyan bin Al-Harith held its rein and Al-'Abbas its stirrup, trying to hold it back. Then he dismounted and asked his Lord for help: "O Allah, send down Your help."
sections.title: Ambush in the Valley

quote.text: I am the Prophet, no lie; I am the son of 'Abdul-Muttalib.
quote.who: The Prophet ﷺ, at Hunain

body: He told Al-'Abbas, who had a great voice, to call them back, and Al-'Abbas called to the men of the pledge under the tree. When they heard him, he said, they turned back like cows to their calves, crying, "Here we are, here we are!" A man whose camel would not turn would throw his armour round his neck, jump down with his weapons and let it go, and run towards the voice. A hundred gathered round the Prophet ﷺ and fought; then the call went out to the Helpers, and last of all to Banu Al-Harith bin Al-Khazraj, and the army poured back into the valley as it had poured out.

Both sides held and fought hard. Watching, he said the fight was hot now. He took a handful of dust and threw it in their faces: "May your faces be disgraced." Their eyes filled with dust and they broke. Within hours Hawazin were routed; seventy of Thaqif alone were killed, and their camels, weapons and herds were taken. On the day of Hunain, Allah said, your numbers pleased you and availed you nothing, and the earth for all its width was narrow for you; then He sent down His calm on His Messenger and the believers, and hosts you did not see [9:25-26].
sections.title: "Men of the Tree!"

quote.text: Now the fight is hot.
quote.who: The Prophet ﷺ, watching Hunain

body: The beaten Hawazin fled, some to Ta'if, some to Nakhlah and Awtas. Abu 'Amir Al-Ash'ari followed those at Awtas and was killed there; riders following those at Nakhlah caught Duraid bin As-Simmah, and Rabi'ah bin Rafi' killed him. The spoils were gathered at Al-Ji'ranah under Mas'ud bin 'Amr Al-Ghifari.

Among the captives was a woman who said she was his foster sister: Ash-Shaima' bint Al-Harith, of Banu Sa'd. He knew her by a mark, spread his own cloak for her and seated her on it, and let her go home to her people.
sections.title: Awtas, and Ash-Shaima'

body: Most of Hawazin and Thaqif shut themselves up in Ta'if with Malik bin 'Awf. Khalid went ahead with a thousand men; the Prophet ﷺ followed through Nakhlah Al-Yamaniyah, Qarn Al-Manazil and Liyyah, where he had Malik's fort pulled down, and camped by Ta'if and laid siege to it, for between ten and twenty days.

Arrows came down from the walls like locusts. Many were wounded and twelve killed, and the camp moved back to the higher ground where the mosque of Ta'if stands today. He set up a catapult and battered a breach; some men crept to the wall under a wooden shelter to burn it, and the defenders poured red-hot iron on them, and shot them as they ran. He ordered their vines cut and burned; they begged him by Allah and their kinship to stop, and he stopped. His caller cried that whoever came down from the fort would be free, and twenty-three came. One let himself down from the wall on a pulley-wheel, so he called him Abu Bakrah, the man of the wheel; he gave each of them to a Muslim to look after.

The fort held, with a year's food inside. He asked Nawfal bin Mu'awiyah Ad-Daili, who said: a fox in its hole; wait and you will catch it, leave it and it will do you no harm. He told 'Umar to announce they would leave in the morning. The men protested: leave without taking it? "Then fight in the morning." They fought and were wounded. When he said again that they would leave tomorrow, they were glad, and he laughed. As they rode away he told them to say: returning, repenting, worshipping, and praising our Lord. Asked to curse Thaqif, he prayed for them instead.
sections.title: The Siege of Ta'if

quote.text: O Allah, guide Thaqif, and bring them to us.
quote.who: The Prophet ﷺ, asked to curse Thaqif

body: He waited ten nights at Al-Ji'ranah before dividing anything, hoping Hawazin would come repentant and take back what they had lost. No one came. Then he gave first, and most, to those new to Islam, to win their hearts: to Abu Sufyan a hundred camels and forty ounces of gold, and when he asked for his son Yazid, the same, and for Mu'awiyah, the same again; to Hakim bin Hizam a hundred, and when he asked, a hundred more; to Safwan bin Umaiyah a hundred, and another, and another; to Al-Harith bin Kildah a hundred; to other chiefs of Quraish and the tribes, a hundred, fifty, forty.

Word ran that Muhammad gave like a man who did not fear poverty, and the Bedouin crowded him so that he was pressed against a tree and they pulled his cloak from his shoulders. Give him back his cloak, he said: had he as many camels as the trees of Tihamah, he would divide them all among them; they had not found him mean, nor a coward, nor a liar. He took a hair from his camel's hump between two fingers. By Allah, he had nothing of their spoils, not even this, but his fifth, and that fifth went back to them. Then Zaid bin Thabit counted out the rest: four camels and forty sheep to each man on foot, twelve camels and a hundred and twenty sheep to each horseman.
sections.title: The Gifts at Al-Ji'ranah

quote.text: If I had as many camels as the trees of Tihamah, I would divide them among you. You have not found me mean, nor a coward, nor a liar.
quote.who: The Prophet ﷺ, at Al-Ji'ranah

body: The Helpers had stood with him at Hunain when others ran, and now they watched those who had run go away with full hands, while they had nothing. Some of them grumbled that he had found his own people again. Sa'd bin 'Ubadah told him. "And you, Sa'd?" "I am one of my people." "Gather them for me."

He came to them and praised Allah. Had he not come to them astray, and Allah guided them; poor, and Allah enriched them; enemies, and Allah joined their hearts? "Allah and His Messenger are more generous and more gracious." Why did they not answer him? He answered for them: they could have said, and said truly, that he came to them rejected and they believed him, deserted and they helped him, a fugitive and they sheltered him, destitute and they comforted him. Did they resent a little of this world, with which he had won people to Islam, when he had left them to their Islam?

"Are you not content, Helpers, that the people go home with sheep and camels, while you go home with the Messenger of Allah? By Him in whose hand is my soul, but for the Hijrah I would be one of the Helpers. If the people took one valley and the Helpers another, I would take the valley of the Helpers. O Allah, have mercy on the Helpers, and their sons, and their sons' sons." They wept until their beards were wet. "We are content with the Messenger of Allah as our portion."
sections.title: "You Go Home with the Messenger of Allah"

quote.text: Are you not content that the people go home with sheep and camels, while you go home with the Messenger of Allah?
quote.who: The Prophet ﷺ, to the Helpers

body: When it was all divided, fourteen men of Hawazin came as Muslims, led by Zuhair bin Surad, his foster uncle among them, and spoke so movingly that he was touched. "You see who is with me. The best speech to me is the truest. Which is dearer to you: your wealth, or your women and children?" Nothing, they said, was equal to kin. After the noon prayer, he told them, stand and ask the Messenger to intercede with the believers, and the believers with the Messenger, for your captives.

They did. Whatever was his and Banu 'Abdul-Muttalib's, he said, was theirs. "And ours is the Messenger's," said the Emigrants and the Helpers. Al-Aqra' bin Habis refused for Banu Tamim, 'Uyainah bin Hisn for Fazarah, and Al-'Abbas bin Mirdas for Banu Sulaim, whose men said, "No, ours is the Messenger's," and he cried that they had undermined him. He told them that anyone who would not give up a captive freely would have six for each from the next spoils, and everyone gave theirs up, 'Uyainah last of all with an old woman he had held on to. He gave each captive a garment.
Then he put on ihram at Al-Ji'ranah and went to Makkah for 'Umrah, left 'Attab bin Asid as its governor, and came home to Madinah in the last six nights of Dhul-Qa'dah, in the eighth year.
sections.title: Hawazin Come as Muslims

quote.text: Which is dearer to you: your wealth, or your women and children?
quote.who: The Prophet ﷺ, to the delegation of Hawazin

parts.title: The Conquest
parts.blurb: A broken treaty, ten thousand fires at Marr Az-Zahran, the idols thrown down, "go, you are free"; then the ambush at Hunain, the siege of Ta'if and the Helpers' tears.

body: Ka'b bin Zuhair, of a family of poets and among the finest poets of the Arabs, had mocked the Prophet ﷺ in verse. After Ta'if his brother Bujair wrote to him: the Prophet ﷺ had put to death some in Makkah who had mocked and harmed him, and the poets who were left had scattered for their lives; if he valued his skin, let him come to him, for he never killed a man who came repenting. They wrote back and forth until the earth felt narrow to Ka'b.

He came to Madinah and stayed with a man of Juhainah, prayed Fajr with him, and went and sat by the Prophet ﷺ, who did not know his face, and put his hand in his. "Messenger of Allah, if Ka'b bin Zuhair came to you repenting, as a Muslim, would you grant him safety if I brought him?" "Yes." "I am Ka'b bin Zuhair." A Helper jumped up to ask leave to cut off his head. "Leave him: he has come repenting, and put the past away."

Then Ka'b recited the poem that begins with Su'ad, praising the Prophet ﷺ and asking his pardon. He praised the Emigrants in it, and spoke ill of the Helpers for the man who had wanted his head; later he made it up to them in another poem.
sections.title: Ka'b bin Zuhair

quote.text: Leave him alone; he has come repenting, and has put away the past.
quote.who: The Prophet ﷺ, of Ka'b bin Zuhair

body: He reached Madinah at the very end of the eighth year, and as soon as the new moon of Muharram rose he sent men out to the tribes to collect the zakah and teach the faith. Some went at once; others were sent later, as their tribes came into Islam. Small columns went out too, to make the roads of Arabia safe: 'Uyainah bin Hisn against Banu Tamim, who were urging others not to pay; Qutbah bin 'Amir against Khath'am at Tabalah, where he was killed; Ad-Dahhak bin Sufyan to Banu Kilab; and 'Alqamah bin Mujazziz across the sea from Jeddah to an island where Abyssinian pirates who robbed the Makkan caravans had gathered, and who fled.
sections.title: To Every Tribe
list: Az-Zibriqan bin Badr and Qais bin 'Asim

body: 'Uyainah bin Hisn rode against Banu Tamim with fifty horsemen, none of them Emigrants or Helpers, marching by night and hiding by day, and fell on them in the desert. They fled, and he brought back eleven men, twenty-one women and thirty boys, who were lodged in the house of Ramlah bint Al-Harith.

Ten of their chiefs came to Madinah and shouted at the Prophet's door: "Muhammad, come out to us!" He came out and talked with them, then left them to pray Dhuhr, and afterwards sat in the courtyard of the mosque. They had come to boast. Their orator 'Utarid bin Hajib spoke, and the Prophet ﷺ had Thabit bin Qais bin Shammas answer him. Their poet Az-Zibriqan bin Badr recited, and Hassan bin Thabit answered him on the spot.

When it was over, Al-Aqra' bin Habis said it all: their orator was better than ours, their poet more gifted, their voices finer. They accepted Islam, and he treated them generously and gave back their women and children.
sections.title: Orators and Poets

quote.text: Their orator is more eloquent than ours, their poet more gifted than ours, and their voices finer than ours.
quote.who: Al-Aqra' bin Habis, of the Muslims

body: He sent 'Ali with a hundred and fifty men, a black flag and a white banner, to pull down Al-Fuls, the idol of Tai'. At dawn they fell on the clan of Hatim, broke the idol and took captives and herds. 'Adi bin Hatim had fled; his sister was taken. In Madinah she begged the Prophet ﷺ to be kind to her: her brother was gone and her father dead, and she was old and could do no work. Who was her brother? 'Adi bin Hatim. "The man who ran from Allah and His Messenger?" and he walked on. The next day she asked again, and the third day he granted it, and gave her a mount, and she went to Syria to find 'Adi. Go to him, she told her brother, willing or afraid: he had done a kindness her father would never have done.

'Adi came without protection or letter, and the Prophet ﷺ took him into his house. "What made you run? Did you run from saying there is no god but Allah? Do you know any god but Allah?" No. "Were you not a Rakusi, and did you not take a quarter of your people's spoils?" Yes. "That is not lawful in your own religion." Then 'Adi knew he was a prophet, who knew what was hidden, and he became a Muslim.

Once a man came complaining of poverty, and another of robbers on the roads. "'Adi, if you live long, you will see a woman ride alone from Al-Hirah to circle the Ka'bah, fearing no one but Allah; you will see the treasures of Kisra opened; and you will see a man hold out a handful of gold or silver, and find no one to take it." In his old age 'Adi said he had seen the woman ride from Al-Hirah, and he had been among those who opened Kisra's treasures.
sections.title: 'Adi bin Hatim
sections.place: The land of Tai', and Madinah

quote.text: You will see a woman travel alone from Al-Hirah to circle the Ka'bah, fearing no one but Allah.
quote.who: The Prophet ﷺ, to 'Adi bin Hatim

body: Mu'tah had shown the Arab tribes of the north that they need not live under Caesar, and Caesar saw the danger on his borders. He resolved to crush the Muslims before they grew stronger, and gathered the Romans and the Ghassanid Arabs.

Madinah was uneasy. That year, when the Prophet ﷺ had sworn to keep away from his wives for a month, 'Umar's Helper neighbour came hammering at his door at night. "Have the Ghassanids come?" asked 'Umar. "Worse: the Messenger of Allah has divorced his wives." The hypocrites waited for the Muslims to fall. They built a mosque of their own, Masjid Ad-Dirar, the Mosque of Harm, and asked him to come and pray in it; he was setting out, and said on his return. Revelation told him what it really was, and when he came back he had it pulled down.

Nabataean traders bringing oil from Syria said Heraclius had gathered more than forty thousand men, with Lakhm, Judham and other tribes, and that his vanguard had reached Al-Balqa'. It was a year of drought and searing heat, and the road was long. But if he waited, Rome might come into the land of Islam, or to Madinah itself, the dying ways of the Ignorance would stir again, and the hypocrites would strike from behind. So, against his habit of hiding where he was going, he told the Muslims plainly: they were going to fight Rome.
sections.title: Rome Gathers

quote.text: Have the Ghassanids come?
quote.who: 'Umar, woken at night; so much did Madinah fear Rome that year

body: Ayahs of Surat Bara'ah came down urging them on, and he urged them to give. The tribes poured into Madinah, and no one stayed home but the hypocrites, and three true believers. Poor men came begging for a mount, and when he had none to give them they went away with their eyes overflowing, grieving that they had nothing to spend [9:92]. Women gave their musk, their bracelets, anklets, earrings and rings. And the hypocrites mocked those who gave much as show-offs, and those who gave little as if Allah needed it [9:79].
sections.title: The Army of Hardship
list: two hundred saddled camels and two hundred ounces of gold, then a hundred camels more and a thousand dinars put before the Prophet ﷺ, who turned the coins over and said nothing 'Uthman did after that day could harm him; nine hundred camels and a hundred horses in all, besides money
everything he had, leaving his family Allah and His Messenger
Al-'Abbas, Talhah, Sa'd bin 'Ubadah, Muhammad bin Maslamah
a handful of dates, all he had

body: He left Muhammad bin Maslamah over Madinah, or Siba' bin 'Urfutah, and 'Ali to look after his family. The hypocrites said he had left 'Ali behind because he thought little of him, and 'Ali took his weapons and caught up with him on the road.

He set out on a Thursday with thirty thousand men, the greatest army the Muslims had ever put in the field. For all that had been given, it was ill-supplied: eighteen men took turns on one camel, and men ate the leaves of trees until their lips swelled, or slaughtered the camels they loved. It was called the Army of Hardship.
sections.title: As Harun Was to Musa
sections.when: A Thursday in Rajab 9 AH · October 630 CE

quote.text: Are you not content to be to me as Harun was to Musa? Only, there is no prophet after me.
quote.who: The Prophet ﷺ, sending 'Ali back to Madinah

body: On the way they passed Al-Hijr, where Thamud had carved their houses from the rock. The men drew water from its wells; he forbade them to drink it or make wudu' with it, told them to feed the dough they had kneaded with it to their camels, and to draw instead from the well where the she-camel of Salih used to drink. Do not enter the dwellings of those who wronged themselves, he said, unless you enter weeping, lest what befell them befall you; and he hurried his camel through the valley.

When they ran short of water he prayed, and a cloud came and rained until all had drunk. Near Tabuk he told them they would reach its spring tomorrow, not before the day was up, and no one was to touch its water until he came. Two men got there first; the spring was a thin trickle. He took a little of it in his hands, washed his face and hands, and poured it back, and the water gushed out for them all. "Mu'adh, if you live long, you will see this place filled with gardens." A wind would blow that night, he warned; let no one stand, and let every man tie his camel. One man stood, and the wind carried him off to the mountains of Tai'. All the way he joined Dhuhr with 'Asr and Maghrib with 'Isha'.
sections.title: The Valley of Thamud
sections.when: On the road to Tabuk, 9 AH
sections.place: Al-Hijr, and the spring of Tabuk

quote.text: Do not enter the dwellings of those who wronged themselves unless you enter weeping, lest what befell them befall you.
quote.who: The Prophet ﷺ, at Al-Hijr

body: At Tabuk he spoke to the army, of the good of this world and the next, warning and giving hope, and lifted hearts worn down by hunger and thirst. But no army came. Hearing that the Muslims were marching, the Romans and their allies lost their nerve and melted back into their own lands. It gained the Muslims more than any battle could have.

Yuhannah bin Ru'bah, lord of Ailah, came to make peace and pay the jizyah, and so did the people of Jarba' and Adhruh. He gave each a writ of protection: in Allah's name, the protection of Allah and of Muhammad, the Messenger of Allah, for the people of Ailah, their ships and caravans by land and sea; none to be kept from any spring they were used to, nor any road they wished to travel.

He sent Khalid bin Al-Walid with four hundred and fifty horsemen to Ukaidir, lord of Dumat al-Jandal: "You will find him hunting wild cattle." It was a moonlit night, and as Khalid came in sight of his castle, wild cattle came and rubbed their horns against its gate, and Ukaidir came out to hunt them. Khalid took him from among his men and brought him to the Prophet ﷺ, who spared him and made peace on tribute. The tribes that had leaned on Rome turned towards the Muslims; the land of Islam now touched Rome's border.
sections.title: Twenty Days at Tabuk
facts: two thousand camels, eight hundred head of cattle, four hundred coats of mail, four hundred spears

quote.text: You will find him hunting wild cattle.
quote.who: The Prophet ﷺ, sending Khalid to Ukaidir

body: On the way home, going up a mountain pass, he was alone with 'Ammar, who held his camel's rein, and Hudhaifah bin Al-Yaman, who drove it; the army had gone on down into the valley. Twelve hypocrites, their faces covered, came up behind to kill him. He sent Hudhaifah back, and Hudhaifah struck at their camels' faces with his staff; Allah cast fear into them, and they fled to rejoin the army. He told Hudhaifah their names and what they had meant, and so Hudhaifah was called the keeper of the secret. They planned what they could not carry out [9:74].

As Madinah came in sight he said, "Here is a cheering sight," and of the mountain, "This is Uhud: a mountain that loves us, and we love it." The women, boys and children came out of the town singing: the full moon has risen over us from the hills of Al-Wada'; thanks are due from us, so long as anyone calls to Allah. It was the last march he led himself.
sections.title: Twelve Masked Men
sections.when: Ramadan 9 AH, on the way home

quote.text: This is Uhud, a mountain that loves us, and we love it.
quote.who: The Prophet ﷺ, coming home from Tabuk

body: Tabuk was a sifting. Whenever he was told someone had dropped behind on the march, he said, "Let him be: if there is good in him, Allah will bring him to you; if not, Allah has spared you of him."

Home again, he prayed two rak'ahs in the mosque and sat to receive people. More than eighty hypocrites came with excuses and oaths. He took them at their word, asked forgiveness for them, and left their hearts to Allah. Three believers had stayed behind with no excuse: Ka'b bin Malik, Murarah bin Ar-Rabi' and Hilal bin Umaiyah. They would not lie, and told him the truth. He told the Muslims not to speak to them until Allah judged them.

No one spoke to them. The earth for all its width grew narrow for them, and their own souls grew narrow. After forty days they were told to keep away from their wives. On the fiftieth day forgiveness came down [9:118]: the happiest day of their lives. And of those kept back by true need, weakness or illness, there was no blame [9:91]; as they neared Madinah he had said that some men there had been with them in every valley they crossed and every road they walked, held back only by their excuse.
sections.title: The Three Who Stayed Behind

quote.text: There are men in Madinah who were with you in every valley you crossed and on every road you travelled; only their excuse held them back.
quote.who: The Prophet ﷺ, returning from Tabuk

body: After Tabuk everyone knew that only Islam would last in Arabia. The Arabs and hypocrites who had hoped Rome would save them gave up hope, and the hypocrites were no longer handled gently: the Muslims were told to take none of their alms, not to pray over their dead or ask forgiveness for them, nor stand at their graves. Masjid Ad-Dirar was pulled down, and much of Surat Bara'ah came down about the march, the hypocrites and those who stayed behind.
sections.title: The End of Leniency
list: The li'an of 'Uwaimir Al-'Ajlani and his wife
each swore against the other before him, as the ayahs had laid down
who confessed to adultery, and was stoned only after she had weaned her child
died; he prayed for him from afar
died, and he grieved deeply; had he a third daughter, he told 'Uthman, he would have married her to him too
died; the Prophet ﷺ prayed over him, though 'Umar tried to stop him; then an ayah came agreeing with 'Umar

body: After Ta'if, 'Urwah bin Mas'ud Ath-Thaqafi had come to Madinah and become a Muslim. He was sure his people would follow him, for they loved him more than their own firstborn. When he called them to Islam they shot him from every side and killed him. Months later, unable to stand against the Muslim tribes around them, they sent 'Abd Yalil bin 'Amr, who would go only with five others, among them 'Uthman bin Abil-'As, the youngest.

A tent was pitched for them in a corner of the mosque, so that they could hear the Qur'an and watch the Muslims pray. They asked for a treaty that would let them keep fornication, wine and usury, keep Al-Lat, and be spared the prayer. He refused every one. They asked only not to have to break Al-Lat with their own hands, and that he granted. Each noon, while the others slept, young 'Uthman bin Abil-'As went to the Prophet ﷺ to learn the Qur'an, or to Abu Bakr if he was sleeping, and he made 'Uthman their chief. Years later, when Thaqif were about to apostatise, 'Uthman told them: you were the last to accept Islam, do not be the first to leave it.

At home the envoys pretended at first that war was coming, until their people's pride broke and they were ready to accept; then they told the truth. Khalid went with men to destroy Al-Lat. Al-Mughirah bin Shu'bah swore he would make them laugh at Thaqif: he struck it with his axe and fell down as if struck dead, and Thaqif cried that the goddess had killed him. He leapt up: Al-Lat was nothing but stones and dirt. They broke it to the ground, dug out its foundations, and carried off its jewels and robes.
sections.title: Thaqif and Al-Lat

quote.text: You were the last to accept Islam: do not be the first to leave it.
quote.who: 'Uthman bin Abil-'As, to Thaqif

body: He sent Abu Bakr to lead the Muslims in the Hajj. After he had gone, the opening of Surat Bara'ah came down, declaring Allah and His Messenger free of obligation to the idolaters who had not kept faith with their treaties. The Arabs' custom was to proclaim such things openly, so he sent 'Ali after Abu Bakr to proclaim it. Abu Bakr met him at Al-'Arj or Dajnan: "Have you come as commander, or with a message?" "With a message."

They made the Hajj together, and on the day of sacrifice 'Ali stood at the Jamrah and read it out to the crowds: the treaties with the idolaters were ended, and they had four months to decide; those who had kept their treaty and helped no one against the Muslims would have it kept to the end of its term. And Abu Bakr sent men to cry through Mina what would end the Ignorance for good.
sections.title: Abu Bakr Leads the Hajj

quote.text: After this year no idolater shall make the Hajj, and no one shall go round the House naked.
quote.who: The cry through Mina, Hajj of 9 AH

body: Najran, a land of seventy-three villages towards Yemen, could field a hundred thousand fighting men. Sixty of them came to Madinah, twenty-four of their nobility, and three who ruled them: the 'Aqib, 'Abdul-Masih, who governed; the Sayyid, Al-Aiham or Shurahbil, who saw to their affairs; and the bishop, Abu Harithah bin 'Alqamah. They talked with him, and when he called them to Islam and recited the Qur'an to them, they refused.

What did he say of 'Isa? He waited a day for the answer, and it came: the likeness of 'Isa with Allah is as the likeness of Adam, whom He created from dust; and whoever argues, let both sides bring their sons and women and selves, and pray that Allah's curse fall on whoever lies [3:59-61]. He gave them a day to think. When they still refused, he came out wrapping Al-Hasan and Al-Husain in his cloak, with Fatimah walking behind him, ready for the mutual curse.

The 'Aqib and the Sayyid took counsel: if he was a prophet and they cursed each other, neither they nor their children would ever prosper. They would not do it, and accepted his terms: two thousand garments a year, a thousand in Rajab and a thousand in Safar, with an ounce with each, and in return the covenant of Allah and His Messenger and freedom in their religion. They asked for a trustworthy man to collect it, and he sent Abu 'Ubaidah bin Al-Jarrah, the trustworthy one of this nation. In time Islam spread in Najran.
sections.title: The Christians of Najran

quote.text: The likeness of 'Isa with Allah is as the likeness of Adam: He created him from dust, then said to him, "Be," and he was.
quote.who: Al 'Imran 3:59

body: More than seventy delegations came, most of them after the conquest of Makkah, many after Tabuk, and the last, of Nakh', two hundred men, in the middle of Muharram of the eleventh year. Madinah had become the capital of all Arabia.
sections.title: The Year of Delegations
list: came twice; to their chief he said, "You have two qualities Allah loves: far-sightedness and tolerance"
At-Tufail bin 'Amr, who had once asked him to curse them and heard him pray for their guidance instead, brought seventy or eighty families of them to him at Khaibar
Rome's governor of the Arabs about Ma'an; won over by Mu'tah, he sent a white mule and word of his Islam, and Rome crucified him at 'Afra' in Palestine
fifteen came and pledged; a hundred of them were at the Farewell Hajj
twelve men, who told him they were the kin who had helped Qusai take Makkah; he gave them good news of the conquest of Syria
asked about hospitality: it is a charity, and its due is three days; a stray sheep is yours, your brother's or the wolf's; leave a stray camel alone until its owner finds it
brought the zakah left over after giving to their own poor; their boy asked only for forgiveness and a contented heart, and was the most content of men ever after
with Zaid Al-Khail, whom the Prophet ﷺ renamed Zaid Al-Khair: "Every man the Arabs praised to me fell short of it, but Zaid; they did not say the half of him"
accepted Islam when 'Ali came to them, and he fell in prostration at the news: "Peace on Hamdan, peace on Hamdan"
came complaining of drought, and he prayed for rain from the pulpit
sent word that they had become Muslims, and he sent Mu'adh bin Jabal and others to them

body: With the delegation of Banu Hanifah came Musailimah, proud and wanting rule: if Muhammad made him his successor, he would follow him. The Prophet ﷺ went to him with a palm stalk in his hand and Thabit bin Qais beside him. "If you asked me for this stalk, I would not give it to you." He had dreamed that two gold bracelets were put on his hands, and they troubled him, and he was told to blow on them, and they flew away: two liars who would come after him. Musailimah was one of them.

Back in Al-Yamamah, Musailimah claimed to be a prophet, made rhymes, allowed wine and adultery, and wrote that the land should be halved between him and Quraish. The answer: the earth is Allah's, He gives it to whom He wills of His servants [7:128]. To his two envoys, who said Musailimah was the messenger of Allah, he said that if envoys could be killed, he would have killed them. Musailimah was killed at Al-Yamamah under Abu Bakr, by Wahshi, who had killed Hamzah. The other liar, Al-Aswad Al-'Ansi in Yemen, was killed by Fairuz a day and a night before the Prophet ﷺ died, and he told his Companions of it.

Banu 'Amir bin Sa'sa'ah sent 'Amir bin At-Tufail, the betrayer of Ma'unah, and Arbad bin Qais, who plotted to kill him: 'Amir kept him talking while Arbad drew his sword. Allah froze Arbad's hand on the hilt. On the way home a thunderbolt struck Arbad and his camel, and 'Amir died of a swelling like a camel's, in the house of a woman of Banu Salul.
sections.title: The Two Liars

quote.text: If you asked me for this palm stalk, I would not give it to you.
quote.who: The Prophet ﷺ, to Musailimah

body: None of his battles was lost through a fault of his plan, his ground or his choice of men. At Uhud the loss came from an order disobeyed, at Hunain from weakness in some of the ranks; and in both he stood his ground and turned the day. The commanders he trained went on to beat Persia and Rome. His wars brought security, made homes and work for the Emigrants, and armed the army, without a grain of injustice. They were not raids for plunder and captives, but a struggle to free the weak from oppression. And he bound them by rules.
sections.title: A Look at His Battles
list: Fight in the name of Allah, for His sake, those who disbelieve in Him; do not steal from the spoils, do not betray, do not mutilate, and do not kill a child
Make things easy, not hard; calm people, do not punish them
If he came upon an enemy by night, he did not attack until morning
No burning with fire; no killing of women or children
Plunder is as unlawful as carrion
Do not finish off the wounded, or chase the fleeing, or kill the captive; an envoy is never killed
Whoever kills one under a covenant will not smell the fragrance of Paradise

body: 'Amr bin Salamah remembered how his people lived by a water on the road, asking every traveller what this man was saying, until he knew the Qur'an by heart from their answers. The Arabs held back from Islam until the conquest: leave him to his own people, they said; if he beats them, he is a true prophet. When Makkah fell they hurried in, his own father first. He came back from the Prophet ﷺ with what to tell them: pray such a prayer at such a time; when the time comes, let one of you give the call, and let the one who knows most of the Qur'an lead you.

Ten thousand marched on Makkah; thirty thousand to Tabuk, less than a year later; and a hundred thousand or more stood with him at the Farewell Hajj, their "Here I am, O Allah" rolling to the horizon.
sections.title: People in Crowds

quote.text: When the time of prayer comes, let one of you give the call, and let the one who knows most of the Qur'an lead you.
quote.who: The Prophet ﷺ, as 'Amr bin Salamah's father brought it home

body: For more than twenty years he had stood up as he was told, to warn, and carried every burden of it: the struggle in men's hearts against the Ignorance, and the battles against those who would kill the faith before it took root. He fought it all by day and stood before his Lord by night.

Now the call had prevailed over all Arabia. The idols were not only abandoned but broken by the hands that once worshipped them. "There is no god but Allah" rang out five times a day across the desert, and reciters of the Qur'an went north and south. Scattered tribes became one people, the worshippers of created things worshippers of Allah alone, all of them His servants, brothers under His law.
sections.title: The Call Fulfilled

quote.text: No Arab is better than a non-Arab, nor a non-Arab than an Arab, nor a red man than a black, except in piety. All are the children of Adam, and Adam was made of dust.
quote.who: The Prophet ﷺ

parts.title: Tabuk and the Delegations
parts.blurb: The Army of Hardship marches against Rome and finds no one to fight; three men are shunned for fifty days; and all Arabia comes to Madinah.

body: The call was complete and a new society stood on "there is no god but Allah." Something in him told him his time in the world was ending. When he sent Mu'adh bin Jabal to Yemen in the tenth year, he told him he might not see him again; he might pass by this mosque, and his grave. Mu'adh wept.
That Ramadan he spent twenty days in i'tikaf in the mosque, where he used to spend ten, and Jibreel went through the Qur'an with him twice, where he used to go through it once.
sections.title: "You May Not See Me After This Year"

quote.text: Mu'adh, you may not meet me after this year; perhaps you will pass by this mosque of mine, and my grave.
quote.who: The Prophet ﷺ

body: He let it be known he would make the Hajj, and people poured into Madinah from everywhere to make it with him. On a Saturday, with four days of Dhul-Qa'dah left, he combed his hair, put on perfume and his garments, saddled his camel, and set out after noon. He reached Dhul-Hulaifah before 'Asr, prayed two rak'ahs and spent the night. In the morning he told them that one had come to him in the night from his Lord, and said: pray in this blessed valley, and say, 'Umrah together with Hajj.

He bathed for ihram, and 'Aishah perfumed his head and body with her own hands, with dharirah and a perfume with musk in it; its traces could be seen in his hair and beard. He put on his ihram, prayed Dhuhr as two rak'ahs, declared his Hajj joined with 'Umrah, and cried, "Labbaik, Allahumma, labbaik," and again on his camel, and again on the open plain. He spent the night at Dhu Tuwa, and on Sunday morning, the fourth of Dhul-Hijjah, entered Makkah: eight days on the road. He went round the Ka'bah and between As-Safa and Al-Marwah, and stayed in ihram, for he had brought his sacrificial animals. He camped above the town at Al-Hajun.

Those who had no animals with them he told to make it an 'Umrah and leave ihram. They hesitated, and he said that had he known then what he knew now, he would not have brought his animals, and would have left ihram himself. Then they did it.
sections.title: The Farewell Pilgrimage
sections.when: End of Dhul-Qa'dah – 4 Dhul-Hijjah 10 AH · 632 CE

quote.text: Here I am, O Allah, here I am, at Your service.
quote.who: The Prophet ﷺ, setting out for the Farewell Hajj

body: On the eighth day he went to Mina and prayed there five prayers, and after sunrise on the ninth rode to 'Arafah, where a tent had been pitched for him at Namirah. When the sun passed its height he had Al-Qaswa' saddled, and went down into the valley. A hundred and twenty-four thousand people, or a hundred and forty-four thousand, were gathered round him, and he spoke to them, Rabi'ah bin Umaiyah bin Khalaf calling out his words after him so all could hear.

"O people, listen to me, for I do not know whether I will meet you in this place after this year." At the end he asked them what they would say when they were asked about him. "We bear witness that you have conveyed the message and fulfilled your mission." He raised his forefinger to the sky and pointed it down at the people: "O Allah, bear witness. O Allah, bear witness. O Allah, bear witness."
sections.title: At 'Arafah
sections.place: Namirah and the valley below it, at 'Arafah
list: Your blood, your wealth and your honour are as sacred to each other as this day, in this month, in this land
Everything of the Ignorance is under my feet; its blood feuds are void, the first I void being the blood of Ibn Rabi'ah bin Al-Harith
Its usury is void, the first I void being that owed to my uncle Al-'Abbas
you took them on Allah's trust; they owe you faithfulness, and you owe them food and clothing in fairness
I have left among you something which, if you hold fast to it, you will never go astray

There is no prophet after me and no nation after you; worship your Lord, pray your five prayers, fast your month, give your zakah gladly, make the Hajj to your Lord's House and obey those set over you, and you will enter your Lord's Paradise

body: When he finished speaking, the ayah came down: This day I have perfected your religion for you, completed My favour upon you, and chosen Islam for you as your religion [5:3]. 'Umar wept. Why? "After perfection there is nothing but decline."

Bilal called the iqamah, and he prayed Dhuhr, and then at once 'Asr. He rode to the place of standing, faced the qiblah and stood until the sun had set and its yellow faded. With Usamah up behind him he went on to Muzdalifah, prayed Maghrib and 'Isha' with one call and two iqamahs, and lay down until dawn. After Fajr he rode to Al-Mash'ar Al-Haram and stood facing the qiblah, praising Allah until it was full light, then went on to Mina before sunrise, Al-Fadl bin Al-'Abbas behind him now, hurrying through the valley of Muhassir.
sections.title: "This Day I Have Perfected Your Religion"

body: He threw seven small pebbles at the great Jamrah, saying "Allahu akbar" with each. At the place of sacrifice he slaughtered sixty-three camels with his own hand and gave 'Ali the rest to slaughter, a hundred in all; a piece of each was cooked in one pot, and they ate of it and drank its broth. Then he rode to the House for the tawaf, prayed Dhuhr in Makkah, and came to his family, Banu 'Abdul-Muttalib, drawing water at Zamzam.
sections.title: The Jamrah and the Sacrifice

quote.text: Draw, Banu 'Abdul-Muttalib. Were it not that people would crowd you out of your right after me, I would draw with you.
quote.who: The Prophet ﷺ, at Zamzam

body: Late in the morning of the Day of Sacrifice he spoke again, from a grey mule, 'Ali calling out his words. Time had come round to the shape it had on the day Allah created the heavens and the earth: twelve months, four of them sacred. What month was this? Allah and His Messenger knew best; he was silent so long they thought he would rename it. "Is it not Dhul-Hijjah?" What land? "Is it not the Sacred Land?" What day? "Is it not the Day of Sacrifice?" Then your blood, wealth and honour are as sacred to each other as this day, in this month, in this land. You will meet your Lord and He will ask you about your deeds; so do not go astray after me, killing one another. "Have I conveyed?" "Yes." "O Allah, bear witness."

A wrongdoer wrongs only himself; no man is to be blamed for what his father or his son did. Satan had despaired of ever being worshipped in this land, but he would be obeyed in things they thought small, and that would please him.

He spent the days of Tashriq at Mina, teaching. Surat An-Nasr came down in them, and he spoke again on the middle day. On the thirteenth he left Mina for the hillside of Banu Kinanah at Al-Abtah, prayed the four prayers there, slept a little, then rode to the Ka'bah for the farewell tawaf, and set out for Madinah: not to rest, but to go on striving.
sections.title: The Day of Sacrifice

quote.text: Let those who are here tell those who are not; perhaps the one told will understand it better than the one who heard it.
quote.who: The Prophet ﷺ, at Mina

body: Rome would not let the Muslims be: it had even put to death its own governor at Ma'an, Farwah bin 'Amr, for becoming a Muslim. In Safar of the eleventh year he raised a great army and gave it to Usamah, son of Zaid bin Harithah, to ride into the borderlands of Al-Balqa' and Ad-Darum in Palestine, to make Rome afraid and give heart to the Arabs on its borders.

People talked: Usamah was too young to command. He answered them, and men came to join Usamah in great numbers. The army marched out and camped at Al-Jurf, three miles from Madinah. Then came the worrying news of his illness, and it waited, to see what Allah would decree. It was the first army Abu Bakr sent as caliph.
sections.title: Usamah's Army

quote.text: If you question his command, you questioned his father's before him. By Allah, his father was fit to command and was among the dearest of people to me; and this son of his is among the dearest of people to me after him.
quote.who: The Prophet ﷺ, of Usamah

body: Surat An-Nasr had told him that his time was near. Early in Safar he went to Uhud and prayed over its martyrs, as if bidding farewell to the living and the dead. Then he climbed the pulpit: he was going ahead of them, and would be a witness over them; by Allah, they would soon meet him at the Pool; he had been given the keys of the treasures of the earth; he did not fear that they would go back to worshipping others after him, but that they would compete for this world.
One midnight he went out to Al-Baqi' and asked forgiveness for the dead there. Trials were coming, he told them, like pieces of a dark night, each following the other, each worse than the last.
sections.title: Farewells

quote.text: Peace be upon you, people of the graves. The morning you wake to is easier than the one the living wake to. We will be joining you.
quote.who: The Prophet ﷺ, at Al-Baqi'

body: On Monday the twenty-ninth of Safar he went to a funeral at Al-Baqi'. On the way back his head began to ache, and the fever rose so high that its heat could be felt through the cloth on his head. He was ill thirteen or fourteen days, and led the prayers for eleven of them.

As the illness grew heavy, he would ask his wives, "Where am I tomorrow? Where am I tomorrow?" They understood, and gave him leave to stay where he wished. He went to 'Aishah's room leaning on Al-Fadl bin Al-'Abbas and 'Ali, his head bound, his feet dragging on the ground, and spent his last week there. 'Aishah would recite the two surahs of refuge and the prayers he had taught, blow into her hands, and pass them over him for their blessing.
sections.title: The Illness

quote.text: Where am I tomorrow? Where am I tomorrow?
quote.who: The Prophet ﷺ, in his last illness

body: On Wednesday the fever burned and he fainted from the pain. "Pour seven skins of water over me, so I can go out to the people." They sat him in a tub and poured until he said, "Enough, enough." Then he went into the mosque with his head bound, sat on the pulpit and spoke. Allah's curse was on the Jews and Christians who made their prophets' graves places of worship; they were not to make his grave an idol to be worshipped. If he had ever struck a man's back, here was his back; if he had ever wronged a man's honour, here was his honour. After Dhuhr he spoke again. A man said he owed him three dirhams. "Pay him, Fadl."

He told them to be good to the Helpers: they were his family, and with them he had found shelter; they had done what was on them, and what was owed them remained; acknowledge the good they had done and pass over their faults. Then he said that Allah had given a servant of His the choice between whatever he wished of this world and what is with Him, and the servant had chosen what is with Him. Abu Bakr wept: "Our fathers and mothers be your ransom!" People wondered at the old man, until they understood that the servant was the Prophet ﷺ himself, and that Abu Bakr was the most knowing of them.
sections.title: Five Days Before
sections.when: Wednesday, five days before his death

quote.text: No one has done more for me with his company and his wealth than Abu Bakr. If I were to take a bosom friend other than my Lord, I would take Abu Bakr; but his is the brotherhood of Islam. Let every door into the mosque be shut, but Abu Bakr's.
quote.who: The Prophet ﷺ

body: On Thursday, in great pain, he said, "Come, let me write something for you after which you will never go astray." 'Umar said that the Prophet ﷺ was in great pain, and they had the Qur'an: the Book of Allah was enough for them. Others wanted it written, and they argued, until he told them to leave him.

He led every prayer until that Thursday's Maghrib, in which he recited Surat Al-Mursalat. At 'Isha' he asked if the people had prayed. "No; they are waiting for you." He asked for water, washed, tried to rise, and fainted. When he came to, he asked again, and again, three times. Then he sent word for Abu Bakr to lead them. 'Aishah begged him three or four times to excuse her soft-hearted father; "You are like the women of Yusuf's story," he said. "Tell Abu Bakr to lead the people." Abu Bakr led seventeen prayers in his lifetime.
sections.title: Four Days Before
sections.when: Thursday, four days before his death
list: drive the Jews, the Christians and the idolaters out of Arabia; honour delegations as he used to honour them
the narrator forgot it; perhaps holding to the Book and the Sunnah, or sending Usamah's army, or the prayer and their slaves

body: On Saturday or Sunday he felt a little better, and came out for Dhuhr leaning on two men. Abu Bakr, leading, began to step back; he signed to him to stay, and had himself seated at his left, and led the prayer, Abu Bakr repeating his "Allahu akbar" so the people could hear.

On Sunday he freed his slaves, gave away the seven dinars he had in charity, and gave his weapons to the Muslims. That night 'Aishah had to borrow oil from a neighbour for her lamp. His coat of mail lay in pawn with a Jew for thirty measures of barley.

At Fajr on Monday, as Abu Bakr led the prayer, they saw the curtain of 'Aishah's room lift. He looked at them standing in their rows, and smiled with joy. Abu Bakr stepped back to the row, thinking he was coming out. The Muslims were so glad they were almost distracted from their prayer. He signed to them to finish it, went back in, and let the curtain fall.
sections.title: A Smile Through the Curtain
sections.when: Saturday or Sunday, and Monday dawn, 12 Rabi' al-Awwal 11 AH

quote.text: He looked at them in their rows at prayer, and smiled.
quote.who: Anas bin Malik, of the last dawn

body: That morning he called Fatimah and whispered to her, and she wept; then whispered again, and she laughed. After his death 'Aishah asked her why. The first time, she said, he had told her he would not recover from this illness, and she wept; then that she would be the first of his family to follow him, and she laughed. He told her too that she would be the lady of the women of the world.

Seeing his pain, Fatimah cried out at how much her father suffered. "There will be no more pain for your father after today." He asked for Al-Hasan and Al-Husain and kissed them, and told those around him to care for them, and called his wives and counselled them. The pain grew so sharp that he told 'Aishah he still felt the food he had tasted at Khaibar. Again and again he told them to keep the prayer, and to be good to their slaves.
sections.title: Fatimah Wept, then Laughed

quote.text: There will be no more pain for your father after today.
quote.who: The Prophet ﷺ, to Fatimah

body: 'Aishah held him against her. Of Allah's favours to her, she said, was that he died in her house, between her chest and her throat, and that Allah mixed her saliva with his at the end. Her brother 'Abdur-Rahman came in with a siwak in his hand, and she saw him looking at it, and knew he wanted it. She took it for him and softened it, and he cleaned his teeth with it as well as he could.

There was a bowl of water by him. He dipped his hand in it and wiped his face: "There is no god but Allah. Death has its agonies." Then he raised his hand, or his finger, and looked up, and his lips moved. She listened, and heard him say: with those You have blessed, the prophets, the truthful, the martyrs and the righteous; O Allah, forgive me and have mercy on me, and join me to the Highest Companion. Three times he said it, the Highest Companion. Then his hand fell.
It was late in the morning of Monday the twelfth of Rabi' al-Awwal, in the eleventh year. He was sixty-three years and four days old.
sections.title: The Highest Companion
sections.when: Late morning, Monday 12 Rabi' al-Awwal 11 AH · June 632 CE

quote.text: O Allah, the Highest Companion.
quote.who: The last words of the Prophet ﷺ

body: The news ran through Madinah, and darkness fell on it. "I never saw a day better or brighter than the day he came to us," Anas said, "and I never saw a day uglier or darker than the day he died." Fatimah cried: O my father, who answered his Lord's call; O my father, whose home is the Garden of Paradise; O my father, to Jibreel we announce your death.

'Umar stood up before the people, beside himself. Some hypocrites, he said, were claiming the Messenger of Allah had died. He had not died; he had gone to his Lord as Musa did, and would come back, and cut off the hands and feet of those who said he was dead.

Abu Bakr rode in from his house at As-Sunh, spoke to no one, went straight into 'Aishah's room, uncovered the face beneath its Yemeni cloth, bent and kissed him, and wept. "My father and mother be your ransom. Allah will not make you taste death twice; the death written for you, you have tasted." He went out. "Sit down, 'Umar." 'Umar would not, and the people left him and turned to Abu Bakr. Then he recited the ayah, and it was as if they had never heard it before; everyone was reciting it. 'Umar said that when he heard it his legs gave way and he fell to the ground, and knew that the Prophet ﷺ was dead.
sections.title: The Darkest Day

quote.text: Whoever worshipped Muhammad, Muhammad is dead. Whoever worships Allah, Allah is Ever-Living and never dies. "Muhammad is no more than a messenger; messengers have passed away before him. If he dies or is killed, will you turn back on your heels?"
quote.who: Abu Bakr, reciting Al 'Imran 3:144

body: Even before he was washed, the Helpers and Emigrants argued over who should lead them, in the roofed hall of Banu Sa'idah, all through Monday into the night, until they gave their pledge to Abu Bakr. All that while his body lay on his bed under a cloth, the door locked.

On Tuesday he was washed in his clothes, three times, with water and lote leaves, from Ghars, the well of Sa'd bin Khaithamah at Quba' that he used to drink from, and shrouded in three white cotton sheets from Yemen, with no shirt and no turban. There was some disagreement over where to bury him, until Abu Bakr said he had heard him say that a prophet is buried where he dies. So Abu Talhah lifted the bed on which he had died and dug the grave beneath it, a lahd with a niche in its side.

They came into the room ten at a time and prayed over him, each alone, with no imam: first his own clan, then the Emigrants, then the Helpers, then the women, and last the children. It went on through Tuesday and long into the night. "We did not know he was being buried," 'Aishah said, "until we heard the sound of digging, in the depth of the night before Wednesday."
sections.title: Buried Where He Died
sections.when: Tuesday – the night before Wednesday, 11 AH
list: Al-'Abbas, 'Ali, Al-Fadl and Qutham, sons of Al-'Abbas, Shuqran his freed slave, Usamah bin Zaid, and Aws bin Khawli
Al-'Abbas, Al-Fadl and Qutham turned him; Usamah and Shuqran poured; 'Ali washed; Aws held him against his chest

parts.title: The Farewell
parts.blurb: The Farewell Pilgrimage and its sermon, a religion perfected, and the last days in 'Aishah's room, until he chose the Highest Companion.

body: In Makkah his household was he and Khadijah bint Khuwailid. He married her at twenty-five, when she was forty; she was his first wife, and while she lived his only one. She bore him sons and daughters. None of the sons lived long.

His daughters were Zainab, married before the Hijrah to her maternal cousin Abul-'As bin Ar-Rabi'; Ruqaiyah and then, after her death, Umm Kulthum, married to 'Uthman bin 'Affan; and Fatimah, married to 'Ali bin Abi Talib between Badr and Uhud, the mother of Al-Hasan, Al-Husain, Zainab and Umm Kulthum. His son Ibrahim, born to Mariyah the Copt, died an infant in Madinah.
sections.title: His Household

body: He was permitted more than four wives, for various reasons. In all he married thirteen women. Eleven he lived with; two of these, Khadijah and Zainab bint Khuzaimah, died before him, and nine survived him. Two marriages, one to a woman of Banu Kilab and one to Al-Jauniyah of Kindah, were never completed.
sections.title: The Mothers of the Believers
people: his first, and his only wife while she lived
10th year of prophethood, days after Khadijah's death
married in Makkah; came to his house seven months after the Hijrah
3 AH, widow of Khunais bin Hudhafah
4 AH; the mother of the poor; died within months
Shawwal 4 AH, widow of Abu Salamah
Muharram 7 AH, by proxy in Abyssinia
not a wife but a bondwoman; mother of Ibrahim

body: He spent his young manhood, nearly thirty years of it, married to one wife older than himself, Khadijah, and then to Sawdah. His later marriages were not the marriages of desire. By marrying 'Aishah and Hafsah he bound himself to Abu Bakr and 'Umar, as by giving Fatimah to 'Ali and Ruqaiyah and Umm Kulthum to 'Uthman he bound himself to them: the four whose sacrifice for Islam is known to all.

Among the Arabs, kinship by marriage was a bond no one would shame by fighting it. Umm Salamah was of Makhzum, the clan of Abu Jahl and Khalid bin Al-Walid; after he married Umm Habibah, her father Abu Sufyan never again met him with hostility; when he married Juwairiyah, the Companions freed a hundred of her people. And he had a whole people to teach, women as well as men, and his wives, trained by him, carried what they learned of his life to everyone; 'Aishah above all.

His marriage to Zainab bint Jahsh was commanded to end a deep-rooted custom of the Ignorance: an adopted son counted as a true son, in marriage, divorce and inheritance. He hesitated, fearing what the hypocrites would say, and was rebuked for it [33:37]. So the custom was broken by his own act: call them by their fathers' names [33:5]; Muhammad is not the father of any of your men, but the Messenger of Allah and the Seal of the Prophets [33:40].
sections.title: Why So Many

quote.text: When Zaid had ended his marriage to her, We married her to you, so that the believers should have no difficulty concerning the wives of their adopted sons.
quote.who: Al-Ahzab 33:37

body: His home was hard to live in. As far as Anas knew, he never tasted a thin flattened loaf in his life, nor saw a roasted goat with his own eyes. "Two months would pass," said 'Aishah, "and we would see three new moons, and no fire was lit in the houses of the Messenger of Allah." What did they live on? "The two black things: dates and water."

Of all his wives, only once did any complain in a way that called for a ruling. The ayahs gave them their choice: if they wanted this world and its glitter, he would provide for them and release them kindly; if they wanted Allah, His Messenger and the Home of the Hereafter, a great reward awaited them [33:28-29]. Not one chose the world. And when small jealousies arose among them, as among any wives, and Allah disapproved [66:1-5], they stopped.
sections.title: Dates and Water

quote.text: The two black things: dates and water.
quote.who: 'Aishah, asked what the Prophet's household lived on

body: No one was ever so loved. Those who knew him would have given their lives to save a fingernail of his from harm. Those who saw him described him so.
sections.title: As His Companions Saw Him
list: neither very tall nor very short; his hair neither tightly curled nor straight; his face somewhat round; his eyes black and large, with long lashes; when he walked he lifted his feet as if going down a slope; when he turned, he turned his whole body. Whoever saw him suddenly stood in awe of him; whoever came to know him loved him
of medium height, broad-shouldered, his hair to his earlobes; I never saw anyone more handsome. Was his face bright as a sword? "No; like the moon"
I looked at him on a moonlit night in a red garment, and at the moon, and to me he was more beautiful than the moon
I never saw anything more beautiful; it was as if the sun moved across his face; and no one walked faster: we wore ourselves out, and he was at ease
when he was happy his face shone like a piece of the moon
I never touched silk softer than his palm, nor smelled musk or amber sweeter than his scent; at his death there were about twenty grey hairs in his head and beard
any road he had taken, those who came after knew by its fragrance that he had passed that way
between his shoulders, towards the left, the size of a pigeon's egg

body: He spoke the purest Arabic, and every tribe's dialect with its own people. Patience and forgiveness came to him most when he had the power to punish; the more he was harmed, the gentler he grew. Given a choice between two things, said 'Aishah, he always chose the easier, unless it was a sin, and then he was furthest of all from it; he never took revenge for himself, only when Allah's sanctity was violated, and then for Allah. He was the last to anger and the first to be pleased.

He gave like a man who did not fear poverty; in Ramadan, when Jibreel came, he was more generous than the free wind, and no one ever asked him for anything and heard "no". When the fighting was fiercest, 'Ali said, they sheltered behind him, and he was always nearest the enemy. One night Madinah woke to a noise and the men ran out towards it, and met him coming back, alone, on Abu Talhah's unsaddled horse, his sword round his neck: there was nothing to fear.

He was shyer than a girl kept in her chamber. Even before prophethood they called him Al-Amin, and Abu Jahl himself said, "We do not call you a liar; we only deny what you bring" [6:33]. He forbade people to stand for him as men stood for kings; he visited the sick and the poor, accepted a slave's invitation, mended his own sandals and his own clothes, and milked his own sheep. On a journey, when one man offered to slaughter the sheep, another to skin it and another to cook it, he said he would gather the wood; they could do it for him, he knew, but he did not want to be set above them.
sections.title: An Exalted Standard of Character

quote.text: And you are surely on an exalted standard of character.
quote.who: Al-Qalam 68:4

body: Hind bin Abi Halah described him: always thoughtful, never at rest; silent for long, speaking only when there was need, and then clearly, with full meaning and no excess. He made much of every blessing, however small; if he did not like a food, he neither praised it nor found fault with it. He never grew angry for himself; only for Allah's sanctity and His religion. His laughter was mostly a smile.

He sat wherever there was room at the edge of the gathering, and told others to do the same. He gave each person there his share of his attention, so that each thought no one was more honoured by him. Whoever came to ask his advice spoke first and spoke last, and he listened patiently until the man had finished; and he never sent anyone away without what he asked for, or a gentle word. His gathering was one of kindness, modesty, patience and honesty: no voices raised, nothing sacred made light of; the old respected, the young treated with mercy, the stranger cared for.

He kept himself from three things: hypocrisy, excess, and what did not concern him; and he spared people three: he did not run them down, did not shame them, and did not seek out their faults. He spoke only where he hoped for reward. When he spoke, those around him bowed their heads as if birds sat on them, and only spoke when he was silent.
sections.title: His Gatherings

quote.text: O Allah, send blessings upon Muhammad and the family of Muhammad, as You sent blessings upon Ibrahim and the family of Ibrahim; You are Worthy of all praise, Most Glorious.
quote.who: The prayer upon him, with which the book ends

parts.title: His Household, His Character
parts.span: As those who knew him remembered
parts.blurb: His wives and children, the home of dates and water, and the man as his Companions described him, on an exalted standard of character.

body: Ibrahim came from Ur, near Kufah in Iraq, and went on to Harran and then Palestine, which he made the base of his call. By Allah's command he left his wife Hajar and their infant Isma'il in the barren valley of Makkah, beside the Sacred House, where the spring of Zamzam burst forth for them.

He came back to visit them several times. In a dream he was shown himself sacrificing his son, and Allah ransomed Isma'il with a great sacrifice. On a later visit father and son raised the walls of the Ka'bah, and Ibrahim called mankind to make pilgrimage to it. The Arabs kept his religion, the worship of Allah alone, for ages, until the idols came.
people.name: Ibrahim
people.role: Prophet, the Friend of Allah; father of Isma'il and of the Arabized Arabs

body: Brought as an infant to the valley of Makkah with his mother, Isma'il grew up among the tribe of Jurhum, who came to live by Zamzam. He learned Arabic from them and married among them. With his father he built the Ka'bah.

He had twelve sons, though in time only the lines of Nabet and Qidar could be traced. From Qidar came 'Adnan, and from 'Adnan, after many generations, Quraish and the Prophet ﷺ. Isma'il kept the House and ruled Makkah all his life.
people.name: Isma'il
people.role: Prophet, son of Ibrahim and Hajar; forefather of the 'Adnani Arabs

body: Hajar was given to Sarah by the Pharaoh of Egypt, and Sarah gave her to Ibrahim as a wife. She bore him Isma'il. By Allah's command, Ibrahim left her and her baby in the empty valley by the Sacred House with a bag of dates and a skin of water. When these were gone, the spring of Zamzam gushed out for them. The book notes the view of Qadi Sulaiman Mansurpuri that she was not a slave but a daughter of Pharaoh.
people.name: Hajar
people.role: Mother of Isma'il

body: Qusai grew up on the borders of Syria and came back to Makkah as a young man. He married the daughter of Hulail, chief of Khuza'ah. After Hulail's death, he took Makkah and the House with Quraish and Kinanah behind him. From about 440 CE, Quraish held them without rival.

He built Dar An-Nadwah, the House of Assembly, beside the Ka'bah, and held every honour of the city: the assembly, the standard, the caravans, the keys of the Ka'bah, and the water and food of the pilgrims. He passed them to his son 'Abd Manaf.
people.name: Qusai bin Kilab
people.role: The chief who won Makkah and the Ka'bah for Quraish

body: A chief of Khuza'ah, loved by his people for his piety and generosity. In Syria he saw people worshipping idols and took it for a good thing. He brought back the idol Hubal, set it up inside the Ka'bah, and called people to worship it. Most of the rites of idol worship among the Arabs are traced back to him, and the Prophet ﷺ is reported to have said that these practices were first invented by him.
people.name: 'Amr bin Luhai
